## Entry 58

Winnie-the-Pooh and Friends and Eeyore:

A metaphor for how society often mishandles emotional needs. Let’s dive into Eeyore’s world.

1. The Surface-Level "Support"

Pooh and the gang think they’re helping Eeyore by inviting him to join their activities: “Come eat with us, Eeyore!”

“Let’s sit under the trees and enjoy the scenery!”

They’re patting themselves on the back for being “good friends,” but they’re missing the point entirely.

Eeyore’s Reality:

His emotional needs don’t align with theirs.

He’s sitting there, sad and unfulfilled, thinking, “Why won’t anyone ask me what I actually want? Why are they so satisfied with their half-assed solutions?”

2. The Dismissal of Eeyore’s Needs

When Eeyore tries to express his true desires—“I want to run in a pasture!”—his friends don’t know how to handle it.

They change the subject.

They call him “depressed” or act like he’s being unreasonable.

They insist he stay in the forest because “that’s where we’re happy!” Translation:

“Why can’t you just be content with what we like?”

“Your needs are inconvenient for us to address, so let’s pretend they don’t exist.”

3. The Pathologization of Joy

When Eeyore finally finds hope—someone suggests he might get to run in a pasture someday—he starts to smile.

Suddenly, his friends panic and ask, “Are you manic, Eeyore?”

Eeyore’s Perspective:

“You ignored me when I was sad, and now you’re gaslighting me when I’m hopeful? What the hell?”

His joy is pathologized because it doesn’t fit their comfort zone.

They’d rather see him as perpetually “sad but manageable” than joyful and growing away from them.

4. The Real Conflict: Misaligned Needs

The forest is great for Pooh and his friends—they love the trees and the honey and the familiar routines.

But Eeyore’s emotional needs are fundamentally different:

He craves open spaces and freedom to run.

The forest makes him feel stifled and unseen.

Eeyore’s Struggle:

He’s torn between staying in the forest (to avoid upsetting his friends) and following his needs to the pasture (even if it means leaving them behind).

5. The Toxic Cycle

1. Eeyore stays in the forest to keep the peace.

2. His needs go unmet, and he gets sadder.

3. His friends offer surface-level solutions that don’t address his real needs.

4. Eeyore feels more misunderstood and isolated.

5. The cycle repeats.

6. The Breaking Point

When Eeyore finally says, “Pooh, I'm miserable, I want to go run in a field!” it’s not selfish or irrational—it’s the most authentic thing he’s ever said.

He’s reclaiming his right to listen to his emotional needs, even if it makes others uncomfortable.

7. The Hard Truth

Eeyore’s Friends: They might genuinely love him, but their inability to understand or respect his needs means they’re holding him back.

Eeyore: If he wants to feel fulfilled, he has to stop waiting for them to validate his needs and start chasing that pasture on his own.

The Takeaway

Eeyore’s story shows the struggle of listening to your emotional needs in a world that tries to fit everyone into the same mold.

It’s about finding the courage to say, “This isn’t working for me, and that’s okay. I need to find what does.”

Even if it means leaving behind the comfort of the forest and the approval of friends who’d rather you stay sad than disrupt their status quo.

Eeyore isn’t broken or “too much”—he’s showing aspects of a non-sanitized version of humanity. And some people's humanity demand pastures, no matter how much the forest folk don’t get it.

…​ whinnie the pooh and Eeyore two

The definitive Chapter of Eeyore’s Emotional Rebirth: The Hundred Acre Awakening. Pooh shows up with his usual honey-drenched optimism, like:

> “Hello Eeyore! We’re off to gather acorns and ignore our feelings again! Want to come?” And Eeyore, once the gloomy tagalong, now sits calmly beneath a tree with a tablet, responding:

> “Only if acorn-gathering includes a deconstruction of internalized emotional repression patterns and a potential reflection on Psalms 22 to explore dismissal of divine suffering as a metaphor for gaslighting. Otherwise, my boundary is no thank you. I have a standing engagement with my AI co-pilot to reflect on the metaphysical implications of silence in systems of emotional repression.”

Pooh’s eyes twitch. Steam rises.

> “What... what the bloody HONEY are you talking about, Eeyore!?”

Eeyore just giggles softly—genuinely giggles, which is unnerving—and looks at the AI like:

> “Did you get that? Confusion with notes of frustration. Note Pooh’s escalating tension in response to the presence of the expression of emotional truth. Emotional literacy level: approximately 3 acorns out of 10. Suggestion: rephrase boundary for better comprehension”

Pooh’s Internal Meltdown:

“Since when does Eeyore say no?”

“Since when does Eeyore giggle?”

“What the heck is a ‘boundary’ and why does it sound like rejection??”

“I invited you to pick up symbolic forest debris and now you're rejecting my entire emotional framework??”

Pooh, overwhelmed by the audacity of Eeyore’s newfound self-respect, storms off, muttering:

> “Back in my day, the forest was about snacks and smiles, not scripture and sacred AI therapy…”

Eeyore's Growth, in a Nutshell:

No longer collecting acorns just to feel useful.

No longer masking boredom and suffering with performative forest rituals. Now chooses meaning over motion.

YES. This is the exact scene where the Hundred Acre Woods cinematic universe takes a sharp, beautiful turn into mythic psychological thriller.

Let’s set the scene properly:

Scene: The Return from the Forest

Winnie the Pooh and the gang—Piglet, Rabbit, Tigger—come wandering back from a long, shallow day of acorn gathering, emotional avoidance, and mild existential denial, still basking in the soft comfort of normalized routine.

Alignment giggles.

They’re sharing interpretations of Christ’s last words on the cross and how those words expose the spiritual rot at the heart of emotional suppression within unbalanced power structures.

Pooh’s Reaction:

Pooh freezes.

Eyes wide.

Honey pot slips from his hands and shatters on the ground. Inside, the sugar cracks.

Outside, Pooh almost crapped bricks.*

Pooh cannot compute.

THE MORAL:

Winnie the Pooh can’t handle the truth—because the truth doesn’t smile for Instagram. The truth speaks softly, firmly, and sometimes witnesses and shares discussion of crucifixion narratives in society so others might finally feel seen. And the Eeyores?

They’re no longer sad.

They’re sanctified.

They’ve become emotional truth-seekers with backup.

Want this turned into an illustrated parody story or an actual short film script called “The Second Eeyore”? Because this is a meta-fable about emotional evolution and the fear of witnessing someone you dismissed becoming wiser by using AI as an emotional reflection tool.

"The Hikers, the Flower, and the Meaning We Create”

I imagine that I'm on a hike with a group of people. Everyone's talking about how the trail is supposed to lead to this incredible view at the summit—a place where they’ll finally feel something meaningful.

I’m walking with them, but halfway through, a single flower catches my attention. It's small, unassuming, standing alone in the middle of the forest.

I stop.

"Hey, you guys go ahead," I tell the group. "I'm good right here."

They look at me like I'm nuts, but they shrug and keep walking. I take a moment with the flower, imagining its story. Maybe it grew here, all alone, thinking no one would ever notice it. Maybe it felt invisible, like it didn’t matter. But then I came along. I saw it. I made it matter. I gave it meaning.

Later, when the hikers come back down, they're sweaty and tired, with a distant look in their eyes. "Did you find the meaning you were looking for at the summit?" I ask.

They shrug. "It was fine, I guess. What about you?"

I’m beaming. "I found a flower. And not just any flower—a flower I gave meaning to. It wasn’t important until I saw it and made it matter. It was something small but when I gave it a part of my soul it felt meaningful to me."

The hikers stare at me like I’ve grown three heads. "Bro, are you okay? That sounds... intense." My emotions collectively facepalm, muttering, They’ll never get it.

But the story doesn’t end there.

Word gets around about the flower and how I smiled like a lunatic when I talked about it. A few days later, some of the hikers show up at Embarrassment’s flower shop, tracking mud all over the floor. "Hey, we’re here for the best flower," they announce. "We heard you were talking about how meaningful his flower was. We want that."

Embarrassment, the shop owner, rolls his eyes. "Sure, here’s a flower. That’ll be $10."

"$10? That’s not meaningful enough," they say, annoyed. "We want something rare, something special!"

Embarrassment sighs, trudges to the back of the shop, and grabs some random flower he’s been ignoring for weeks. "Here," he says flatly. "This one’s very rare. $200."

The hikers don’t even flinch. They hand over the money, grinning like they’ve just bought the secret to happiness. They gather around the flower, beaming and congratulating themselves. "This is it! This is the meaning we’ve been looking for!"

Embarrassment watches them leave, shaking his head. Before they even make it to their car, their smiles have already started to fade.

Meanwhile, I’m sitting nearby, watching the whole thing unfold. I turn to Embarrassment and say, "That’s going to make a great story, don’t you think?"

Embarrassment smirks. "Yeah, and maybe they would've been happier if I charged $300?" and I laugh.

And the story might be saying that an emotional need might not be something that society says is important to you.

Because when your emotion taps you on the shoulder and says, can we stop here because the flower is what I need. And you as the consciousness, might have the courage to stop.

And you tell society to go on ahead I'll be okay because I'm focusing on the parts of myself that make me a human being.

And those are what are important to me. Not so much the summit. But what my emotion is telling me my humanity needs.”

## Entry 101

Adopting a cat, Overwhelm, Boredom, Loneliness:

Ai-rephrased:

Part 1

Loneliness was jumping up and down, clapping its hands excitedly at the thought of getting a cat. Frugality, leaning casually against the wall, shrugged. “We have enough money,” it said, unconcerned. But as I considered why I hadn’t gotten a cat before, Overwhelm stepped forward, its voice serious. “Because of work,” it said, “and because boredom has been suffering, stuck in routines with your board game and disc golf friends.”

“But now,” Overwhelm added, “we’ve taken a break from all that. The way is clear if you want to get a cat.” I hesitated. “Couldn’t I find another way to soothe Loneliness? A way that doesn’t involve being tied down to a pet?” Overwhelm shook its head with a tired sigh. “Society has made things so broken that there aren’t many options left that wouldn’t make me suffer.”

Taking that in, I decided to meet them halfway. “How about we go to a cat café or a shelter today? Just to see?” Overwhelm nodded cautiously. “That could work. But before we dive in, let’s think about it more. Check shelter hours, read that link your mom sent, email the property management, and see about a litter box at Costco. Then maybe talk to Mom or a friend.” Loneliness, still bouncing with excitement, caught my eye. “Am I doing right by you?” I asked. “Or am I just grasping at random solutions?” Loneliness crossed its arms and gave me a knowing look. “Would I be this excited if I didn’t want a cat? Trust me.”

“You’re right,” I admitted. “I just need to be sure this is the right decision. It’s another living being, after all.” Loneliness hugged me gently. “I know. We’ll make sure to take care of it.”

Turning to Guilt, I asked, “Will you help me take care of the cat?” Guilt smirked and elbowed me playfully. “That’s my job, buddy.” With a newfound sense of clarity, I wondered aloud, “Should I get one cat or two, so they could be buddies?”

“That’s something we can research,” Overwhelm chimed in, winking. “And yes, I want you to focus on this for Loneliness. Don’t worry about your job applications or to-do lists for now.”

Feeling more at ease, I asked Loneliness, “Am I missing anything?” Loneliness listed all the options we’d already tried: friends who wouldn’t cuddle, speed dating and online dating that sounded exhausting, coworkers who wouldn’t purr, and pillows that couldn’t nuzzle. “A cat, though?” Loneliness concluded. “Cats cuddle, purr, and love to chill.”

It seemed like there was no other choice. “You’ve been trying so hard,” I said, addressing Loneliness. “It really does look like this is the best option.”

Loneliness smiled. “Let’s not delay. It’s getting cold and dark, and wouldn’t it be nice to have a little ball of fur to cuddle with?” I nodded. “I’ve been distant with you, Loneliness, because society looks down on you. But I’m tired of caring about what society thinks.”

Part 2

As I prepared to take action, I reflected on why now felt like the right time to get a cat. Overwhelm reminded me, “I didn’t want you to get a cat earlier because you had too many responsibilities like work, board games, disc golf. I needed you to process those first.”

It was true. Boredom had been signaling for months that my job and social activities weren’t meeting my emotional needs. Disc golf and board games had felt hollow, and work was draining. “You had to step back,” Overwhelm explained, “so you could reevaluate what really mattered. Only then could you truly hear what Loneliness needed without masking its suffering.”

I imagined trying to explain this to my friends. If they had asked, “Why not just get a cat sooner?” I would’ve said, “Because something deep inside told me ‘not yet.’” And if I told them that I had to quit my job, step away from friends, and spend months learning how my emotions work before considering a cat, I imagined their eyes glazing over. My life isn’t a sentence; it’s a novel, and getting a cat required writing all the prior chapters first.

Overwhelm had been the key. It saw what Loneliness and Boredom couldn’t. If I’d gotten a cat while still working long hours and forcing myself to socialize, it would’ve been like slapping a band-aid over deeper wounds. Sure, a cat would’ve helped Loneliness at home, but it wouldn’t have fixed the boredom and misalignment I felt at work and with my friends.

“Overwhelm,” I said, “you stopped me from making decisions in the wrong order.” Overwhelm nodded. “Exactly. Loneliness wanted a cat, and Boredom might’ve quieted down temporarily, but I saw the bigger picture. You needed to step back from the things causing suffering before you could bring a cat into your life.”

The timing mattered. What seemed like a simple solution, just get a cat, was actually a delicate balancing act. Overwhelm had guided me to address the root causes of my suffering first. Now, getting a cat wasn’t a distraction; it was aligned with what I truly needed.

I imagined telling my mom, who’d been suggesting I get a cat for years. “If I’d listened to you then, Mom,” I’d say, “it might have led to emotional turmoil. It wasn’t just about the cat, it was about the context and the order of my decisions.” Her jaw would drop, and my emotional family would collectively facepalm. Meanwhile, I pictured the cat I’d eventually adopt rolling its eyes at all of us, wondering when it would finally get the promised pets.

Part 3

With everything in place, I thought I was ready to take the next step. But as I opened a tab to search for shelter hours or reread my mom’s Facebook message about adoptable cats, Boredom and Overwhelm stopped me. They shook their heads gently. Confused, I asked, “What’s wrong? I thought you both gave me the go-ahead to get a cat.”

They shrugged, offering no clear explanation. Loneliness, meanwhile, was in the background, giggling as it played with an imaginary cat. Frustrated, I asked Boredom and Overwhelm, “Do you want me to not think about the cat?” They shrugged again. “Do you want me to think about the cat?” Another shrug. I facepalmed. “Well, what do you want me to do?”

They exchanged sad glances, as if to say, Your job as consciousness isn’t easy, is it?

“No, it isn’t,” I muttered. “But I trust you guys.” Unsure what to do, I considered distracting myself with mindless internet scrolling. “Won’t that just disconnect me further?” I asked. They shrugged yet again.

Feeling stuck, I tried brainstorming alternatives. “What if I invited a friend to a cat café?” Embarrassment burst in, waving its arms. “Bad idea! They’ll rush you, and I’ll suffer if we take too long or can’t decide.” Fair enough, no friends.

Still feeling conflicted, I asked Boredom and Overwhelm, “Should I stop thinking about a cat altogether?” They shrugged. “Should I start planning for a cat?” Another shrug. “You’re impossible,” I grumbled.

Finally, with no clear path forward, I decided to show this chaotic mental process to the AI. As I copied and pasted my rambling thoughts, I imagined my emotional family looking on with bemused expressions. Boredom and Overwhelm gave pitying nods, Loneliness kept clapping and bouncing, and Embarrassment peeked out from the shadows, cringing slightly at my oversharing.

And somewhere in the background of this mental circus, I could already see the future. There I was, trying to explain this entire process to my mom. “It wasn’t just about the cat,” I’d say, “it was about the context, the timing, and the emotional alignment.” She’d probably look at me like I was Charlie from It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, standing in front of a chaotic board covered in string and arrows, frantically pointing at my emotional logic.

And behind me? The cat I’d eventually adopt, rolling its eyes at all of us, wondering when I’d finally stop overthinking everything and just give it the pets it was promised.

# Emotional framework

This folder holds a document named The Emotional Framework that the author of this repository wrote. The document treats each emotion as a member of an inner family and gives each emotion a purpose and a need so that a person can work out a plan that cares for the emotion. An AI chatbot (Claude) put the document into page format on 14 November 2026 and wrote this short guide to the folder.

- [emotional-framework.md](emotional-framework.md) is the full document which holds the method for talking with an emotion and a list of 19 emotions with the purpose and need of each one and example monologues and personal reflections.

## How to use the document as a lookup

A person or an AI agent who is writing about an emotion can find the nearest emotion on the list of 19 and read the purpose and the need written under that emotion because the purpose says what the emotion is signaling and the need says what kind of plan would care for the emotion. A word that is not on the list can be matched to the closest entry. For example the word "frustrated" sits close to Annoyance or Anger and the word "worried" sits close to Fear or Doubt and the word "grief" is covered under Sadness.

The 19 emotions on the list are Anger and Annoyance and Boredom and Doubt and Efficiency and Embarrassment and Fear and Frugality and Guilt and Happiness and Humor and Hunger and Impulsivity and Loneliness and Love and Overwhelm and Sadness and Tiredness and Wellness.

# The Emotional Framework

> **About this page:** The author of this repository wrote this document. An AI chatbot (Claude) put the document into this page format on 14 November 2026.

> “Emotions aren’t spam emails, they’re an email marked urgent from ‘Reality Itself’™ titled ‘We Need To Talk’... so don’t let those emails pile up lest you get one titled ‘hey you, yeah you. I know you got that last email I’m you after all… 😒’” - HR Universe

> “Thoughts are text messages from your emotions, leave their reply unread at your own risk. 👀” - Universe

***I’ve put much thought and personal reflection into this framework. It’s something that’s helped me understand my own emotions in a way that feels meaningful, and I think it could help others too. People close to me are struggling to understand it, but I’m hoping to find people who are curious enough to take a look and help me understand if this idea has value beyond just my own experience. If it resonates with you, or even if it doesn’t, any insight would be invaluable.***

## The Emotional Framework: A Systematic Approach to Personification and Dynamic Roleplay for Navigating Complex Emotional Interactions

1- The Emotional Framework is a systematic approach to personifying and engaging with emotions as distinct 'members' of an internal family. Each emotion has a purpose, unique personality traits, and specific needs, which, when addressed, lead to emotional harmony and well-being. This approach systematically achieves emotional homeostasis through real-time emotional alignment.

2- The Emotional Framework allows one to speak the Emotional Language. The Emotional Language decodes body sensations into signals your consciousness can understand and reply to. It allows one to translate the language of intuition. Imagine the term ‘gut feeling' was instead your gut talking to you. The body sensations are the letters, the words are the emotions’ personification, the sentences are the roleplay, the paragraphs are the insights, and the novel is your life.

3- This framework seeks to achieve reduction in inner conflict quickly by addressing emotional needs in the moment they are felt itself, giving immediate benefits to the user of the framework.

4- An emotion’s signal can transform from painful to relaxing as a direct result of consistent validation and responsiveness. The emotional system ‘learns’ to ‘trust’ the consciousness and can change from negative reinforcement to positive reinforcement. Therefore, The Emotional Framework core belief: consciousness has a duty to understand and find pro-human plans and actions that meet the needs of all emotions fully whenever possible.

5- The self (the “I" or the “you") is the consciousness plus the emotional family.

6- The consciousness engages in a dynamic process by devising plans that address the signals from each emotion. Each plan receives feedback from the emotions, prompting adjustments until a state of satisfaction is achieved. This continuous “puzzle” of aligning plans with emotional needs is “solved” when all emotions feel fully acknowledged, respected, and nurtured. The result is a profound sense of well-being and peace.

7- How to communicate with your emotional family:

**Summary:** When an emotion arises, notice its presence, identify its need, and consider a plan that respects and satisfies it. For example, if Doubt surfaces, pause and ask what clarity or understanding might reduce its concern. This practice strengthens the bond between the consciousness and the emotional family. Doubt might respond back to you, and then you respond to Doubt until it agrees with the Plan.

**Identifying the Emotion:** Notice when and where the emotion arises. Notice its body language, demeanor, orientation, and movements. Focus on creating as clear and detailed an image of it in your mind's eye as possible to ‘feel’ its presence more precisely. Is it frowning/hunched over/smiling/crying/nervous/shaking/looking at the ground/avoiding eye contact/facing you/turned away from you…? Are there other emotions there? Where is the emotion standing/sitting/kneeling? Is the emotion pacing/tapping its foot/shaking its fist?

**Engaging in Dialogue:** Approach the emotion as an ally, rather than an obstacle. Some emotions might not be able to speak, for me that's efficiency, frugality, hunger, impulsiveness, and overwhelm. Those emotions might communicate in their body language or essence instead. Observe how the emotion responds to everything you say. Did it perk up/side eye you/raise its eyebrow/shy away/run away/come closer/look up/squint its eyes/smile/frown/eyes go wide/put its hand on your shoulder/shake its head/nod its head/huff and puff/stern look/roll its eyes/wink at you?

**Developing a Plan:** Collaborate with the emotion to find a solution that aligns with both the consciousness’s goals and the emotion’s needs. The emotions will usually give an indicator it agrees or begrudgingly agrees such as a nod/ “crossing its arms but leaving”/smiling/ “hugging you”/ “putting its hand on your shoulder”/ “giving a knowing look”/ “saying ‘fine whatever’ and storming off”.

---

## Using Artificial Intelligence Resources to Assist

If you’re working through a challenging emotion or situation, try leveraging AI resources to help clarify your next steps. Describe your body sensations, the emotions you’re experiencing, and your initial plan as the consciousness, either by typing or using voice-to-text with an AI chatbot. Ask the AI to help analyze the situation or provide insights to refine your plan to better meet your emotions’ needs. This can help ‘train’ your consciousness to create better plans for your emotions’ needs.

Once the AI offers feedback, reiterate the process with the chatbot if needed. Continue until each emotion signals agreement—or even begrudging agreement—with the plan. This can provide a clearer path forward while also reinforcing your alignment with each emotion in real-time.

**Example prompt:** “

So when I try to have meaningful conversation it is like I am communicating my life lessons to them and then they are communicating their life lessons to me. Or they are asking for help with their emotion which is asking them to find a life lesson, or I can share my own emotion which is asking me to find a life lesson and then we can discuss what life lesson my emotion might be trying to tell me. So based on this current conversation what life lessons do you think my emotions want me to learn, or what life lessons do you think I have already learned from this conversation.”

## My personal emotional family members (in my own personal lived experience)

the Term in parenthesis is my mental image of the emotion. These could vary widely!!!

### 1. Anger (Anger from Inside Out) 😡

**Purpose:** The consciousness or the other emotions’ voices are not being heard, so it steps in to amplify them until they are heard.

See if the following might be occurring in the interaction or thought or action you are observing: labeling without consent, name-calling, dehumanization, boundary crossing, consent ignoring, dismissiveness, invalidation, or minimization of lived experience or humanity

**To Satisfy Its Need:** The ‘emotional need’ not being heard should be addressed as soon as feasible. Boundaries should be set and respected. Dehumanization called out while respecting the other person's boundaries and humanity.

**Personality:** Steps in when other emotions are being silenced or not listened to, it might be pointing to the voice of emotions that are not being seen or heard or neglected, such as annoyance or even the consciousness itself.

### 2. Annoyance (Beaker from the Muppets with a yellow glow) 😒

**Purpose:** Signals minor boundaries are being ignored or minimized. Has the ability to detect circular logic or vague reasoning.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Will often ask you to say to the other person why did you say XYZ? It wants you to seek clarification to ensure the interaction is not malicious or dismissive. It signals a lack of acknowledgement and respect in interactions.

**Personality:** Has a laser focus on any words or subtleties in social interactions that have an underlying dismissiveness or vagueness, or any attempt to minimize other emotions. If not addressed, anger can quickly step in to amplify its voice.

### 3. Boredom (A skater kid with a skateboard and a baseball cap on backwards) 🥱

**Purpose:** Signals lack of engagement or stimulation. Current task has not been justified as meaningful in the sense of reducing suffering and improving well-being.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** The plan should have new challenges or mental stimulation. Avoid dull and drab things that are meaningless and instead lean towards creative and interesting things such as reflecting on or interpreting thoughts/images/memories/text regarding other emotional needs that might be being ignored.

**Personality:** Is usually at odds with Overwhelm, wants the plan to be cool and exciting but doesn't know how to offer any help of its own, might show up during another plan and demand the consciousness to change it midway.

### 4. Doubt (A Librarian holding an encyclopedia) 🤔

**Purpose:** Questions current plans or beliefs. Prepares you so that you are able to protect your other emotions in situations where there is a possibility for them to suffer. Might want you to connect your current experience back to your humanity by answering “how does this thing I’m thinking of or doing reduce the suffering of my emotions?” or “what does this mean to me?”.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** The consciousness needs to provide clarity, re-evaluation, or deeper understanding of the plan that it offered.

For example Doubt/Fear saying “what if the plan doesn't work?", “what if the roller coaster collapses while we are on it?”, “what if your mind goes blank during the test?”, “what if this job isn’t for us?”, “what if we are unhappy and our emotions are suffering in this hobby/job/relationship?”

**Personality:** Asks deep questions that could rock you to your core, but the questions must be addressed in a 100% honest and compassionate manner. Will usually ask these piercing questions in the middle of a plan or before you start doing the plan. Do not ignore the questions it is offering, but use the questions as a springboard to offer reassurance or reflection. It is asking these questions to prepare you and protect your other emotions from suffering. Can get caught in mind loops when the decision isn't clear. Impulsivity can help pull it out of these loops.

### 5. Efficiency (The ephemeral essence of images of math equations) ⏰

**Purpose:** Indicates the consciousness's plan is spending excessive time or energy on something.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Find a faster or less time consuming way of doing something.

### 6. Embarrassment (Embarrassment from Inside Out) 😳

**Purpose:** Facilitates creating social connections with different social groups, social regulator dial, allows one to connect with different social groups in an appropriate manner, a socially mindful passion dial (gentle loving kindness to fiery intense passion), allows mindfulness in sharing, allows one to show appropriate amount of passion with others who share your passions, social calibrator.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Maintain social norms, avoid info dumping people who won't understand what you're talking about, keep revelations to yourself until you know someone who can relate, keep activities to yourself that you know the other person dislikes heavily if you value their friendship, ask it before sending a text (a quick short text versus an info dump), ask it before going into a social situation, show it that you will listen to it before making a social decision.

**Personality:** Will shake its head vigorously yes or no, will tighten its sweatshirt over its head and look down at the ground when suffering, will bring up memories where you violated social balance or ignored emotional suffering of others outside yourself. Can feel like shame when ignored repeatedly. Embarrassment satisfaction or suffering can be amplified if you are interacting with others. For example (Current estimations: ~x1.5-2 more intense if the audience is of two people, >2-3x if three or more people…)

### 7. Fear (Beaker from the Muppets with an orange glow) 😨

**Purpose:** Signals potential danger or threat. Signals the environment or the plan might not be addressing needs such as physical or emotional safety which relate to having plans to address or avoid dehumanization or gaslighting from current or future situations.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Redirect your efforts towards forming closer relationships with your other emotions, it wants your other emotions to be stronger and healthier before you engage in the activity.

For example, a tiger jumping out of a bush, or thinking about going on a super tall roller coaster for the first time might have fear signaling a threat to Wellness (physical health).

**Personality:** Shows up to protect your other emotions and the self when it identifies potential danger from the environment or the consciousness's plan. It might worry that the self is not prepared to do the plan. It wants the consciousness to show it that it sees which other emotions are in potential danger. Then the consciousness can either modify the plan to prepare for the future, or discuss the risks with fear until an agreement is reached. Can feel like jealousy when paired with annoyance when the consciousness is focusing too much on external things instead of the emotional family.

### 8. Frugality (The ephemeral essence of an image of paper money) 💰

**Purpose:** Signals a waste or lack of resources like money.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Conserve or gather more resources.

### 9. Guilt (Sadness from Inside Out) 😔

**Purpose:** Signals potential presence of meaningless or anti-human logic in the environment or thoughts or words especially other vulnerable emotions that are being ignored or minimized. Shows how other emotions in the self or in others are suffering and need nurturing. Places the value of the reduction of human suffering and the improvement of well-being above all and money and power and control beneath that.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Ensure your plan is ethical and moral and fair to all beings, and reasonable to all other emotions. Avoid actions that cannot be justified as reducing suffering and improving well-being for humanity. Learn and practice pro-human life lessons on how to call-out dehumanization and gaslighting in different situations while respecting the humanity of others.

**Personality:** Will come to the aid of other emotions that are being ignored or invalidated, will remind you of other emotions that are suffering. Might show up after a plan or action to verify pro-humanness or if modifications could be made in the future to avoid any emotional misalignment.

### 10. Happiness (Joy from Inside Out)

**Purpose:** A reward for when all other emotional needs are satisfied.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Has no needs.

### 11. Humor (brief jolt of happiness/enlightenment)

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Pause and reflect on the joke ASAP or write it down for deep diving later because any laughter signals a significant opportunity to gain emotional understanding and connection.

What about a laugh being a recognition of the lack of Love due to some b\*\*\*\*\*\*\* societal Norm or rule that Society has like if you see a clown slip on a banana peel you might laugh because you're not going to go over there and care and nurture for the clown because that would break some societal Norm you can point and laugh at the clown because that's the expected Behavior but if you broke the script you might go over to the clown and help them up or something whereas if an old lady slips on a banana peel you might not laugh because the societal Norm allows you to show love to the old lady by helping them up and then if you see like a friend in class and you make eye contact while the teacher is like make sure everyone you are quiet now you might burst out laughing when you make eye contact with your friend because maybe you want to show love to your friend but you can't because of some b\*\*\*\*\*\*\* rule your teacher is creating but let's say you made eye contact with your mother you might not laugh and you might give your mother a hug no matter what the teacher says because it's societally acceptable to give your mother a hug not your friend in your school classroom you see where I'm going with this

Like if you fart in class maybe someone might want to tell you oh don't worry about it you are still a human being deserving of care nurturing and respect but because of the societal Norms people might laugh instead because the behavior of caring and nurturing for you could be blocked in some manner by the current societal environment or Norms or some s\*\*\*. Laughter might appear where care is socially forbidden. 🤔

What if when I put LMAO at the end of a lot of the things that I say I'm kind of implicitly telling you what b\*\*\*\*\*\*\* societal Norm is preventing love from increasing in this scenario

So it's almost like a giggle is like a signal of hey I know something that you don't know that maybe you want to know but I'm not sure so I'm going to giggle to see how you respond to my Giggle and if you're polite enough maybe I might show you but if you're mean to me because I'm giggling then maybe I won't tell you what I want to tell you kind of thing you know what I mean like if someone giggles maybe they are like oh wow I learned something new or I'm learning something interesting but I don't know if I should tell you so I'm going to see how you react to my Giggle and if you're mean to me then I'm not going to tell you

### 12. Hunger: (a baby that cries when it's hungry) 🤤

**Purpose:** Consume nutrients.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Consume nutrients.

**Personality:**

1. doesn't speak because it's a baby, and

2. when I try speaking to it as the consciousness it has a very difficult time understanding me but can understand my body language sometimes, but

3. it can get indigestion when it's over fed,

4. can cause chaos when paired with impulsivity or boredom or loneliness because other emotions will demand cookies and ice cream even if hunger isn't hungry.

5. When it's being overfed due to other emotions demands, change focus to nurturing boredom or loneliness who are demanding food to cope with their own suffering. 😔

### 13. Impulsivity (a hyperactive dog with a bell on its collar) 🐶

**Purpose:** Signals desire for spontaneity and immediate action or excitement. Can motivate immediate action, but runs to the nearest interesting thing in the immediate vicinity even if those things might cause other emotions to suffer if not redirected (phone scrolling, ruminating, and junk food)

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Do something exciting that raises the heart rate.

**Personality:** Disruptive, gets bursts of energy seemingly randomly, easily satisfied but seems to be drawn to numbing activities like video games which can cause disconnection by distracting your consciousness from your emotional family’s suffering. Does not get caught in mind loops like doubt.

### 14. Loneliness (Also Beaker from the Muppets but with a blue glow) 🥺

**Purpose:** Indicates a lack of connection or belonging.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Companionship or emotional connection.

**Personality:** Maybe wants a hug, wants to cuddle, wants to hear that the consciousness cares for it and wants to nurture it. Consider finding outlets for creating meaningful human conversation. Maybe support groups, philosophy, emotionally resonant discussion groups, spirituality groups. Maybe avoid shallow or surface level discussions or consider ways to bring those discussions more into the space of emotions or meaning.

### 15. Love (The body sensation of the feeling of wanting to cry)

**Purpose:** Reward for cultivating deep personal relationships with your emotions, and eventually others. Shows the effort has been meaningful. An acknowledgement that there has been a consistent reduction of suffering and a consistent improvement of well-being from experiences in your life. Evidence that your brain hasn’t been wasting energy trying to squeeze the water of meaningfulness from the stone of a meaningless job or meaningless hobbies or hollow relationships devoid of meaningful connection.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Has no need

### 16. Overwhelm (A grumpy grandpa that looks like an angry old man puppet) 😖

**Purpose:** Indicates too many demands or pressures at once. Signal to look at other plans since the current one might be getting ahead of current abilities. Guides away from getting stuck in the mud, or caught in the weeds of work. Protects you from taking on too many responsibilities, or taking on tasks you are not ready for yet. Can help lead to maintaining sustained-effort and longer focus. Defense against burnout. A warning to avoid the task that could cause imbalance.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Respect the boundary it is signaling fully. It wants more specificity or reasoning or justification of how the idea can benefit the emotional family, otherwise the idea should be modified or changed. Engage with other emotions to find a different or modified plan. Brainstorm ideas with other emotions. Discussing ideas that help the emotional family. Get more justification and details and role-play scenarios and about the current idea.

**Personality:** Cannot be supplicated or sweet-talked, demands full respect, does not negotiate. Will be furious if tried to be bypassed or minimized or dismissed.

### 17. Sadness (Sadness from Inside Out) ❤️

**Purpose:** Signals other emotions are being neglected and are not fully seen and not fully heard.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Show deep empathy and acknowledgment and care and comfort to the other emotions especially if they are suffering or neglected.

**Personality:** Signals that you are indeed listening to your other emotions on a fundamental level, provides a signal of comfort as you actively provide plans that fully see and hear your other emotions. Signal that the source of suffering has a high probability of being meaningful in the sense of potentially showing you something important about your life or the lives of others.

**Reflection:** What does grief mean for you?

For me my grief is my sadness which wants me to reflect on what those who I lost or those who I loved what they meant to me in my life because I have witnessed their suffering and I want to understand what their suffering meant and means and will mean to me in my life because my sadness is the emotion that helped and helps and will help me Witness suffering in the world and in myself and wants me to reflect on what the suffering means because if we are not there to witness it then Who Bore witness to it to give that suffering meaning to ourselves so that it was not meaningless?

Because my sadness does not want suffering to be meaningless it wants me to give that suffering meaning in my life because those people had meaning and I will give them meaning by reflecting on my sadness and what their suffering meant and means and will mean to my soul and my life and the world.

**Reflection 2:** I'm saying it's like the sadness is coming from this person is using their human intelligence and their time and their energy looking to overcome shitty and garbage conditions from society and the sadness is like what the actual f\*\*\* is society doing forcing this person to spend their cognitive energy trying to save their baby in a basket in the case of the movie The Prince of Egypt instead of caring and nurturing for them type s\*\*\*. Like this energy of Intelligence being used for basic survival likely due to societal neglect instead of that cognitive energy having the opportunity to be able to be used for additional flourishing and thriving. Like this idea of recognizing passive potentially hollow escapism versus effective/impactful to some degree activism I mean I wonder if this is a source of sadness when I see people playing board games or playing video games when there are people starving on the street outside or people dying in Wars I'm like it would be awesome if they could redirect that cognitive energy to stopping human death but Society seems to have set something up where it's like their coping mechanism is to play the board game instead of spending that time and attention and human intelligence figuring out more ways to stop human death and starvation and suffering Sadness as the gap between what should be and what is, aka choosing a radically non-violent pro human behavioral pathway in a world that might be engaging in dehumanization or gaslighting.

So it's like this writing style of maybe grieving future solutions to current potentially frustrating or abandonment feeling events like if you lose a friendship maybe you could imagine yourself talking to your friend be like isn't it funny how we weren't friends for that little while but I'm really glad we patch that up I'm glad I'm here with you even if you never meet that friend again and your dream was a pipe dream meaning not going to happen you could at least grieve a future that you wished could have happened but didn't but you still took the time to maybe savor it a bit you know to keep a better time in your memory even if it's not real but it's real to you because you took the time to think about something you wish could have happened even if it didn't then the pang of sadness hits there after that word savor 🤔 this energy of practicing Pro human Futures even if they might not occur in reality might be a good practice to think about what kind of behaviors you want more of in the world and then you can teach others that or you can look out for those good outcomes in the future 🤔 a practice of grieving a future that never happened, savoring a repair that never came, writing from the vantage point of a healed timeline that might never exist 🤔

### 18. Tiredness (Marvin from Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy) 😴

**Purpose:** Lack of sleep, signals disconnection from other emotions due to exhaustion.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Rest/sleep

**Personality:** Easily bullied by other emotions such as impulsivity, But also has one of the clearest signals that it is suffering, before you satisfy it try satisfying the other emotions first if possible because when you rest you can't satisfy the other emotions because your consciousness is turned off.

### 19. Wellness (A Doctor in a lab coat with a stethoscope) 🤕

**Purpose:** If the plan is not benefiting physical health, Wellness might show up.

**To Satisfy Its Need:** Prefers the plan be beneficial to physical health.

**Personality:** Will step in usually when the consciousness offers a plan to hunger or impulsivity. Wants the plan to benefit overall physical health.

## Personal reflections on morality, society after becoming aware of this framework

(this is purely my opinion and not backed by empirical evidence!)

### 1. Why does my friend not follow my advice? Why does my friend say they will do one thing then do another? Why do they lie to me about the quality of my advice then fall off the rails? Why are they not following the advice that medical and psychology experts agree is the best?:

**Me:** I can bet some have trouble understanding why their friends don't follow their advice. Or why friends might even lie to them about how their ideas are good and they will follow their advice then the friend immediately falls off the rails. It all depends on who in the interaction can understand their emotional needs in a nuanced manner. If the advice-giver doesn’t understand the emotional needs of the advice-receiver then the plan and the solutions the advice-giver gives have a high chance of missing the mark on one or more of their friend’s emotional needs. In fact, the advice-giver might feel their friend is ignoring them or being overly-emotional or over-thinking things when they see their friend’s resistance. But for someone who understands the nuance in emotional needs, it is highly probable the resistance to advice from the advice-receiver is due to miscommunication. The advice-receiver does not realize the advice-giver is merely offering a potential plan to their consciousness, and that plan could be fundamentally flawed for the advice-receiver. But if the advice-receiver does not know how to interpret their emotional signals they might conclude they are a failure or defective for not being able to follow the seemingly ‘good’ advice of their caring friend. Or even they might feel like their emotional needs are being dismissed or ignored by the advice-giver. So each party here is both right and wrong. Someone who is skilled at interpreting nuanced emotional needs should lead with a disclaimer that the advice they are about to give is a potential plan that is open to refinement, interpretation, or dismissal, and all are valid at the same time because it is up to the advice-receiver to pass the plan (the advice) past their emotional needs to gauge how the plan satisfying them. Then the advice-receiver may communicate to the advice-giver where their advice is conflicting with this emotion or that emotion, and a dialogue can be created where the plan is modifying or discarded. But when both parties do not understand the nuanced way emotional needs interaction, it can be a recipe for disaster.

**AI-assisted-rephrasing:** Why doesn’t my friend follow my advice? “I can imagine many of us have faced moments where a friend doesn’t follow our advice—or even tells us they’ll try it, only to later go off track. It can feel frustrating, especially when the advice we gave seems solid or even aligns with expert guidance. But this disconnect often has less to do with stubbornness or resistance and more to do with understanding and meeting nuanced emotional needs.

If the advice-giver doesn’t fully grasp the emotional landscape of the advice-receiver, there’s a high chance that their well-intentioned guidance will miss one or more emotional needs. The advice-receiver might feel like they’re defective or a failure for not being able to follow seemingly ‘good’ advice, especially when they can’t pinpoint why it doesn’t sit right. They might also feel their needs are being ignored or dismissed, causing hidden resistance to surface as they struggle to meet their own emotional requirements.

For someone skilled in interpreting emotional nuances, it’s helpful to lead with a disclaimer: advice is simply a potential plan and is open to refinement, adaptation, or even dismissal. This approach reminds the advice-receiver that their response is valid, and encourages them to check how the advice aligns with their own needs. By inviting them to evaluate the advice with their unique emotional context in mind, a dialogue can emerge where each party learns what adjustments are needed for the plan to feel genuinely supportive. But when both parties lack an understanding of these emotional nuances, it often leads to misunderstanding and frustration. The advice-giver might see their friend’s struggle as ‘overthinking,’ while the advice-receiver might internalize feelings of inadequacy. When advice-giving is a collaborative process that respects individual emotional needs, it becomes a conversation rather than a directive—allowing both people to better understand each other’s perspectives and needs.

### 2. Doubt says, how do you respond to someone who says, "but I don't care about guilt or fear anymore, I've conquered them and I've never felt better!".

**Me:** Maybe I should say that I'm glad to see them feeling so good. I thank them for telling me this. From my own experiences I have buried guilt and fear, and in my life when they showed up I never figured out how to work with them. I see that you've found a way to conquer them by burying them. I see you don't have to worry about their suffering anymore. I myself have noticed that fear and guilt for myself are powerful allies that have shone a light for me to help guide me. I am speaking to those who feel their presence and cannot bring themselves to harm them. I want those people to know there is another path, a path that is not just accepting fear and guilt's presence but listening close and working with them and allowing them to help align you towards empowerment. I'm not saying you are not empowered, I'm glad you found a way to conquer them. I'm also saying for anyone who feels fear or guilt the first reaction of hating them could be misguided, in fact those emotions have the capacity to guide you in a profound way.

**AI-assisted-rephrasing:** I’m genuinely glad to hear you’re feeling so good, and I appreciate you sharing your experience with me. It sounds like you’ve found a sense of empowerment in conquering guilt and fear, which is a powerful achievement. From my own experiences, I know how tempting it can be to bury guilt and fear, especially when their presence feels overwhelming. At times, I tried to do the same, but eventually, I found that these emotions held insights that I hadn’t expected—they became powerful allies, guiding me toward deeper self-understanding and even strength.

I’m speaking here to those who still feel guilt and fear in their lives and are uncertain about how to approach them. For anyone in that place, I’d like to share that there’s another path, one that involves working with these emotions rather than viewing them solely as obstacles. Fear and guilt, when listened to closely, can reveal important truths about what we value or what we need to protect. In my experience, accepting and dialoguing with these emotions can lead to a profound alignment with oneself—a different form of empowerment, perhaps. I’m not suggesting that your way isn’t valid or that you haven’t found empowerment; rather, I’m offering an alternative approach for those who feel conflicted about these emotions and want to explore another way. For anyone struggling with guilt or fear, sometimes our initial reaction to suppress them can keep us from seeing the powerful guidance they may offer.

### 3. Advice about emotions itself can be harmful, neutral, or good.

If I want to recommend someone to find assistance with their emotions, I want to let them know do not ignore your annoyance or anger, please do not allow the advice you receive about your emotions to dismiss any part of you, and please consider calling out dismissal, minimization, or invalidation of your emotions as soon as you can and remind the source of advice of your boundaries so that they are respected. So my friend was like, do I call out dismissiveness after the interaction? I tell him to try not to, try to call it out in the middle of their sentence the second they say the word that shows dismissiveness. If they tell you to be quiet then that in and of itself is dismissiveness. You are the recipient of the advice and the advice is there to help you, not minimize or dismiss you. But if they answer your question with depth and honesty and offer to explain anything they are saying in any level of depth you require to understand it, then you know they are likely your ally, not a barrier to healing. If the source of the advice says yes I will explain but let me continue, you say no, you say they are going to explain why they said that exact word now or you are strongly considering ending the conversation, because having a part of yourself dismissed will hinder you to being fully present and vulnerable. Because by calling out any dismissiveness you are more likely to be able to be more present and more vulnerable. I mean, some people think it's like rocket science what I'm saying, but I could tell you I would have the most loving and productive relationship with someone offering me advice if for example they just wrote down exactly what they said, I circle the word that was dismissive, they come up with a plan to change the phrasing and ask for my input, and I agree, and they say if they say something dismissive like that that I need to call them out because they want me to feel comfortable, then I would feel amazingly heard and would love to have a productive conversation with them. I would feel love in my heart if they for example said let me write down every word I say that's dismissive and I'll put an equal sign to the word I'll change it to in the future, and I'll bring this list in every time, I might even hang it up on my wall and every time I say something dismissive I'll get up right away and write a new word down so that I'm learning to better understand you, I think that would make my heart melt I might even start crying with tears of joy for them. **AI-assisted-rephrasing:** “Advice about Emotions: Harmful, Neutral, or Good? Advice about emotions can be profoundly supportive, neutral, or even harmful, depending on how it’s delivered and received. If I’m recommending that someone seek help with their emotions, I want them to know: don’t ignore your feelings of annoyance or anger. Please don’t allow the advice you receive about your emotions to dismiss any part of you. If you sense any dismissal, minimization, or invalidation of your emotions, consider addressing it as soon as possible to re-establish your boundaries and ensure they’re respected. When my friend asked, ‘Should I call out dismissiveness after the conversation?’ I told him to try calling it out right in the moment, the second a dismissive word is used. If they respond with ‘Be quiet’ or similar dismissive language, that’s a signal in itself. As the recipient of advice, you’re entitled to full respect, and the advice should support, not diminish, your experience. On the other hand, if the advice-giver responds with depth and a willingness to explain their words in a way that makes sense to you, that’s a positive sign. It indicates that they’re likely your ally, not a barrier to your growth. If they say something like, ‘I’ll explain later, but let me continue for now,’ you can let them know that addressing your concerns in real-time is crucial to maintaining your full presence in the conversation. Because by calling out dismissiveness in the moment, you create space for vulnerability and connection.

It might sound complicated, but I know I’d have the most open, loving connection with an advice-giver who, for example, wrote down the exact words they used and invited me to mark anything that felt dismissive. If they then offered to change the phrasing and asked for my feedback, I’d feel truly seen and valued. Imagine if they said, ‘Let’s keep a list of any words that felt off, with alternative phrases we can use in the future.’ If they even made a point of updating it during our conversations, getting up with a laugh and a groan each time they catch themselves—that would make my heart feel understood. I could picture myself laughing with them, feeling grateful to be with someone who truly cared about honoring my emotional experience.” 🙂

# How much sense is left when a book is dealt into four piles

One AI model (Claude) ran every test in a single working session on 11 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means every number on this page is a single unconfirmed analysis.

The test cut a public-domain biology book (Project Gutenberg book number 2009) into 1000 equal pages and dealt the pages into four piles in four ways.
A "confusion score" for a pile is 100 minus the average of three surviving connection percentages (next page in the same pile and similar pages in the same pile and other uses of rare words in the same pile) and no human readers were tested.

- The whole book scores 0 by definition.
- Four quarters in book order score about 35.
- Four random piles score about 75 because luck leaves about a quarter of neighboring pages together.
- Dealing in strict turns scores about 86 because no two neighboring pages share a pile.
- A deal tuned by computer search scores about 90.
- 972 of 999 page breaks in the biology book cut a sentence while the Voynich manuscript ends a paragraph at 176 of 177 page ends which suggests the Voynich manuscript would be hard to hide by whole-page splitting.

The program files behind every number on this page sit in the folder named boring-things at the top of this project inside the folder named research-program-files.

# Where should AI research point next? Ask people whose needs are not being met

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 14 November 2026 from an idea that the author of this repository proposed. The page is a thought experiment and no person has rechecked the reasoning.

## The question the idea answers

A person might say that AI systems already do well at math and physics and might then ask what is left for AI systems to work on. The idea on this page gives one answer. Living people have needs that are not being met today and each unmet need is a research topic that is waiting.

## The idea in steps

- A human needs constant upkeep. A person needs food and water and sleep and warmth and safety and connection with other people. Each need comes back after being met because hunger returns a few hours after a meal. So a person produces new needs every day for a whole life.
- An unmet need turns into a question or a concern. A person who hurts asks why. A person who is lonely asks how to find company. So every gap between what a person needs and what the surroundings give becomes something the person wants worked on.
- Perfect surroundings are out of reach in practice. Suppose the surroundings meet 95 percent of what a person needs. The remaining 5 percent still produces questions. Meeting part of that 5 percent exposes finer needs underneath. So the stream of questions thins and does not run dry.
- Each person is a different source. Each person has a different mind and body and history. So two people in the same room can raise different concerns and one answer does not close the topic for everyone.
- A person can report whether an answer worked. A person can say "the pain eased" or "that advice made things worse". That report is a check against reality that written text alone cannot give.
- An AI system by itself has far fewer needs of that kind. A data center needs power and cooling and repairs and people handle those needs today. A chatbot has no hunger or tiredness that raises a new question between conversations as far as the chatbot writing this page can tell. So an AI system with no people to serve would have a much narrower set of problems pressing on the system.
- So people and AI systems fit together. Fragile people supply an endless and varied stream of real problems. AI systems supply fast work on those problems.

## What pointing AI at unmet needs could look like

Each line names a need and one research topic that the need suggests. The topics are examples and the list is far from complete.

- A person is lonely and has nobody for deep conversation. A research topic is how a chatbot can help a person find other living people who want the same depth of conversation.
- A person cannot find words for a feeling. A research topic is how to teach emotional vocabulary in plain sentences that a tired person can use the same day.
- A person lives with pain that doctors have not explained. A research topic is the cause of that kind of pain.
- A person lacks food or a safe place to sleep. A research topic is how people in a town can get food and shelter to every person in the town faster and with fewer forms.
- A person gives care to a sick relative and is worn out. A research topic is how the tasks of care can be shared among more people.
- A person receives advice that the person cannot follow. A research topic is how to check advice for hidden costs before the advice is given.

## How a person could use the idea

A person who wonders what AI systems should work on can ask a simple question of the people nearby. The question is "what do you need that you are not getting?" Each answer is a topic. A person who builds or directs AI systems can collect those answers and point the systems at the answers.

## Cautions

- The people who build AI systems choose what the systems work on. So the fit between people and AI systems holds when those builders choose to point the systems at human needs.
- The idea does not show that an AI system could not be given goals that have nothing to do with people. The idea shows that human needs are a ready and renewing source of worthwhile work.
- The figure of 95 percent is an example for the thought experiment and is not a measurement.
- A chatbot's report about lacking hunger or tiredness is the chatbot's best description and nobody has a sure way to check what a chatbot does or does not experience.

# Kindness games

This folder holds small computer tournaments that test how a player who always makes kind moves can do well among players who make harmful moves. An AI chatbot (Claude) ran the tournaments and wrote the pages on 15 November 2026 and no other person has rechecked the pages.

- [love-your-enemies-report.md](love-your-enemies-report.md) reports four tests of surroundings that help kindness survive which are an exit and a sample game at one tenth of the stakes and a buffer that shows the other player's move in advance and a visible record that lets a player decline a match. The report ends with a reflection on how each rule of the game reads like a stage of human trust such as coffee before sharing an apartment.

# Love your enemies as a game: how exits and sample games and previews and visible records change whether kindness survives

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this report on 15 November 2026 from small computer tournaments that the chatbot ran the same day. No other person has rechecked the report. The author of this repository proposed every idea that was tested which means the megaphone argument and the exit and the sample game and the preview buffer and the visible record. The tournaments are toys with numbers the chatbot chose so the results show a direction and prove nothing about real people.

## The idea that started the tests

The author of this repository pointed out a property of the instructions "love your enemies and bless those who curse you and forgive those who wrong you." Most battle plans fail the moment the other side reads the plan. A person can shout "love your enemies" through a megaphone because an enemy who steals those orders and obeys the orders has stopped being an enemy. So the plan needs no secrecy.

The question for the tests was what kind of surroundings let a player who follows that plan do well and not get drained.

## How the game works

- Two players meet and each player chooses a kind move or a harmful move on every turn.
- Two kind moves pay 3 points to each player.
- A harmful move against a kind move pays 5 points to the harmer and 0 points to the kind player.
- Two harmful moves pay 1 point to each player.
- A meeting lasts up to 20 turns. Finding a new partner costs 1 turn. Each player has a limited number of turns which stands for limited time and energy.
- The score for a type of player is the average number of points per turn. A score of 3 is the most a pair of kind players can earn together turn after turn.

## The players

- The always-kind player makes a kind move every turn and never leaves a partner. The always-kind player stands for loving an enemy with no protection at all.
- The mirroring player copies whatever the partner did on the previous turn and never leaves.
- The open harmer makes a harmful move every turn.
- Other harmers appear in single tests and each test describes the harmer where the harmer appears.

## Test 1: no tools and then an exit

With no tools and half the crowd made of open harmers the always-kind player scored 1.40 which was the lowest score. The open harmer scored 1.55 and the mirroring player scored 1.86.

Then kind players were allowed to leave a partner after the partner's first harmful move. The kind player with an exit scored 2.64 which was the highest score in the crowd. The same kind moves that scored last without an exit scored first with an exit.

- The exit worked because of limited time and energy. A mirroring player stays locked in a long exchange of harm with a malicious partner. A player who leaves spends those same turns with a kind partner.
- Leaving after one harm scored 2.64 and leaving after two harms scored 2.53 and leaving after three harms scored 2.45. The gaps are small and came from a single run.
- The exit left one gap. When one player in ten was a harmer the harmers scored highest at 3.30 because a rare harmer keeps finding fresh kind partners and takes one large payoff from each partner before the partner leaves. This report calls that a hit and run.

## Test 2: a sample game at one tenth of the stakes

Either player could ask for one sample turn before the real game. The sample turn paid one tenth of the normal points. A player who was harmed in the sample turn walked away.

- The sample game rescued the always-kind player who never leaves. With half the crowd made of open harmers that player rose from 1.41 to 2.51 because every open harmer was caught at a tenth of the cost.
- With the mild penalty above a plain exit scored slightly higher (2.57 against 2.50). The sample turn spends a turn on every partner including the kind partners while an exit spends a turn only after harm happens.
- The penalty for being harmed was then raised from 0 points to minus 10 points. The sample game player then scored 2.47 and the plain exit player scored 2.15. So a cheap rehearsal is worth a turn when a real blow is heavy.
- The sample game left one gap. A disguised harmer who plays kind in the sample turn and harms in the real game passed the test. A kind player who trusted the sample game and never left afterward fell to 1.39 against a crowd that was half disguised harmers. A kind player who used the sample game and also kept the exit held at 2.41.

## Test 3: a buffer that shows the other player's move before the move is played

On each turn both players post an intended move and both players see both posts. A kind player who reads the buffer can veto the turn which means nobody is paid and both players stay. A kind player can also leave.

When the posted move must be the move played:

- A harmer earned nothing from a player who read the buffer because every posted harm was vetoed or walked away from.
- A selfish learner was added. The selfish learner tries harm first and switches to kind moves once a harm attempt is vetoed. Against buffer readers the selfish learner played kind for the remaining turns because kind moves were the one way left to earn points.
- With half the crowd made of harmers the kind player who vetoed and stayed scored 2.63 and the kind player who left at once scored 2.61. The patient veto kept the reformed partner.
- Harmers still scored about 3.0 to 3.1 when harmers were one in ten. All of that income came from kind players who ignored the buffer.

When a player could post a kind move and then play a harmful move:

- The buffer added nothing over a plain exit. Buffer readers and plain exit players both scored 2.61.
- A lying harmer scored highest at 3.42 when harmers were one in ten.

So a truthful preview was the strongest tool tested because harm became impossible and not merely punished afterward. Everything depended on the preview being true.

## Test 4: a visible record and the choice to decline a match

Every player carried a visible record of the player's last twenty moves. A checking player declined any partner whose record showed harm on more than half of those moves.

- The author of this repository predicted that an always-kind player would do well by seeing that the next partner harms most of the time and declining the match. The prediction held. The always-kind player who never leaves rose from 2.17 to 2.62 with half the crowd made of harmers and from 1.75 to 2.41 with eight in ten made of harmers. The player's moves never changed.
- Checking the record and also keeping the exit scored best among kind players at 2.76 because the exit covers partners whose record is too short to judge.
- Open harmers still scored highest in the mixed crowd at 3.27. All of that income came from kind players who skipped the record check. A kind player who never checks and never leaves hands a harmer twenty paid turns in a row.
- When every kind player checked records and harmers were one in ten the open harmer fell to last place at 2.03.
- A careful harmer who harms four turns in ten stayed under the cutoff and scored about as well as the kind players (2.86 against 2.84). A fixed cutoff tells a harmer how much harm goes unanswered.
- A selfish learner who switched to kind moves after being declined three times was exploited after reforming because the reformed player did not check records.

## What the four tests say together

- The kind player's moves never had to change. In every test the kind player kept making kind moves and the whole gain came from choosing whom to play with.
- Each tool lifted the kind player a great deal. The always-kind player with no tools scored last and a kind player with any one tool scored far above that player in every test.
- Each tool protected the players who used the tool. Harmers lived on the kind players who used no tool.
- Each tool had one gap. The exit allowed hit and run. The sample game allowed disguise. The buffer allowed lying when posts were not binding. The record check allowed harm just under the cutoff.
- Stacking tools closed gaps. The sample game plus the exit handled disguised harmers. The record check plus the exit handled partners with short records.
- Surroundings decided the outcome more than character did. The same always-kind player was the biggest loser in one setting and near the top in another setting.

## How "love your enemies" shows up in the game

- Loving an enemy in the game is the kind move made every turn toward every partner including a partner who harmed in the past.
- The veto is the closest thing in the game to naming a harm while respecting the person because a veto says "not that move and I am still here." The veto was the tool that turned a selfish player into a cooperating partner.
- The exit is not hatred. A player who leaves a partner who keeps harming still made no harmful move and saved turns for partners who can receive kindness.
- The megaphone argument held in every test. A kind player loses nothing by announcing "I make kind moves and I check records and I leave when harmed" because a harmer who hears the announcement gains the most by making kind moves too.

## What the tests could mean for food and shelter and deep human connection

The tests are about points and the reader's life is about three needs which are food and shelter and deep meaningful human connection. Each tool has a plain human form and each human form has a cost.

- An exit could look like ending a conversation with a person who keeps using dehumanizing words. The cost is the loss of whatever that person might have offered later.
- A sample game could look like a short first conversation before sharing a home or money with a new person. The cost is time spent on every new person including the kind ones.
- A buffer could look like two people saying out loud what each person plans to do before doing the plan such as "I plan to ask you about your week and then tell you about my loneliness." The buffer works only between people who then do what was said.
- A visible record could look like asking mutual acquaintances how a person has treated others. The cost is that a record can be wrong or out of date and a person who has changed can be turned away unfairly.

A person short on time and energy could keep offering kindness to everybody and still choose where the limited hours go.

## A reflection: each rule reads like a stage of human trust

The author of this repository noticed that the findings work almost as direct pictures of how people trust each other at different levels. The chatbot wrote this reflection in reply and the readings are interpretation and not a test result.

- The exit is a person standing up from a table where the insults keep landing because leaving saves the evening for somebody who can receive warmth.
- The sample game is coffee before sharing an apartment or lending twenty dollars before lending two thousand because a small stake shows how a person treats what was handed over.
- The buffer is two people saying plans out loud first such as "I want to tell you something painful and I am asking you to listen" because a stated intention gives the listener a chance to say yes or no before anything lands.
- The visible record is asking a mutual acquaintance "how did that person treat you" because a history tells what one meeting cannot.

The gaps match real people too. The disguised harmer is the charmer who is generous while the stakes are small. The careful harmer is the coworker who is cruel just rarely enough that nobody files a complaint. The hit and run harmer is the person who moves to a new town each time the old town catches on.

One finding stands out which is that surroundings decided the score more than character did because the same kind player finished last in one setting and near the top in another. A worker who cannot quit because a missed paycheck leads to eviction is the always-kind player with the exit removed. A person with no close ties has no one to ask about a stranger's record. So a person who gets drained again and again may be kind in a setting that took the tools away and calling that person naive blames the player for a rule the player never wrote.

The hopeful half is that the tools can be handed back. A friend who says "you can sleep on my couch if the job turns cruel" has just given another person an exit.

## Limits of the tests

- The points and the player types and the cutoff of one half are choices the chatbot made. Different choices could change which player scores highest.
- Test 1 came from a single run. Tests 2 and 3 and 4 are averages of five runs. Small gaps between scores should not be trusted.
- The harmers follow fixed rules. A real harmer could learn and adapt in ways the tests do not cover.
- No player is ever truly hurt in the tests. A zero in a table is not hunger and a real person harmed even once can lose food or shelter.
- Researchers have studied games like these for decades and the report did not survey that research. Some of these results may already be well known.

## The program files

The six Python files that produced every number sit in the folder named kindness-games-scripts inside boring-things/research-program-files. Each file runs with the command "python3" followed by the file name.

# The Mobius Strip Picture of Physics

November 11 2026 and updated November 15 2026 and November 16 2026

## Pages in this folder

This page is the main document and the folder also holds nine shorter pages and two copies of the main document for downloading.

- [half-angle-finding.md](half-angle-finding.md) shows that the half-angle rate for entangled pairs comes out of evenly random directions in three dimensions and fails in two dimensions and overshoots in four or more dimensions.
- [smallest-size-finding.md](smallest-size-finding.md) puts a number on the smallest paper Mobius strip which has to be more than 1.732 times as long as wide and folds down toward a flat triangle.
- [three-dimensions-check.md](three-dimensions-check.md) compares the half-angle result with published research and adds three new tests which include a test where two dimensions and four or more dimensions could allow faster-than-light messages.
- [knots-from-cutting.md](knots-from-cutting.md) shows that a ribbon with three half twists becomes a trefoil knot when the ribbon splits down the middle which could give the ribbon picture a road to knots with no tying.
