A protein adds one ability that matters for the next step because many proteins hold another molecule and change the held molecule in one particular way such as cutting the held molecule in two. Several proteins can also lock together into a team in which each protein does one part of a longer task.

The protein step suggests that a single non-living structure can carry pieces of emotional logic through folded shape alone. The protein step also shows a limit because a protein cannot make a copy of the protein without the rest of the cell so the full set of survival jobs only appears when many shaped parts work together.

Step five: a complex non-living structure

The last step asks whether the four survival jobs could still get done with life removed entirely and a sufficiently complex Mobius strip structure is the example. A ribbon structure could defend a boundary because stored tension could spring an intruding strip back outward. A ribbon structure could avoid danger because early ripples from a violent region could tighten the ribbon structure or push the ribbon structure away before the violent region arrives. A ribbon structure could seek resources because converting nearby flat space into new loops could keep fresh flat space flowing inward. A ribbon structure could recognize a matching partner because a strip seals edge to edge only with a complementary strip and breaks apart from a strip that does not match.

Nothing at the ribbon step is imagined as sensing or choosing because every response could come from shape. The ribbon step could therefore be the most stripped-down version of emotional logic because the protective behaviors remain while everything resembling experience has been taken away.

Below the ladder: a rock and a crystal

A rock sits below the bottom of the ladder because the inside of a rock is arranged the same way in every surrounding so nothing in the rock connects a dangerous condition to a different behavior. A growing crystal sits one small step above the rock because a growing crystal accepts only molecules that fit the pattern of the crystal which is recognition by shape with none of the other three survival jobs. The rock and the crystal suggest that complexity alone is not enough because a structure has to respond differently to different conditions before emotional logic can begin.

What stays the same on every step

The same loop appears to show up on every step in full or in part because a condition that threatens or feeds the structure causes a shift that protects or builds the structure. The machinery carrying the loop changes from a reflecting nervous system in a human to a simpler nervous system in a lizard to chemistry inside a cell in a bacterium to one folded molecule in a protein to bare shape in a ribbon structure.

The four survival jobs may also feed one another because a structure that defends a boundary lasts long enough to gain danger avoidance and a structure that finds resources can support the extra parts needed for recognizing a partner. Emotional logic could then be described as one system that tends toward complexity because each survival job protects the complexity already built and makes room for more complexity. Natural selection could favor the loop wherever the loop appears because structures carrying the loop outlast structures without the loop whether the structures are alive or not.

Ribbon structures as proteins: shaping other strips and selecting for complexity

A sufficiently complex ribbon structure looks a lot like a protein and the resemblance connects the five-step comparison above to the idea that a non-living structure could copy the structure's own form. This part is an experimental reflection like the two parts before because no one has observed ribbon structures in space.

How a ribbon structure resembles a protein

A protein in a living cell is one long chain that folds into coils and flat pleated sheets and the coils and sheets then pack together into one working shape. Paper Mobius strips cut two or three times fall into shapes with a similar look because the cut strips form spirals and folded bands and loops nested beside each other like puzzle pieces. Ribbons can also join in two ways much as the parts of a protein do because some ribbons share one continuous band or are chained through each other which is a permanent join while other ribbons only rest against each other and can come apart again which is a temporary join.

A ribbon structure as a catalyst

A catalyst is something that makes a particular change happen more easily without being used up by the change. A protein that works as a catalyst holds another molecule in a pocket and the fit of the pocket makes one particular change to the held molecule far more likely. A ribbon structure could work as a catalyst in the same way because a ribbon structure with a pocket of the right shape could nestle a passing strip and bend or twist or cut or join the passing strip in one particular way. The simplest case appears in the earlier part of this document about waves and particles where a closed strip works like a mold that helps a traveling ripple close into a new matching strip.

Teams of several ribbon structures

Proteins in a cell often work in teams because several proteins lock together into one larger unit and each protein in the unit does one part of a longer task. Several ribbon structures could lock together in the same way so that one ribbon structure holds a strip while a second ribbon structure twists the strip and a third ribbon structure seals the strip. A team of ribbon structures could then build shapes that no single ribbon structure could build alone.

Why selection could lean toward complexity

A complex ribbon structure that does not shape other strips could be a dead end if every complex structure slowly decays and a structure that leaves no copies disappears when the structure breaks down. A complex ribbon structure that shapes other strips into more structures of the same kind could leave copies behind and the copies could go on shaping further strips. After a long time the ribbon structures still present could mostly be the ribbon structures whose complexity helps reproduce that same complexity. No goal and no intention needs to be assumed for complexity to spread in such a way because the spread could follow from reproduction alone.

Selection could also favor teams because a group of ribbon structures in which each member helps make another member of the group could rebuild the whole group again and again. A group that rebuilds every member could outlast any lone ribbon structure that cannot make a copy without help.

What a self-copying ribbon structure could need

Any form that copies the form's own shape needs three things which are a template meaning an existing shape that guides raw material into the same shape and a steady supply of raw material and a way for the finished copy to come free so that the copy can make further copies. The ribbon picture offers a candidate for all three because a shaping ribbon structure could be the template and inflowing flat space could be the raw material and cutting plus jostling from neighbors could free the copy.

Two questions remain open about a self-copying ribbon structure and the first question is how a complex form could be copied when a simple loop is easy to copy and a braided knot is not. One possibility is a chain of simple loops copied one loop at a time the way a zipper closes one tooth at a time because each single step could only require the easy kind of copying. The second question is how exact the copying has to be because selection needs copies that are mostly the same and occasionally different so that a version that survives better can appear. The same two questions are asked about how non-living chemistry on the early Earth became the first living cell.

A worked example: a ribbon structure that behaves like a courting lizard

This part of the document imagines one specific complex ribbon structure and follows the ribbon structure through feeding and signaling and traveling and reproducing because a concrete story shows how the survival behaviors described earlier could chain together. The name lizard ribbon structure is used here for a non-living ribbon structure complex enough to copy the signal-and-approach behavior that real lizards show when a lizard advertises readiness to mate and another lizard of the same species moves toward the advertisement. This part is an experimental reflection because nobody has observed any such ribbon structure and nothing here claims that the lizard ribbon structure feels or decides anything.

Feeding: taking smaller strips into the structure

A lizard ribbon structure could feed by absorbing smaller Mobius strips that drift into contact with the lizard ribbon structure which is similar to how a real lizard eats an insect. A pocket on the lizard ribbon structure could hold a small strip in place and the lizard ribbon structure could then unfold the small strip and join the ribbon of the small strip into the larger body. The motion and tension stored in the small strip could become part of the lizard ribbon structure so the lizard ribbon structure could gain energy and material with every small strip absorbed.

Signaling: releasing small strips with one particular shape

A lizard ribbon structure that has absorbed more energy than the lizard ribbon structure needs for upkeep could shed the surplus by pinching off small strips from the outer edge. The pinched-off strips could work as signaling strips because every signaling strip from one kind of lizard ribbon structure could carry the same recognizable shape such as a particular number of twists or a particular tightness of spiral. The signaling strips could drift outward in every direction so the space around a well-fed lizard ribbon structure could hold a cloud of signaling strips that is thickest near the lizard ribbon structure and thinner farther away. The cloud could work as an announcement that a lizard ribbon structure with spare energy for reproduction is nearby even though no ribbon intends to announce anything.

Detecting: a pocket that fits only the matching signal

A second lizard ribbon structure of the same kind could detect the signal because the second lizard ribbon structure could carry a pocket shaped to fit the signaling strip of that kind and no other strip. A signaling strip from a different kind of ribbon structure could have the wrong number of twists so the wrong signaling strip could slide past the pocket without lodging. The fit could work like a key in a lock which means the lizard ribbon structure could respond only to signals from the same kind of structure and could ignore every other strip drifting by.

Traveling: a spiral tail that turns when a signal lodges

A signaling strip lodging in the pocket could release a held tension inside the second lizard ribbon structure and the released tension could set a spiral tail turning. The turning spiral tail could push the lizard ribbon structure forward the way a corkscrew pushes through thick pudding because the pudding-like resistance of flat space gives the spiral tail something to push against.

The lizard ribbon structure might not need to know where the signal came from because the thickness of the cloud of signaling strips can do the steering. A lizard ribbon structure heading toward the source could meet signaling strips more and more often so the spiral tail could keep turning and the lizard ribbon structure could keep going. A lizard ribbon structure heading away from the source could meet signaling strips less and less often so the spiral tail could slow and the lizard ribbon structure could tumble to a new random heading. Repeating the keep-going and tumble behavior many times could carry the lizard ribbon structure up the cloud toward the source which is the same trick a swimming bacterium uses to find food.

Meeting: complementary shapes locking together

The traveling behavior could raise the odds that two lizard ribbon structures of the same kind bump into each other because both structures end up in the thickest part of the cloud. Two lizard ribbon structures that touch could lock together when the outer edges carry complementary shapes which means a ridge on one structure fits a groove on the other structure. A ribbon structure of a different kind could carry edges that do not fit so the mismatched pair could bounce apart and no energy could be wasted on a partner that cannot help make a copy.

Reproducing: pooling spare energy to build a new structure

The locked pair of lizard ribbon structures could then pour spare energy into the space between the two structures and the spare energy could twist nearby flat space and nearby small strips into new ribbon. The shapes of the two locked structures could guide the new ribbon the way a mold guides clay so the new ribbon could fold into a third lizard ribbon structure resembling the two parents. Using two parents as the mold could mix features from both parents which could make each new lizard ribbon structure slightly different from either parent.

The new lizard ribbon structure could break free once the new structure is complete because jostling from surrounding strips could work the new structure loose. The two parent structures could separate with less spare energy than before so the two parents could stop shedding signaling strips until feeding builds the surplus back up.

Why the whole chain could be favored

Every link in the chain could raise the number of copies left behind because feeding could supply the energy and signaling plus traveling could bring matching structures together and locking plus pooling could build the copy. A kind of ribbon structure missing any single link could leave fewer copies so over a long time the kinds of ribbon structures carrying the whole chain could become the common kinds. The slight differences between each new structure and the parents could give natural selection something to work on because a version that feeds or signals or travels a little better could leave a few more copies than the other versions.

The whole picture in one paragraph

Space in the ribbon picture could have begun as a smooth flat sheet under tension and the flat sheet could have been relaxing into twisted ribbons ever since because a twisted ribbon is imagined as a more relaxed shape than a stretched flat sheet. The first Mobius strip could have been the Big Bang itself because the first Mobius strip started the chain in which each Mobius strip catalyzes more Mobius strips. A closed twisted ribbon could be a particle of matter and an open traveling ribbon could be light. The half twist itself could be the electron and the rapid movement of the twist around a spinning Mobius strip could be the electron cloud and a left-handed twist and a right-handed twist could cancel into a plain loop the way an electron and a positron cancel into light. A strip of either handedness can spin in either direction so the handedness could be the electric charge and the literal spinning direction could be the spin of the particle. A left-handed strip and a right-handed strip could be matter and antimatter and the joined strip could collapse and snap open and release light once the two opposite spins cancel because the outward push of the spinning would be gone and the Higgs field would press the loop inward. One ribbon stretched between two places and then pinched into a left-handed strip and a right-handed strip could be the linked pair of particles that physicists call entangled and several ripples stacked on one ribbon could be the many-states-at-once behavior that physicists call superposition. The flat strips of space-time could be the Higgs field and the flat strips flowing inward toward less densely packed crowds of Mobius strips could be gravity. Ripples and hums could travel through flat strips and Mobius strips alike so ribbons humming the same note could be magnetism. A flat strip that bumps or glides against a curved Mobius strip could be bent into a new Mobius strip so every Mobius strip and knot could be a catalyst and a star or a planet could be a Mobius strip factory. Mass could be the squeeze of the inward-flowing Higgs field on loops that cannot merge and new simple Mobius strips flying off as very light fast particles such as neutrinos could relieve the squeeze and leave room for more of the Higgs field to flow in. The spinning of the Mobius strips inside a particle or a knot could add further mass and stability because a spinning bicycle wheel is more difficult to move than a still bicycle wheel. Simple unknotted loops could fill out the unseen part of the universe while braided knots could make atoms and knots fused into one seamless sphere could make a black hole. Complex ribbon structures that happen to protect and copy the structures' own shape could outlast the ribbon structures that do not which is how survival behaviors resembling primitive emotions could arise without life. Every one of the pictures comes from the same act of twisting a flat strip and joining the ends which is why a strip of paper and a piece of tape are enough to start exploring the whole story. The whole universe could be one continuous rippling cloth of space in which matter is space itself tied into loops and knots. A world with depth could be written on two-dimensional strips which is the ribbon picture of the holographic principle.

# Physics ideas from the author's earlier notebook

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 16 November 2026 from a long notebook that the author of this repository typed at different times. Every idea on this page belongs to the author of this repository and the chatbot only sorted the ideas by topic and put the ideas into plain sentences. The page uses no equations and no exact figures. No experiment has tested any idea on this page so each idea is offered as a way of imagining and not as proven physics. Some ideas are earlier or alternative pictures that differ from the main document in this folder and the page says so where that happens.

## How the first Mobius strip could have started

- A very long strip needs almost no twisting to become a Mobius strip because the half twist is spread along the whole length. An extremely long piece of flat space could therefore have shifted by a tiny amount and locked into the first Mobius strip and a huge Mobius strip could look almost like a plain circle with one twist that is barely noticeable.
- Paper shows that a Mobius strip can be easier to make than a plain loop. Two ends laid side by side and each turned a quarter turn join smoothly while a plain loop forces one end to sit on top of the other end. Nature could favor shapes that are easier to make.
- A plain paper loop is stiffer than a paper Mobius strip which bends and adapts more easily so the twisted shape could survive more bumps.
- Joining a strip with a small overlap tucks a little length into the curve so the finished Mobius strip could be slightly shorter than the flat strip that made the Mobius strip. A shorter strip could hold less energy which could be why the twisted shape is favored over flat space. The size of the overlap could be linked to a famous number in physics that sets the strength of the electric force.
- Strings that are shaken at random tie themselves into knots so anything built from Mobius strips could grow more tangled and more complex through random jiggling alone.

## Why light travels and matter stays in place

- Every Mobius strip could be corkscrewing through flat space at the speed of light the whole time. A closed loop turns the corkscrewing into going around and around so the closed loop stays in one spot. A loop that is cut open has the same motion straightened out so the open strip flies off in a line at the speed of light.
- The notebook compares the two cases to the whipping tail of a tiny swimmer and a spinning propeller because the same kind of motion can drive a thing forward or turn a thing in place.
- The motion going around inside a closed loop could act like a gyroscope which is a spinning wheel that resists being tipped. The resistance could be what a person measures as mass.
- The direction that a freed strip travels could be set by the direction the loop was corkscrewing at the moment of the snap. One end of the traveling strip could be slightly rounded by the pudding-like resistance of flat space the way the front of an airplane wing is rounded.
- Nature treats left-handed and right-handed things differently in some experiments. A person who could freeze a traveling strip of light could therefore make a good guess about the direction of travel from the handedness of the corkscrew.
- Light could glide through flat space without stirring flat space so light could make no new Mobius strips. A closed loop stays put and keeps jostling the flat space around the loop so a closed loop could keep making new strips which the main document treats as the source of gravity.
- Bumpy and dense structures could rub against flat space more than smooth structures so bumpy and dense structures could make more new strips and carry more mass.

## Light and heat and glue

- Light could bud off from the surface of a Mobius strip when a wave on the surface grows too tall the way a drop leaves a splash. The bud could be shaped like an egg or a teardrop. Some structures could reach tall waves more easily which could be why some materials glow more than others.
- The corkscrewing of light could leave ripples in flat space the way a spinning paddle leaves ripples in water. The ripples could be what physicists call the electromagnetic field which is the invisible field that carries electric and magnetic effects.
- A crystal is a solid whose pieces sit in a repeating pattern. A crystal could act like a roller coaster track for light because the lined-up ribbon structures could steer light along set paths which could be why crystals scatter light in exact directions.
- Heat could be the simplest Mobius strips. Complex structures could be unable to feed on heat because heat is too simple to build with.
- Strips could need to meet within certain angles and energies before the strips can join.
- A strip could carry a small hook or spiral at one end that works like glue. The hook could be the ribbon picture of the gluon which is the particle that physicists say holds the inside of a proton together.

## Time

- Time could be change in the makeup of a strip. A traveling strip of light touches nothing and so cannot change. From the point of view of light no time passes and light could seem to arrive the instant light leaves.
- Time could be the equal sign between two snapshots of the universe. One snapshot alone holds no meaning because nothing can be compared. Meaning appears when two snapshots are compared.
- The rules of the universe could work like the equal sign in a sum because the rules take the last snapshot and produce the next snapshot.
- The speed limit of light could be a rule that keeps each snapshot close to the snapshot before. Without the limit each snapshot could differ so wildly from the last that no observer could ever form.
- Turning an object in three dimensions gives a different result when the turns are done in a different order. The need for an order could be one reason the universe needs time.

## Measurement and superposition

- Every strip could be chaotic which means a tiny nudge leads to a large change. Any way of measuring a strip is a nudge. A measurement could therefore change the strip greatly which could be the ribbon picture of what videos call the collapse of the wave function.
- Superposition could be a question mark and not two things at once. A thing in superposition could be waiting for more information before one answer becomes true.
- A word with many meanings gives a picture of superposition. The word takes one meaning only when two people share a context. A sentence with no ending is open in the same way and the ending settles the meaning.
- A Mobius strip has no fixed front or back. The observer could supply the front and the back by choosing where to stand so the answer could depend on the frame of reference of the observer.
- A ball inside a sealed box could be moving or still depending on what the box is compared with. The motion could stay undecided until an observation is made.
- An alternative picture places unobserved light in a rules dimension that has no space. Light could pop into space only when light touches matter. An entangled pair could sit in the same spaceless dimension until measured which could explain the instant link without a stretched ribbon.
- A thing could exist in space only in relation to another thing in space.

## Black holes

- New simple strips made by a black hole could be thrown out from the top and the bottom of the black hole. The thrown strips could curve back around like the lines of a magnetic field. The outflow and return could help explain why many galaxies are flat spirals.
- A black hole could resemble a living thing that eats and expels because a black hole takes in complex knots and gives out simple strips.
- An earlier picture treats a black hole as a ring-shaped Mobius strip with one side nearer to the viewer. The nearer side could look brighter and the spinning and twisting could fling out bright jets. The main document pictures a seamless sphere instead.
- The magnetic field of the Earth has a doughnut shape and the shape could arise from the Earth acting like a rotating Mobius strip.
- A black hole could be invisible because a smooth sphere has no place where one direction of space crosses another. Seeing could require a twist or a crossing because a twist gives texture and context. Light and Mobius strips could be things that cross from one dimension into another.
- A collapsing star could flatten the detail of every strip into one smooth surface. The surface area of the sphere could track how much mass and energy the black hole has swallowed.
- A black hole could be an engine that turns flat space into simple strips and the faint glow called Hawking radiation could be the waste of the engine. Black holes could therefore be makers of dark energy.
- Two black holes that collide could fling huge numbers of strips into space. Gravitational waves which are ripples in space that detectors pick up from such collisions could be those strips flying outward.
- Each black hole could hold a universe inside. A collision of two black holes could resemble the birth of a new universe.
- The edge of a black hole could resemble the edge of a famous fractal which is a shape that shows more detail the closer a person looks. The dark middle of that fractal could stand for things that stay self-contained. An atom could be a small self-contained region that takes in light and gives light back out.

## More on the holographic principle

- The folds of a brain add surface area. A brain could be storing information on a surface the way a black hole could.
- Each human sense could be a flat sensor. The feeling of depth could be rebuilt by the brain from flat inputs. Human experience could therefore be a flat record of a world with depth.
- A flat pattern that changes over time could hold the information of a world with depth because the changes between moments carry the missing direction. The surface of a black hole could store information as such a changing pattern.
- A bumpy ball can be shaped so that the ball rolls along a chosen winding path. The bumps on the surface hold the whole path which is one more case of a surface storing a journey through space.
- Two flat sheets of dots laid over each other at a slight turn show a new large pattern that neither sheet holds alone. Stacked flat layers could create behavior that looks like a new dimension. Physicists found that two sheets of carbon one atom thick conduct electricity with no loss when one sheet is turned by a tiny angle.
- Scientists work out the shape of a crystal in depth from flat patterns of spots which is one more case of flat data describing a world with depth.

## Gravity and dark energy and the growth of space

- Gravity could be like hunger. Matter could eat flat space and turn flat space into strips and give off the simplest strips as heat. A star could take in flat space and send the new strips out as particles and energy.
- Waves on a strip could need extra surface. The need for extra surface could pull on the neighboring space.
- The number that physicists call the cosmological constant describes how fast space stretches. The cosmological constant could be the rate at which matter turns flat space into strips.
- Gravity could measure how much things interact. Dark energy could measure how little things interact. Less interaction could mean more room. The stretching of space could be dark energy minus gravity.
- Space could be made of smallest cells. Each cell could divide like a living cell at a rate set by the dark energy inside the cell.
- Each smallest cell could hold the same share of dark energy and matter. The universe could look even in every direction because every cell started with the same share.
- The beginning of the universe could have been one smallest cell and might not have held all the energy of today.
- The speeding up of the stretching of space could partly be an effect of seeing more of the universe as time passes.
- Short-lived particles that pop out of empty space could add strips and add room. The energy of empty space could be the energy of an almost flat strip at rest.
- The notebook estimates the energy of empty space by starting from the densest energy that physics allows which is the energy packed into one smallest cell. The estimate lands within about ten times of the measured value when the densest energy is divided by the square root of the count of smallest cells in the visible universe across the whole history of the visible universe. The square root appears because random ups and downs spread over many cells grow only as fast as the square root of the count of cells. A published approach that builds space and time from smallest cells predicted the same square root rule years before astronomers measured the speeding up of the stretching of space.
- A container with the air pumped out could hold fewer strips so the denser surroundings press inward. Air could stay near the Earth because the Earth keeps drawing flat space inward.
- The universe might never run down into a cold still end because strips keep making more strips.
- An alternative picture treats dark matter as matter still in superposition and dark energy as energy still in superposition. The main document treats both as simple loops instead.
- The early universe could have been foggy to light until energy was packed into complex structures which cleared paths for light.
- Matter could clump because clumping stores energy. Gravity could store energy one way and the electric force two ways and the strong force three ways.
- A slightly egg-shaped mass could roll through space along a stretched oval path. The notebook asks whether that could be why planets travel in ovals.

## Forces as density of context

- The strength of a force could depend on how much context is packed into how little space.
- The strong force which holds the center of an atom together could be the most context in the least space.
- The electric force could be a middle amount of context in a middle amount of space.
- Gravity could be a little context spread across a great deal of space.
- Dark energy could be context spread too thin to pull anything together.
- A tiny region could be ruled by the strong force and by jitter. A huge region could be ruled by gravity and dark energy. The total could stay the same at every size.
- Storing a great deal of information could need either great complexity or a great deal of room.
- The constant that sets the strength of gravity could measure how strongly matter is tied to the shrinking of space. The speed of light could be the rate at which cause leads to effect. The Planck constant could be the grain size of space.

## A balance of opposites

- Each basic property could run between two opposites that add up to nothing. Examples are space shrinking and space stretching and positive charge and negative charge and spin up and spin down and matter and antimatter.
- Each property could change only in smallest steps which could be why quantum physics deals in fixed amounts.
- The list of known particles could be the names people gave to the different mixes of those properties.
- The universe could hold more matter than antimatter because the first Mobius strip happened to twist one way.

## The same rules in every box

- The speed of light is the same everywhere and every electron matches every other electron. The rules could therefore be identical in every box of space at every size.
- The universe could be a fractal which means the same logic repeats from the smallest scale to the largest scale.
- The existence of an observer shows that the rules of the universe allow observers. Physicists call that line of thought the anthropic principle.

## Complexity and life

- A complex structure could need to keep taking in complexity to hold together and could give off the leftover as heat.
- Living things cannot eat rocks because rocks could be too simple to feed a complex structure.
- The molecule that carries the plans of living things could be a ribbon arrangement that keeps its shape and also found a way to rebuild faster than the arrangement decays.

## What this page leaves out

- Formulas and exact figures stayed out because the page describes each idea in words.
- Ideas about pure mathematics stayed out because the page is about physics.
- Ideas about emotions and consciousness stayed out for the same reason and the later parts of the main document in this folder cover ribbon pictures of emotions.

# Packing test: how much room do Mobius strips need compared with flat strips and plain loops?

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) ran these computer tests and wrote this page on 14 November 2026. No other person has rerun the tests which means every number on this page is unconfirmed.

## The prediction being tested

The author of this repository predicted that Mobius strips are fluffy which means that a pile of Mobius strips needs more room than a pile of flat strips. The reason offered was that the half twist makes a Mobius strip bump into neighbors more readily. The prediction matters for the ribbon picture in this folder because flat pieces of space turning into twisted loops could then need more room.

## The six shapes

Every shape was made from the same strip which means the same length and the same width and the same thickness. Every shape was rigid so no shape could bend or be pressed flat.

- A straight flat strip.
- A flat ring like a washer.
- An untwisted loop that looks like an open-ended cylinder.
- A Mobius strip which is a loop with one half twist.
- A loop with two half twists.
- A loop with three half twists.

The strip was about 6.3 units long and 0.5 units wide. The loops were about 2.5 units across.

## Main test: pour and shake in a big bin

The author of this repository pointed out that the first bins were so small that pieces kept getting stuck on the walls. So the test was rerun in a bin 11 units wide which has four times the room of the largest earlier bin. Each run held roughly 850 to 1250 pieces. The packing was measured in the middle of the pile away from the walls and the floor and the top. The numbers are strips per unit of space so a larger number means tighter packing.

- Straight flat strip: 1.59. A time limit stopped the run before the pile was jostled so the true number could be a little higher.
- Untwisted loop like an open-ended cylinder: 0.945
- Mobius strip which has one half twist: 0.940
- Loop with two half twists: 0.900
- Loop with three half twists: 0.792
- Loop with four half twists: 0.766
- Loop with five half twists: 0.696
- Loop with six half twists: 0.674

Mixes with equal numbers of two shapes poured together:

- Mobius strips mixed with untwisted loops: 0.946
- Mobius strips mixed with straight flat strips: 1.10. The middle of that pile held about 70 percent straight strips and 30 percent Mobius strips because the two shapes did not stay evenly mixed.

## An equation for the loops and how the equation did when tested

The first draft equation was fitted to the loops with zero to three half twists. The draft said that the space per strip grows with the cube of the number of half twists. The draft predicted 0.66 for four half twists and the measured value was 0.766. So the first draft failed the test.

The second equation was fitted to the loops with zero to four half twists:

space per strip = 1.02 + 0.07 x (number of half twists)

The packing number is 1 divided by the space per strip. The second equation was then tested on two new runs.

- Five half twists: the equation predicted 0.73 and the measured value was 0.696.
- Six half twists: the equation predicted 0.70 and the measured value was 0.674.

So the second equation landed within about 5 percent on both new runs and predicted slightly tighter packing than was measured. A fit to all seven loops gives space per strip = 1.01 + 0.08 x (number of half twists). So each half twist costs roughly 8 percent more room per strip. The fit is loosest at the start because the first half twist cost almost nothing.

A rule for mixes was also tested. The rule says that the space taken by a mix is the sum of the space each shape takes alone. The rule predicted 0.943 for Mobius strips mixed with untwisted loops and the measured value was 0.946. The rule predicted 1.32 for Mobius strips mixed with straight strips and the measured value was 1.10. So the rule held for two kinds of loop and failed for loops mixed with flat strips.

## Five sizes of one shape in the same bin

This test asks how well a shape lives beside larger and smaller copies of the same shape. Five sizes of one shape were poured into the big bin in equal numbers. The sizes were 0.6 and 0.8 and 1.0 and 1.2 and 1.4 times the usual size and every measurement of a piece including the thickness was scaled together. The result is compared with the room the same pieces would need if each size were kept in a separate pile.

- Untwisted loops in five sizes: about 1 percent tighter than separate piles.
- Mobius strips in five sizes: about 6 percent tighter than separate piles.
- Straight flat strips in five sizes: about 6 percent tighter than separate piles.

So mixing sizes helped a little for every shape because small pieces can settle into gaps between large pieces. The gain for the untwisted loop is small enough to be chance. The Mobius strip and the straight strip gained about the same amount.

The sizes also sorted by height. The smallest pieces ended up lowest in the pile and the largest pieces ended up highest for all three shapes. That sorting happens in many shaken mixtures because small pieces fall through gaps that large pieces cannot pass.

## Ranking from tightest to fluffiest

The number is the amount of strip per unit of space measured in the middle of the pile in the big bin. Runs with five sizes are counted by the amount of strip material so the numbers can be compared.

1. Flat ring: about 1.9. This number comes from the medium bin because the flat ring was not finished in the big bin.
2. Straight flat strips in five sizes: 1.68
3. Straight flat strip in one size: 1.59
4. Mobius strips mixed with straight flat strips: 1.10
5. Mobius strips in five sizes: 0.99
6. Untwisted loops in five sizes: 0.96
7. Mobius strips mixed with untwisted loops: 0.946
8. Untwisted loop: 0.945
9. Mobius strip: 0.940
10. Loop with two half twists: 0.900
11. Loop with three half twists: 0.792
12. Loop with four half twists: 0.766
13. Loop with five half twists: 0.696
14. Loop with six half twists: 0.674

Neat stacking by hand beats every shaken pile for flat pieces because straight flat strips stacked like sheets of paper leave no gaps at all.

## Earlier test: pour and shake in small bins where the walls affected the counts

A physics program dropped pieces at random angles into a square bin under gravity. The program jostled the pile and added more pieces until pieces stuck out above the rim. The count is how much strip sat below the rim in units of whole strips.

Small bin (4 units wide):

- Flat ring: about 96 strips.
- Mobius strip: about 56 strips.
- Untwisted loop: about 52 strips.
- Loop with two half twists: about 48 strips.
- Loop with three half twists: about 47 strips.
- Straight flat strip: about 12 to 16 strips because the strip is longer than the bin is wide so the strips jammed at steep angles.

Medium bin (6 units wide):

- Flat ring: about 413 strips.
- Mobius strip: about 188 strips.
- Untwisted loop: about 176 strips.
- Loop with two half twists: about 165 strips.
- Loop with three half twists: about 152 strips.
- Straight flat strip: about 140 strips. The strip is still slightly longer than the bin is wide so many strips rested at an angle.

Large bin (7 units wide so that a straight strip can lie flat):

- Straight flat strip: about 355 strips.
- Mobius strip: about 299 strips.
- Untwisted loop: about 285 strips.
- Loop with two half twists: about 266 strips.
- Loop with three half twists: about 251 strips.
- The flat ring was not run in the large bin because the run needed more computer time than was available.

## Test 2: orderly stacking

A program looked for the smallest step at which identical copies of one shape can be stacked and then measured how close two stacks can stand.

- Flat pieces stack one thickness apart like sheets of paper.
- Every closed loop needed a step of one full strip width because some part of the ribbon stands edge-on to the stacking direction. The check covered 163 stacking directions.
- The space per piece in the tightest stacks found was 0.20 for the straight strip and 0.37 for the flat ring and 2.08 for the untwisted loop and 2.26 for two half twists and 2.47 for the Mobius strip and 2.56 for three half twists.

## Test 3: random placement with no gravity

A program placed pieces at random spots and random angles in a box and stopped when no more pieces fit. Between 84 and 92 pieces fit for every shape so the six shapes came out the same within the noise of the test.

## Findings

1. Straight flat strips packed tightest among the shapes finished in the big bin. Straight strips fit about 68 percent more strip per unit of space than any plain loop.
2. The Mobius strip and the untwisted loop packed the same away from the walls (0.940 and 0.945). So the prediction that a Mobius strip is fluffier than an untwisted loop was not supported. The small edge that the Mobius strip showed in the small bins looks like an effect of the walls.
3. More twist made loops fluffier in a steady way. Each extra half twist cost roughly 8 percent more room per strip and a loop with six half twists needed about 40 percent more room than an untwisted loop.
4. So the room needed goes up in two steps. Closing a flat strip into a loop costs the most room. Adding twists beyond the first half twist costs more room again.
5. Mixing Mobius strips with untwisted loops changed nothing because the mix packed like either shape alone.
6. Mixing Mobius strips with straight flat strips packed about 17 percent looser than the simple sum rule predicts. Here is a possibility for the cause. Flat strips pack tightly by lying in layers and loops scattered among the strips break up the layers.
7. The two shapes in that mix did not stay evenly mixed because the middle of the pile ended up with more straight strips than Mobius strips.
8. The orderly stacking test ranked the Mobius strip as needing about 19 percent more room than the untwisted loop. Neat stacks and shaken piles are different arrangements so the two tests answer different questions.

## Limits of the tests

- Each run in the big bin was done once so a difference of a few percent between two shapes could be chance.
- The runs with five sizes and the last straight strip run used finer physics steps than the first loop runs which could shift the numbers by a small amount.
- The two straight strip runs reached a time limit before the piles were jostled.
- The flat ring and a flat half ring were not finished in the big bin because flat pieces pack so tightly that the runs needed more computer time than was available.
- Each loop count in the small and medium bins is the mean of two random starts. The counts in the large bin and the flat ring in the medium bin come from one start except for the straight strip which had two starts.
- One run of the straight strip in the medium bin was thrown out because pieces passed through each other in the physics program.
- Jostling raised each count by a few percent. A longer or harder shake could settle the piles further.
- Pieces were rigid. A paper loop can be pressed flat with creases and a pressed loop would pack far tighter.
- The Mobius shape was the standard textbook shape. A relaxed paper Mobius strip settles into a different shape and could pack differently.
- The stacks in test 2 are the tightest found and no proof shows that tighter stacks do not exist.
- A single web search found no published study of packing many Mobius strips together.
- The link from paper-like shapes to space itself is an idea in this folder and the tests measure paper-like shapes alone.

## How to rerun the tests

The programs sit in the folder named packing-test inside the mobius-strip-calculations folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository. The page named README.md in that folder says what each program does.

# The smallest paper Mobius strip is 1.732 times as long as wide

November 12 2026

## The question

The main document in this folder says that "a paper strip that is made too short compared with the width of the strip cannot hold the half twist without tearing or passing through the surface of the same strip". The main document then suggests that a particle made of ribbon "could therefore have a smallest possible size". This page asks how short the strip can get and puts a number on the answer.

## The answer from published mathematics

A smooth paper Mobius strip that does not pass through its own surface has to be more than 1.732 times as long as wide. The number 1.732 is the square root of 3. Mathematicians guessed this limit in 1977 and a full proof was published in January 2025 in a mathematics journal named Annals of Mathematics. The proof is here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12641

The same proof shows what the tightest strip looks like. A strip that gets closer and closer to the limit gets closer and closer to a flat triangle with three equal sides and three layers of paper. The tightest Mobius strip is therefore not a round loop.

## What the computer check confirmed

The chatbot did not check the proof because the proof is advanced mathematics. The chatbot checked the flat triangle with a small program because a flat fold can be checked with simple geometry.

- The program took a strip with a width of 1 and a length of 1.732 and folded the strip flat along three slanted creases. Each crease runs from one long edge to the other long edge at 60 degrees and the three creases form a zigzag.
- The two short ends of the strip landed on exactly the same line with one end flipped (the gap was 0.0). The flipped join is the join that makes a Mobius strip. The unflipped ends missed each other by a full strip width (a gap of 1.0).
- The folding stretched nothing because the distance between nearby points inside each piece changed by less than one part in a thousand million million.
- The folded shape is a triangle with three equal sides. The height of the triangle equals the width of the strip and each side is 1.155 times the width of the strip.

## A paper version to try

A person can cut a strip 10 centimeters wide and 17.3 centimeters long. The first crease runs from the bottom left corner up to the top edge at 60 degrees. The second crease runs from that spot on the top edge down to the bottom edge at 60 degrees. The third crease runs from that spot on the bottom edge up to the top right corner. Folding along the three creases in a zigzag stacks the paper into one triangle and the two short ends then meet along one side of the triangle with one end flipped. Taping the two short ends together makes the triangle Mobius strip. The chatbot did not try the fold with real paper.

## What this could mean for the ribbon picture

The smallest size in the main document now has a number. A ribbon that behaves like paper could not be shorter than 1.732 widths which means a ribbon particle with a fixed width could not shrink below a length of 1.732 widths. The tightest ribbon particle could look like a flat three-layer triangle and not like a round loop.

## What stays unproven

- The limit holds for paper which means a sheet that cannot stretch and cannot pass through its own surface. Nobody knows whether a ribbon of space would follow paper rules and a stretchy ribbon could be made shorter.
- The chatbot checked only the flat triangle and relied on the published proof for the claim that no smooth strip can be shorter.
- No other person has rerun the program which means the numbers from the program are unconfirmed.

## How to check this page

The program is named smallest_paper_strip.py and sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/mobius-strip-calculations in this repository. The program needs only Python with the numpy package.

# Spin rates: how fast a ribbon loop would need to circulate for each mass

November 15 2026

## The question

The main document in this folder says that mass could have two sources which are the squeeze of the inward-flowing Higgs field and the spinning of the Mobius strips inside a particle or a knot. This page puts rough numbers on the spinning source. The page asks how many laps each second a ribbon would need to make around a loop for the energy of the motion to equal the measured mass of a particle. The page then asks whether a longer strip that holds more energy lets atoms of different sizes share one spin rate.

Every number on this page is a sample calculation and is not a test of the ribbon picture because each calculation starts from assumptions that nobody has checked against an experiment.

## How laps each second relate to the speed of light

Every calculation on this page assumes that the ribbon travels around the loop at the speed of light which is about 300 million meters each second. The distance around the loop times the laps each second therefore always equals the speed of light. The lap counts look enormous because the loops are tiny and not because any part of a ribbon moves faster than light.

Light circles the whole Earth about 7.5 times each second because the Earth is about 40 million meters around. A track the size of the core of a hydrogen atom is about 4 followed by 22 zeros times shorter than the Earth is around so the same light-speed traveler finishes about 4 followed by 22 zeros times more laps in the same second.

A ribbon moving slower than light could not do the job on a small loop because a solid hoop as small as the largest size that collision experiments allow for an electron would need an edge speed about 190000 times the speed of light to carry the measured spin of an electron.

## First calculation: all of the mass from spinning

The first calculation gives the ribbon no energy of its own which means all of the mass has to be the energy of the circulating motion. The loop is round and the ribbon moves at the speed of light and the loop carries the amount of spin that experiments measure for these particles which physicists call one half unit of spin. Those assumptions fix the size of the loop and the lap rate with no free choices left.

The rule that falls out is that a heavier particle needs a smaller loop and a faster lap rate because the lap rate grows in direct proportion to the mass.

- Neutrino with an assumed mass of 0.05 electron volts: radius 2.0 x 10^-6 meters and 2.4 x 10^13 laps each second.
- Electron: radius 1.9 x 10^-13 meters and 2.5 x 10^20 laps each second.
- Muon which is a heavier cousin of the electron: radius 9.3 x 10^-16 meters and 5.1 x 10^22 laps each second.
- Proton treated as one loop: radius 1.1 x 10^-16 meters and 4.5 x 10^23 laps each second.
- Tau which is the heaviest cousin of the electron: radius 5.6 x 10^-17 meters and 8.6 x 10^23 laps each second.
- Top quark which is the heaviest known basic particle: radius 5.7 x 10^-19 meters and 8.3 x 10^25 laps each second.

The widest strip that each loop could hold is the distance around the loop divided by 1.732 because the page named smallest-size-finding.md in this folder reports that a paper Mobius strip has to be more than 1.732 times as long as wide. The electron loop could therefore hold a strip up to about 7 x 10^-13 meters wide.

## Where the first calculation meets measured physics

- The two-lap rule lands on a known number. An ant walking along the surface of a Mobius strip needs two laps to return right side up (a whole Mobius strip spun like a top looks the same after one turn so the two laps count travel along the surface and do not count turns of the whole strip) so the full-return rate is half the lap rate. The full-return rate for the electron is 1.24 x 10^20 each second which equals the internal frequency that standard quantum physics assigns to an electron (the mass energy of the electron divided by the quantum constant). The match holds for every mass because the two-lap rule cancels a factor of two in the formula.
- The proton does not fit inside one loop. The measured radius of a proton is about 8.4 x 10^-16 meters which is 8 times the radius of the single loop. The gap could fit the picture of a proton as a knot of several strips because a bundle of strips takes more room than one loop.
- The electron loop is far too wide for collision experiments. Collision experiments find no structure inside the electron down to about 10^-18 meters and the electron loop is about 200000 times wider than 10^-18 meters. The ribbon picture would need a reason why collisions see a point when the loop is so wide. The main document now pictures the electron as the half twist and not as the whole loop which could ease the strain because a twist can sit in a short stretch of a wide loop.

## Second calculation: a longer strip that holds more energy

The second calculation gives every stretch of strip a fixed amount of energy which means a longer strip is a heavier strip. The amount used is a measured number from the strong force which is the force that holds the pieces inside a proton together. The stretched strong-force field between the pieces inside a proton stores about 0.91 billion electron volts for every femtometer of length. A femtometer is a millionth of a billionth of a meter. The mass energy of one proton is about 0.94 billion electron volts so the measured number is roughly one proton of mass for every femtometer of strip.

Strip length needed for the core of each atom:

- Hydrogen: about 1 femtometer.
- Helium: about 4 femtometers.
- Carbon: about 12 femtometers.
- Iron: about 57 femtometers.
- Uranium: about 244 femtometers.

## Three shapes compared

- Shrinking loop with no energy in the strip which is the first calculation: hydrogen needs 4.5 x 10^23 laps each second and uranium needs 1.1 x 10^26 laps each second. Uranium must lap 236 times more often than hydrogen.
- One big open loop of long strip: hydrogen makes 2.9 x 10^23 laps each second and uranium makes 1.2 x 10^21 laps each second. Uranium laps 236 times less often than hydrogen because the speed is capped at the speed of light and the track is longer.
- Long strip coiled around a loop the size of the hydrogen loop like rope wound into a coil: every atom from hydrogen to uranium makes 2.9 x 10^23 laps each second because every turn of the coil is the same size. Uranium is then about 234 turns of the same loop.

The coiled shape is the shape that lets atoms of different sizes share one spin rate because the mass rises with the number of turns while the lap rate stays the same.

## Where the second calculation meets measured physics

- The mass of the core of an atom grows in step with the count of protons and neutrons in the core which matches mass growing in step with strip length.
- The core of every atom has about the same density which fits a fixed amount of strip for each unit of room.
- A real family of heavy short-lived particles shows spin rising with the square of the mass which is the pattern that one spinning stretched strip produces.
- Physicists find that the Higgs field supplies only a small part of the mass of a proton while most of the mass of a proton is the energy of the motion and binding of the pieces inside the proton. That measurement fits a picture in which most of the mass of an atom sits in strip energy and motion.

## Where the second calculation strains

- A coil with every turn circulating the same way would give uranium about 234 times the spin of hydrogen. The measured spin of the common forms of carbon and iron and uranium is zero. The coil would therefore need neighboring turns that circulate in opposite directions so the spins cancel in pairs. Measured protons and neutrons do pair up with opposite spins inside the core of an atom.
- One big open loop fails more strongly. The spin of one big loop grows with the square of the mass and the uranium loop would be about 39 femtometers in radius while the measured core of uranium is about 7.4 femtometers in radius.
- The electron and the muon and the tau carry the same spin at very different masses. A longer strip alone cannot explain those three particles without the same kind of canceling.

## What stays unproven

- Nobody knows whether a ribbon of space carries energy for each unit of length. The second calculation borrowed the measured number from the strong force and a ribbon of space could have a different number.
- The calculations did not include the squeeze of the inward-flowing Higgs field which is the other source of mass in the main document. A share of mass from the squeeze makes the loop wider and the lap rate lower by the same share. A proton with half of the mass from spinning needs a loop twice as wide that laps half as often.
- The way a coil could make neighboring turns circulate in opposite directions is still to be determined.
- The measured values on this page such as the radius of a proton and the size limit for the electron are standard published values that the chatbot recalled and did not look up for this page.
- No other person has rerun the programs which means every number from the programs is unconfirmed.

## How to check this page

The two programs are named spin_rate_for_mass.py and longer_strip_model.py and both programs sit in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/mobius-strip-calculations in this repository. Both programs need only Python.

# Checking the three-dimensions result against published research and three new tests

November 12 2026

## What this page is

The page named half-angle-finding.md in this folder reports that one simple rule about a random arrow matches experiments on entangled pairs only when space has three dimensions. That page also says the chatbot never searched published research. This page reports that search and reports three new computer tests of the same rule.

Entangled pairs are two particles created together whose measurement results stay linked after the two particles are carried far apart.

## The rule in one paragraph

The rule uses three arrows because an arrow is the simplest picture of a direction. The twist arrow is the direction of the twist of the far ribbon strip. The detector arrow is the direction the far detector points. The hidden arrow points in an evenly random direction at the moment of measurement. The far strip agrees with the twist arrow when the tip of the hidden arrow sits lower along the detector direction than the tip of the twist arrow sits.

## What published research already contains

The search used a web search tool on 12 November 2026 and the search was short which means published work that the search missed could exist.

- The rule for one particle in three dimensions is already in print because physics papers describe a well-known model of one spinning particle where a hidden arrow is drawn evenly from all directions on a ball and the result depends on which side the hidden arrow falls. Two papers that describe the well-known model are linked in the sources part at the bottom of this page.
- One physics preprint first posted in 2001 and revised in 2024 states the same three-way pattern in the summary at the top of the preprint. The summary says a theory of entangled pairs built on a hidden space would stay under the classical limit with fewer than three dimensions and would match quantum physics with exactly three dimensions and would pass the quantum limit with more than three dimensions.
- The chatbot could not compare the method of the 2001 preprint with the rule on this page because the full text that the chatbot could open did not contain the calculation across dimensions. The method of the 2001 preprint could be the same as the rule on this page or could be different.
- A separate group of published papers reaches the number three by another road because those papers replace the ball of states of one quantum particle with a ball in any count of dimensions and find that entangled pairs exist only when the ball has three dimensions.

Here is a guess about what the search means: the three-way pattern is probably not a new discovery because the summary of the 2001 preprint states the same pattern. The tumbling ribbon picture and the short program could still be useful because any person with Python can rerun the program in under one minute.

## New test 1: exact formulas for the combined test score

Physicists use a combined test score to judge entangled pairs. Any rule where the results are set in advance cannot score above 2 and quantum physics cannot score above 2.828 and experiments agree with 2.828.

The earlier page gave the scores as rounded numbers from a computer. This page adds exact formulas for four counts of dimensions and the computer numbers match the exact formulas to four decimal places.

- In two dimensions the score is exactly 2.
- In three dimensions the score is exactly 2 times the square root of 2 which is about 2.8284.
- In four dimensions the score is exactly 2 plus 4 divided by pi which is about 3.2732.
- In five dimensions the score is exactly 5 divided by the square root of 2 which is about 3.5355.
- The score keeps climbing toward 4 as dimensions are added because the computer gave 3.9402 in ten dimensions and a number within 0.0001 of 4 in fifty dimensions. The number 4 is the largest score that arithmetic allows for any rule.

## New test 2: the far-end average in every count of dimensions

The earlier page checked only in three dimensions that no message can be sent. This page ran two million simulated pairs for each of five detector angles in two and three and four and five and six dimensions.

The average result at the far end stayed within 0.003 of zero in every run. The far-end average staying at zero means the far person sees an even split no matter where the near person points the near detector. So the rule in four or more dimensions scores above the quantum limit and still sends no message with fully linked pairs.

## New test 3: two mixes with the same average arrow

Quantum physics has a property that could be named arrow averaging. Arrow averaging means that a detector cannot tell apart two different mixes of particles when the two mixes share the same average arrow.

The test built two mixes of twist arrows.

- Mix one has the twist arrow tilted 60 degrees to the left of straight up half of the time and 60 degrees to the right of straight up the other half of the time.
- Mix two has the twist arrow straight up three quarters of the time and straight down one quarter of the time.
- Both mixes have the same average arrow because both averages point straight up with half the full length.

The test then pointed a detector straight up and counted how often the far strip agreed.

- In two dimensions mix one agreed 66.67 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In three dimensions mix one agreed 75 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In four dimensions mix one agreed 80.45 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In five dimensions mix one agreed 84.38 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.
- In ten dimensions mix one agreed 94.13 percent of the time and mix two agreed 75 percent of the time.

A second run with the detector tilted 40 degrees gave the same pattern because the two mixes matched in three dimensions (69.15 percent for both) and differed in every other count of dimensions tested.

Three dimensions is the only count where the two mixes cannot be told apart. The reason is that the agree rate in three dimensions rises in a straight line with the height of the twist arrow and a straight-line rate depends only on the average arrow.

## Why test 3 could matter

The two mixes in test 3 were not picked at random. Quantum physics describes partly linked pairs which means pairs where the two results match more often than chance and less often than always. For one such partly linked pair quantum physics says the far particles form mix two when the near person points the near detector straight up. Quantum physics says the same far particles form mix one when the near person points the near detector sideways.

So here is a possibility worth testing. If the ribbon picture hands partly linked pairs the same arrows that quantum physics hands partly linked pairs then the rule in four dimensions could let the near person send a message faster than light. The near person could send the message by choosing between straight up and sideways and the far person could read the message by counting agreements (about 80 percent against 75 percent). The same reasoning could apply in two dimensions and in five or more dimensions because the two mixes differ there too.

The general idea behind test 3 is already in print. One linked paper in the sources part argues that any rate that is not a straight line lets people signal with linked pairs. The chatbot did not find the specific test with a random arrow in several counts of dimensions in print and the search was short.

Test 3 gives a second and separate reason for the number three. The combined test score says four or more dimensions would disagree with experiments. Test 3 says two dimensions and four or more dimensions could also break the ban on faster-than-light messages for partly linked pairs.

## What stays unproven

- The rule is still an assumption because nothing shows that space is built from ribbons or that a ribbon face tumbles evenly.
- The main document describes only fully linked pairs. Test 3 assumes that the ribbon picture would treat partly linked pairs the way quantum physics does and nobody has worked out whether a ribbon could do that.
- The rule still needs the whole ribbon to respond as one object at the same instant because a proven result in physics says no rule with results set in advance can score above 2.
- No person has rerun the new program which means every number on this page is a single unconfirmed analysis by one AI chatbot.

## How to check this page

The program is named dimension_followup.py and sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/mobius-strip-calculations in this repository. The program needs only Python with the numpy package and prints every number on this page in about one minute.

## Sources

- The 2001 preprint with the three-way pattern in the summary: https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0105020
- A review paper that describes the well-known model of one particle with a hidden arrow on a ball (part 2.6 of the review): https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.03202
- A second paper that describes the same well-known model in a part about one particle: https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.4222
- A paper that finds entangled pairs only when the ball of states has three dimensions: https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4060
- A paper that derives the number of dimensions of space from properties of one quantum particle: https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.0630
- A paper arguing that any rate that is not a straight line lets people signal with linked pairs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12636

# Joining twists: a left-handed and a right-handed Mobius strip cancel while two left-handed strips add

November 15 2026

## The question

The main document in this folder now pictures an electron as the half twist of a Mobius strip. The twist of a left-handed Mobius strip could be an ordinary electron and the twist of a right-handed Mobius strip could be the mirror-image partner of the electron which physicists call a positron. This page asks what happens when two Mobius strips join into one strip. The page compares a left-handed strip joining a right-handed strip with two left-handed strips joining each other.

## How the strips were joined

The computer cut each Mobius strip once across the width and joined the cut ends straight across so the parts became one longer closed band. No extra flip was added at a joint. A joint taped with one end flipped over would add one more half twist and would change every result on this page.

The program built each joined band as points in space and then measured three things. The program checked whether the band has one side or two sides and counted the edges and counted how many times the edges wind through each other.

## Result one: the shape of the joined band

- One left-handed strip alone has 1 half twist and one side and one edge. One right-handed strip alone is the mirror image.
- A left-handed strip joined to a right-handed strip has 0 half twists. The joined band is a plain loop with two sides and two edges and the two edges do not wind through each other at all. The two twists cancel completely.
- A left-handed strip joined to a left-handed strip has 2 half twists which is one full twist. The joined band has two sides and two edges and the two edges wind through each other once. The full twist cannot be removed without a cut because the two edges are linked like two links of a chain.
- A right-handed strip joined to a right-handed strip is the mirror image of two left-handed strips joined.
- Two left-handed strips and one right-handed strip joined together have 1 left-handed half twist. The joined band is a left-handed Mobius strip again because one left twist and the right twist cancel and one left twist is left over.
- Three left-handed strips joined have 3 half twists and one side. Four left-handed strips joined have 4 half twists and two sides.
- Two left-handed strips and two right-handed strips joined have 0 half twists and make a plain loop.

So the joined band is not a mess in either case. The joined band follows one simple rule which is that half twists add like numbers with a plus or minus sign. A left twist counts as minus one and a right twist counts as plus one and the joined band holds the sum.

## Result two: the energy in a simple elastic model

The second test treated the band like a springy rod in which twisting costs energy and bending into a loop costs energy. The twist was free to spread along the joined band. The two starting strips each had a length of 1 and the joined band had a length of 2.

- Left joined to right: the twist energy fell from 9.87 to 0.00 as the two opposite twists spread into each other. All of the twist energy was freed (100 percent). The joined band settled into a plain relaxed loop.
- Left joined to left: the twist energy settled at 9.87 which equals the twist energy of the two separate strips. None of the twist energy was freed (0 percent). One full twist spread over a band of double length stores the same twist energy as two half twists on two bands of single length.
- The bending energy fell by the same amount in both cases (from 39.48 to 9.87) because one large loop is bent more gently than two small loops. Handedness made no difference to the bending energy.

## How the results line up with measured physics

- Twists adding like signed numbers matches electric charge because electric charge also adds like signed numbers and the total electric charge never changes in any measured reaction.
- Left joined to right matches an electron meeting a positron. A real electron and a real positron destroy each other and all of the energy leaves as light. The joined band lost all of the twist and all of the twist energy and the main document pictures an untwisted loop as carrying only ripples.
- Left joined to left matches two electrons. Two real electrons never destroy each other and the total charge stays at two. The joined band kept both twists locked in and freed no twist energy.
- Sides match a known rule about pairs. A band with an odd number of half twists has one side so an ant walking along the surface of the band needs two laps to return right side up. A band with an even number of half twists has two sides so one lap is enough. Real particles follow the same odd and even rule because one electron needs two full turns to look the same while a pair of electrons acting together needs one full turn. Paired electrons acting as one object are what make some metals carry electricity with no resistance at very low temperatures.
- A real electron can also merge with a proton inside the core of some atoms. The merged pair becomes a neutron which has no charge and one very light fast particle called a neutrino flies off. The neutrino flying off echoes the main document where new simple strips leave as very light fast particles.

## Where the results strain

- Two real electrons push each other apart and no particle with the charge of two electrons and the lightness of an electron has ever been found. The ribbon picture would need a reason why two left-handed strips rarely join or why the joined band quickly splits back into two left-handed strips.
- The elastic model is a springy rod and is not a paper ribbon. A real paper ribbon links twisting and bending together so the energy numbers for paper could differ.
- The joining was straight across. Nobody knows whether strips of space would join straight across or with a flip.
- The tests show that the twist counting matches charge counting. The tests do not show why a twist would push or pull on another twist the way electric charges push and pull on each other.

## A paper version to try

A person can make two Mobius strips from paper with one twisted to the left and one twisted to the right. Cutting each strip once across the width and taping the four cut ends into one long loop with no extra flip could give a plain loop with no twist. Doing the same with two left-handed strips could give a loop with one full twist. Cutting the loop with one full twist down the middle could give two loops linked like a chain which shows that the full twist was locked in. The chatbot did not try the paper version with real paper.

## How to check this page

The program is named twist_joining.py and sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/mobius-strip-calculations in this repository. The program needs only Python with the numpy package. No other person has rerun the program which means every number on this page is unconfirmed.

# What happens to a person's story when each listener holds a different pile of pages?

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection. The idea comes from the page named [hiding-a-book.md](hiding-a-book.md) which found that a pile of pages makes far less sense when neighboring pages are kept apart.

Picture a life as a book. A person tells one part of the book to a coworker and a different part to a relative and a third part to a stranger online. Each listener holds a pile of pages. No listener holds the pages that sit next to each other.

The experiment with the dealt book showed something that fits here. A pile of pages is hardest to understand when each page has lost the page that came before and the page that came after. Meaning lives in the connection between neighboring pages.

A life works the same way because a feeling makes sense beside the event that caused the feeling. A coworker who sees a person go quiet has the page about the quiet and lacks the page about the phone call the night before. So the coworker can read the quiet as coldness when the quiet is grief.

Many people deal their pages out on purpose because handing one person the whole book feels risky. A person who holds the whole book could judge the whole book. Spreading the pages keeps any one listener from knowing too much.

That safety has a cost because a person whose pages are scattered is known in pieces and understood by nobody as a whole. Loneliness can sit inside a crowded life when every person in the crowd holds a different small pile.

So here is the question. Who has been handed enough neighboring pages to follow the story?

A person can start small since nobody has to hand over a whole book at once. Handing one listener two pages that belong together is a start such as "I was quiet today because I got hard news last night". That one pairing of an event with a feeling gives the listener something that makes sense.

Listening carries a matching act of care. A listener who hears one page can ask for the page beside that page with a question such as "what happened right before that?" That question tells the speaker that the listener wants the story to connect.

## Quick points

- A person who tells one part of a life to a coworker and another part to a relative and another part to a stranger has dealt the pages of one book into separate piles.
- A pile of pages is hardest to understand when each page has lost the neighboring pages because meaning lives in the connection between pages.
- A coworker who has the page about a person's quiet and lacks the page about the hard phone call can read the quiet as coldness when the quiet is grief.
- Spreading pages across many listeners feels safe and leaves a person known in pieces and understood by nobody as a whole.
- A person can hand one listener two pages that belong together such as "I was quiet today because I got hard news last night" and a listener can ask "what happened right before that?"

# Social media vibes

This folder holds written reflections on subjects such as loneliness and empty advice and loving an enemy and the folder also holds counts of what behaviors the commenters in a social media thread are asking other people to carry out because a count of requested behaviors shows the mood of a thread more clearly than a count of positive and negative words.

## Reflections to read

The 50 pages in this list are written reflections that a visitor can read in a few minutes each and each page can be read alone. The reflections sit inside the [deep-dives](deep-dives) folder.
