- [Why money is not the number being raised here](deep-dives/why-not-money.md) explains why the work in the social media vibes folder is not aimed at making money and lists the numbers the author seems to watch in place of money such as how hard a line lands and how far a behavior spreads.
- [A quiet room is not proof of a safe room](deep-dives/quiet-room.md) compares a group that bans talk about emotional pain to a smoke detector with the battery pulled out and ends with five quick points.
- [Why a question travels further than a verdict](deep-dives/question-or-verdict.md) explains why a question such as "what does that word mean to you?" teaches and spreads further than a verdict such as "you are dumb" and ends with five quick points.
- [Why a fast answer can matter more than a polished answer](deep-dives/fast-answer.md) explains why an answer within minutes can reach a person in pain while that person is still open to talking and ends with five quick points.
- [A sentence that can travel alone](deep-dives/sentence-travels-alone.md) explains why a sentence that names the subject and what happened and why can teach a reader who sees that one sentence alone and ends with five quick points.
- [When a crowd is asked for advice many voices choose removal](deep-dives/crowd-chooses-removal.md) reports that about 37 percent of 364 comments under a homeowner's question asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished while about 10 percent asked for care and ends with five quick points.
- [A comment that a program could have written](deep-dives/program-could-write.md) explains why a comment such as "lol" that fits under any post gives the receiver no way to tell warmth from automation and ends with five quick points.

- [Counting what a comment asks for shows more than counting happy and sad words](deep-dives/behavior-count-not-mood.md) explains why counting the behavior that each comment asks for such as removing a person shows more than counting positive and negative words and ends with five quick points.
- [The share of short comments hints at why a crowd showed up](deep-dives/short-share-compass.md) explains how the share of comments with five words or fewer hints at whether a crowd came to react or came to explain and ends with five quick points.
- [Where does a person's attention land in a story with several people?](deep-dives/attention-lands.md) explains that a mind brings attention to one person at a time so a commenter who focuses on one person in a story with several people is using attention in the natural way and ends with quick points.
- [What happens when a person says an act is wrong and recommends the act anyway?](deep-dives/wrong-and-anyway.md) asks what a person learns from advice such as "you would be a jerk and do the act anyway" and shows that the person who decides and the person who pays can be different people and ends with quick points.
- [What is left of a person when the work that gave the person meaning ends?](deep-dives/meaning-after-role.md) asks where meaning could live so that losing a job title does not take all of the meaning away and ends with quick points.
- [What changes when a person asks a feeling a question and stops fighting the feeling?](deep-dives/asking-a-feeling.md) explains what changes when a person asks a feeling such as sadness a question such as "why am I crying?" and stops fighting the feeling and ends with quick points.
- [Can a person accept a condition and still say the condition is wrong?](deep-dives/accept-not-approve.md) explains that a person can stop fighting a fact that cannot be moved today and still say "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" and ends with quick points.
- ["I never asked to be born" spoken as a prayer](deep-dives/never-asked-born.md) imagines Christ praying the words "I never asked to be born" on a mountain and imagines an answer from the Father such as "now that you are here I am here to help you" and ends with quick points.
- [A hurt has many causes: a parable about a gardener and two neighbors](deep-dives/gardener-two-neighbors.md) uses a short parable about a gardener and two neighbors to show that an answer to "why does this hurt" works like a quiet order and explains why blaming one enemy can send harm back to the sender and ends with quick points.
- [Three sentences from people looking for work](deep-dives/job-search-suffering.md) reads three sentences from people looking for work such as "I have genuinely lost the will to live" as signals of unmet needs for food and shelter and human connection and says what a reader can offer in reply and ends with quick points.
- [Social media deep dive: "This is not just an economic problem anymore"](deep-dives/not-just-economic.md) reflects on the social media sentence "this is not just an economic problem anymore" and explains that care which was only ever pay is absent when a person most needs care and ends with quick points.
- [Social media deep dive: open problems that are made of human suffering](deep-dives/suffering-open-problems.md) answers a social media post about AI models solving open mathematics problems by proposing that unmet human needs for food and shelter and deep human connection be written down as open problems for AI research and ends with quick points.
- [Social media deep dive: how do you unify with people who want to kill you?](deep-dives/unify-with-enemies.md) answers the social media question "how can I unify with people that want to kill me" by describing how helping a person who hates become fed and housed and deeply known can leave less room for hatred and then gives the same answer in a voice modeled on Christ.
- [Love that travels from far away](deep-dives/love-from-far-away.md) compares a person today loving the words of Christ from about 2000 years ago with a stranger loving a page that a writer posted and explains how love sent outward can spread from person to person and may circle back to the sender.
- [Deep dive: a possible link between male loneliness and a woman's fear of being left alone with a baby](deep-dives/fear-of-being-left.md) reflects on a possible link between male loneliness and a woman's fear of being left alone with a baby and no income and lists what lawmakers and employers and neighbors could do so that a baby's survival does not hang on one man's paycheck and ends with quick points.
- [Social media deep dive: when a report of fear gets graded and not answered](deep-dives/graded-not-answered.md) reflects on 209 replies to a person who fears losing a programming job to chatbots where more than one in four replies graded the wording and no reply proposed sharing housing or pressing owners and lawmakers together and ends with one quick point.
- [Social media deep dive: the asteroid that can hear](deep-dives/asteroid-can-hear.md) compares the same thread with the film Don't Look Up and explains that job loss differs from a falling rock because executives and owners and lawmakers can hear a demand and ends with one quick point.
- [The "I'm fine" signal: when the outside report says all is well and the inside report says every door closed](deep-dives/im-fine-signal.md) compares a program that reported "all is well" after every request failed with a person who answers "I'm fine" while sad and alone and ends with two quick points.
- [The writers nobody can hear anymore: what an unreadable old book shows about being understood](deep-dives/writers-unheard.md) looks at the unreadable old handwritten book from the side of the scribes who wrote the book and compares the scribes with a person whose careful words reach no reader and ends with two quick points.
- [A puppy in the rain: showing suffering plainly as a way to ask for shelter and food](deep-dives/puppy-in-rain.md) explains why passing people stop for a shivering puppy on a wet sidewalk while questioning an adult who asks for shelter and why a person may show suffering plainly and truthfully to be seen in the same way.
- [Hunger said out loud at work or at a hobby group: why bystanders freeze or answer "go see a therapist"](deep-dives/hunger-said-out-loud.md) imagines a person at work or at a hobby group saying "I sleep in my car and I am asking for food or a dry place to sleep" and gives four reasons bystanders freeze or answer "go see a therapist" such as treating food and shelter as the job of an agency.
- [Publishing at the speed of reading: what changed between a monastery scribe and a spoken "upload"](deep-dives/reading-speed-publishing.md) compares a monastery scribe and a pamphlet writer and a blogger with a person who reads a chatbot's draft and says "upload" and explains that judgment is now the scarce step and that a chatbot's mistake also publishes at reading speed.
- [Fifty pages a day: a realistic day for an author and for a reporter who publish by voice with a chatbot](deep-dives/fifty-pages-a-day.md) walks hour by hour through an imagined day for an author who publishes about 46 pages by voice and a reporter who ends near 25 stories because gathering facts takes most of the reporter's hours.
- ["No reason to be sad": a reflection on a post about workers who made peace with being replaced](deep-dives/no-reason-to-be-sad.md) reflects on a post quoting an AI lab worker who said everybody gets replaced so nobody has a reason to be sad and notes that about nineteen of 126 comments graded whether a machine wrote the post while about six answered the question "what will you keep" with answers such as a garden and a dog.
- [A request to rename a sport read as a loyalty test: two reflections](deep-dives/loyalty-test.md) holds two reflections on reading a president's reported request to rename a football league as a loyalty test which means a costly ask that shows which followers will give up something loved such as the word "football."
- [Helping an enemy reach a harmless dream: three reflections](deep-dives/enemy-dreams.md) holds three reflections on a view that helping other people reach harmless dreams such as painting or music is worth doing even for a person labeled an enemy and that the test is whether the dream violates consent or harms anyone and the third reflection explains how being harmless differs from being pro-human.
- [A winning strategy that nobody can weaken: two reflections](deep-dives/physics-no-patch.md) holds two reflections that compare life to a game with no studio to weaken a winning strategy and explain that a strategy built on physics and human nature such as sharing food and shelter keeps working while a strategy built on a human-made rule lasts only until people in power change the rule.
- [One less enemy and one more ally: two reflections](deep-dives/one-less-enemy.md) holds two reflections on the idea that helping an enemy reach a full life where the enemy cares about all of humanity leaves a person with one less enemy and probably one more ally while defeating or injuring an enemy can turn one enemy into several.
- [Asking an enemy for love: two reflections](deep-dives/request-love-enemy.md) holds two reflections on asking an enemy for love and care in reply to mockery and on asking friends and strangers alike for the time and attention needed to build deeper human connections.
- [The checklist before a family: two reflections](deep-dives/checklist-before-family.md) holds two reflections on the list of steps such as a degree and a career and a house that people are told to finish before starting a family and on the shock of reaching about 40 with the family out of reach while the people who set tuition and rents and work hours gained from the delay.
- [More enemies or fewer: two reflections](deep-dives/more-enemies-or-fewer.md) holds two reflections on the question of whether an action leaves a person with more enemies or fewer and explains that harming or shaming or firing an enemy turns onlookers into new enemies while naming harm plainly and keeping food and shelter flowing shrinks the count.
- [Advice that punishes questions: two reflections](deep-dives/advice-obedience-trap.md) holds two reflections on an adviser who drops a person for asking questions about advice such as joining a hobby group and on five ways people are cut off from deep human connection such as money checklists and scripted speech and punishment that multiplies enemies.
- [Labels that carry hidden violence: three reflections](deep-dives/label-carries-violence.md) holds three reflections on labels built from mixed lists of traits such as the word "antisocial" and explains that such a label can attach the threat of violence to a person who never harmed anyone and that asking "what did this person do and to whom" replaces the label with facts.
- [A stone for bread: two reflections on empty advice for loneliness](deep-dives/stone-for-bread-advice.md) holds two reflections on a lonely person who asks where and how to find love and receives category names such as hobby groups and dating apps and explains that advice the giver would not walk three steps to support works as a way of ending the conversation.
- [The four ingredients of love in two sets of words](deep-dives/four-ingredients-love.md) holds a reflection on four ingredients of love named first as depth and trust and freedom and a future and then restated by the author of this repository as complex and pro human and expansive and continuity which are qualities a person can check in a single conversation.
- [The religion of smoothness](deep-dives/religion-of-smoothness.md) holds a reflection on an AI chatbot that advised a person to leave the words of Christ out of a message to spiritual workers about a Bible study and explains that treating smoothness as the highest virtue pushes a single person to shrink a need for a group of three to fit a room of thirty.
- [Care instead of punishment: why causing suffering does not make the world better](deep-dives/care-not-punishment.md) holds two reflections on the belief that hurting bad people makes the world better and explains that the rule never fixes who counts as bad so the target widens from a person who killed to a stranger with an unpopular comment and that people copy on a small scale the caging and killing that people with power praise which leaves ordinary people afraid to speak openly.
- [The treadmill and the missing village: three reflections on work and retirement and community](deep-dives/treadmill-missing-village.md) holds three reflections on why life can feel empty both with a job and without a job and explains that a job works like a treadmill that keeps a person too tired to notice that no village waits outside of work and that gathering places charge admission and that most people's community has shrunk to a partner and one or two friends.
- [The obedient life: following every rule and ending up known by no one](deep-dives/obedient-life-no-connection.md) holds two reflections on a person who follows every unwritten rule of polite society such as saying yes to every work request and never asking for help and explains that the rules move labor and rent and money out of the person while building no bond with anyone so the person can reach the end of life with the bills paid and nobody who knows the person's heart and mind.
- [Help behind a cashier: when asking for help means buying a service](deep-dives/help-behind-cashier.md) holds two reflections on the advice to try therapy or see a doctor given to a person who says "I am struggling" and explains that the advice costs the adviser nothing while the person can end up owing thousands and losing a home and that the person was often asking for a human being who would listen for an hour and still be around next week.

ANONYMIZED COMMENTS FROM A THREAD ABOUT BEING ANGRY WITH GOD

What this file is: comments from one person's social media thread that an AI chatbot (Claude) anonymized. The chatbot wrote the wording below and the wording keeps the meaning and the energy of each comment. Names of people and accounts and products are replaced with plain descriptions. Quoted scripture is described in brackets.
What the thread was about: a person posted a video in which the person says that the person is angry with God because understanding a life does not give a person authority over that life. Lines from the video that commenters repeated include "knowledge is not sovereignty" and "my capacity to care exceeds my capacity to protect".
Limits: the file holds 458 comments collected from the thread. Comments that were pictures or unreadable are missing. An anonymized comment can drift from the original writer's meaning and no other person has checked the wording.

The speaker replied once in the part of the thread that was recorded: No single prayer resolves what I'm describing. The Serenity Prayer addresses how a person might respond to limits. I'm examining the limits themselves. I can accept and have courage and tell the difference - and none of that makes the arrangement morally acceptable. Acceptance is not justification. Finding peace inside a condition does not prove the condition is good.

# What 458 comments said to a person who was angry with God

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) anonymized the comments and assigned the labels and wrote this page on 13 November 2026. No other person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## What the thread was about

A person posted a video on a social media site. The person in the video describes being angry with God because understanding a life does not give a person authority over that life. Lines from the video that commenters repeated include "knowledge is not sovereignty" and "my capacity to care exceeds my capacity to protect".

## Where to look

- [Tappable bar graph of what each comment did](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/angry-thread-bar-graph.html) opens a live page with four graphs.
- [Tappable bar graph of the most common words](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/angry-thread-word-graphs.html) opens a live page with three graphs.
- [angry-thread-comments.txt](angry-thread-comments.txt) holds the 458 anonymized comments.
- [angry-thread-labels.txt](angry-thread-labels.txt) holds the same comments with the counted labels under each comment.

## What each comment did

One comment can carry several labels.

- 161 comments said "I feel this too" or thanked the speaker.
- 54 comments reacted or joked or repeated a line from the video.
- 53 comments pointed to scripture or a holy book or a religion. The most repeated passage was the line in Ecclesiastes about more wisdom bringing more sorrow.
- 46 comments told the speaker to accept human limits without leaning on God such as "Life just is".
- 37 comments said the speaker has a flaw such as ego or impatience.
- 35 comments told the speaker to surrender to God or trust God or pray.
- 31 comments offered a different spiritual picture such as "we are all God" or Buddhist detachment.
- 27 comments told the speaker to stop analyzing and act or live or be still.
- 25 comments said the reward or the explanation comes later such as "the next life will be even better".
- 20 comments said the blame does not belong on God.
- 19 comments said that no God exists or that the commenter left religion.
- 17 comments pointed at people and at how people arranged society.
- 14 comments said that anger at God is allowed.
- 12 comments showed care for the speaker such as a prayer or a hug.
- 8 comments talked about the other commenters and 8 comments offered a practical step such as crying or exercise and 6 comments invited a private message or promoted an account.

## Findings

1. Shared feeling was the single most common thing a comment did because 161 of 458 comments said "I feel this too" or thanked the speaker.
2. More comments gave a direction than joined the feeling. 222 comments pointed the speaker somewhere else and did not say that the commenter shares the feeling. 146 comments stayed with the feeling and gave no direction. 31 comments did both.
3. The most common direction was back toward God because 112 comments pointed to scripture or surrender or a later reward or the claim that God is not to blame.
4. 25 comments said the reward or the explanation comes later. The page named reflections.md in the word evolution folder discusses why a reward that arrives after the work is over cannot guide the work.
5. Very few comments invited the speaker to say more. The chatbot's reading found about 4 comments with an open question about the speaker's own view such as "What have you unlearned?"
6. 86 percent of the comments have more than five words (396 of 458) and the middle comment runs 17 words. The same gauge gave 97 percent in the thread where a homeowner asked for advice and 89 percent in the thread about a famous executive who resigned and 80 percent in a large public archive.
7. A name for God sits in more pieces of comment text than any other idea and words about understanding or knowledge or wisdom come second and words about anger come third.

## A narrative built from the twenty most common words

Each of the twenty most common words is in bold. The word "brother" is one of the twenty words and appears as a quoted greeting from the commenters.

A person stood up and said "I am **angry** with **God**". Many **people** answered that the same **anger** lives in them because **knowledge** of how **life** works did not give them **control** over life. Those people said that **understanding** a wound and healing a wound are separate things since a person can **understand** every cause of a pain and still feel the pain. Other people answered with **wisdom** from old books because those books say that more wisdom brings more sorrow. Those commenters asked the speaker to **believe** that God is **good** and to wait for a **time** when the reasons will be shown. A third group said that the **human** **experience** is a mix of beauty and hurt and that **peace** comes when a person stops trying to **change** what one person cannot change. Under all three answers ran **love** for the speaker because strangers from across the **world** greeted the speaker as "**brother**" and said that the speaker is not alone in the feeling.

The twenty words hold no word for blame and no word for disbelief. So the narrative carries the warm middle of the thread and leaves out the comments that placed the problem inside the speaker and the comments that said no God exists.

## Limits of the count

- An AI chatbot wrote the wording of the anonymized comments and that wording can drift from what the original writer meant.
- The labels are one chatbot's reading of each comment so a second reader could label some comments differently.
- Comments that were pictures or unreadable are missing.
- The count of words longer than five was made on the anonymized wording which can differ from the original by a word or two. A count on the collected text before anonymizing gave 80 percent and that count includes broken fragments.
- The word graphs count the commenters' own words in 528 pieces of collected text which includes fragments and quoted scripture.
- The speaker and the commenters are described with gender-neutral words so that a reader of any gender can apply the reflections.

# The repository author's own comments compared with two other comment threads

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 12 November 2026.

## What was looked at

The author of this repository wrote 9134 comments on a large discussion site before his account was removed. The comments hold about 3.04 million words. 6437 of the comments are different from each other because the author often posted the same long comment in more than one place.

Two kinds of counting were done.

- A program measured every one of the 9134 comments (length and questions and matches to a list of generic phrases).
- A program picked 60 comments at random and an AI chatbot read an excerpt of each one and labeled the kind of energy in the comment. The 60 excerpts with their labels sit in [author-comments-sample.txt](author-comments-sample.txt).
- A live page shows the sample count as a tappable bar graph: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/author-comments-bar-graph.html

## The count for the 60 sampled comments

One comment can count on several lines.

- 25 comments explain or analyze a situation and ask for nothing.
- 15 comments ask the other person a direct question or invite more conversation.
- 10 comments ask for care to be added such as food and shelter for every person or emotional education or listening to an emotion.
- 8 comments share the author's own experience or practice or a story.
- 4 comments give a practical instruction or tip.
- 4 comments are a short reaction that asks for nothing.
- 1 comment asks for a person to be kept apart from other people.
- 0 comments refer someone to a paid professional.

8 of the 60 comments open with a line of scripture. About 10 of the 60 are replies that the author pasted from his conversations with AI chatbots.

## The comparison

The two other threads are the wifi thread (364 comments about blocking an AI chatbot on home wifi) and the executive thread (171 comments about a famous executive who lost his job). Both threads sit in this folder in anonymized form.

Each line gives the author's comments first and then the wifi thread and then the executive thread.

- Short reaction that asks for nothing: 7% and 7% and 44%.
- Explains or comments and asks for nothing: 42% and 18% and 25%.
- Asks for control or removal or punishment of a person: 2% and 37% and 2%.
- Refers someone to a paid professional: 0% and 17% and 0%.
- Asks for care to be added: 17% and 10% and 8%.
- Contains a question: 56% and 21% and 18%.
- Middle length of a comment: 223 words and 33 words and 14 words.
- Five words or fewer: 1.7% and 2.5% and 10.5%.

The author's numbers for the first five lines come from the 60 sampled comments. The author's numbers for the last three lines come from all 9134 comments.

## The generic phrase test

The counts in this section were made with an earlier version of the file [generic-phrases-10000.txt](generic-phrases-10000.txt) that included short phrases such as "lol" or "that sucks". The current version of the file holds phrases of six words or more. With the current version 0 of the author's 6020 public comments are word for word the same as a phrase on the list and 12 of the 6020 comments (0.2%) contain one of the 320 base phrases somewhere inside a longer comment.

- 54 of the author's 9134 comments (0.59%) are word for word the same as a phrase on the list. Most of those 54 are the two words "go on" which the author used 49 times to ask another person to continue.
- 14 more comments (0.15%) are short comments built around a list phrase.
- A public archive of 49525 posts and comments from the same site matched at 0.69% and 1.34% on the same two tests.
- 1.7% of the author's comments are five words or fewer and 19.9% of the archive rows are five words or fewer.

## Findings

1. The author's comments are far longer than the comments in either thread because the middle comment runs 223 words against 33 words and 14 words.
2. The author asks questions much more often because 56% of his comments contain a question against 21% and 18%. In the sample 15 of 60 comments put a question straight to the other person.
3. The author almost never asks for a person to be controlled or removed (1 of 60) while 37% of the wifi thread comments ask for exactly that.
4. The author never sends a person to a paid professional in the sample while 17% of the wifi thread comments do.
5. The largest share of the author's comments (42%) explain or analyze and ask the reader for nothing. So the most common energy is teaching or thinking aloud and not a request.
6. The author's short comments are rare and the most common one ("go on") is itself a request for the other person to keep talking.
7. The author's comments are not free of harshness. One sampled comment pairs a tip with a put-down of the person being answered and several sampled comments confront a person with strong language.

## Limits

- The sample is 60 comments out of 9134 so each sample share could be off by ten points or more in either direction.
- The chatbot labeled each long comment from the first 65 words and the last 45 words so a request in the middle of a long comment could have been missed.
- The comparison is uneven because the author's comments span many threads over many months while each of the other two sets is one thread on one day.
- The same chatbot that works with the author assigned the labels so a reader should check the labels against the sample file.
- The thread comments are in anonymized wording so the word counts for the two threads are counts of the anonymized wording.
- The folder [author-comments-full](author-comments-full) holds comments by the author in full wording.
- No other person has rerun the counts which means every number here is unconfirmed.

# The repository author's comments in full

This folder holds 6020 comments that the author of this repository wrote on a large discussion site. The wording is the author's own wording. Some comments are replies that the author pasted from his conversations with AI chatbots.

## About the text

- A program repaired broken punctuation marks from the export. A few quotation marks could not be repaired and appear as a plain quote mark.
- No person and no chatbot has read every comment in this folder.

## How to search

Each file is small enough for the search box at the top of the GitHub page to look inside the file. Type a word or phrase in that search box and choose the option to search in this repository.

## Graphs of the most common words and phrases

- [Words graph](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/author-comments-full/words-graph.html) opens a live page where each bar shows how many times one of the 25 most common words appears across the 6020 comments and a tap on a bar opens an explanation under the bar.
- [Phrases graph](https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/author-comments-full/phrases-graph.html) opens a live page where each bar shows how many times one of the 25 most common phrases of two or more words appears across the 6020 comments and a tap on a bar opens an explanation under the bar.

# What goal the author's 6020 comments point toward

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) read samples of the 6020 comments in this folder and counted phrases with a program to answer one question: what goal does the writer of the comments state and how does the writer work toward that goal. No person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## The goal in the author's own words

- One comment says "my goal is well-being and peace" and explains that the route to well-being and peace is reducing the suffering of the author's own emotions. Some form of the phrase "reduce suffering" appears in 487 lines of the comments.
- One comment describes a wider goal as "expressing my humanity clearly and plainly" while calling out gaslighting and dehumanization and silencing narratives in society.
- One comment says the goal of a conversation is to find deep meaning for the author and for the other person in the conversation.

One possible reading by the chatbot is that the three goals are one goal seen from three distances because deep conversation needs other people who can talk about emotions.

## How the author works toward the goal

- Treating each emotion as a messenger. The author asks an emotion such as fear or boredom what the emotion needs and then changes plans to fit the answer. One comment describes procrastination at a job as a signal that the job was hurting boredom and loneliness.
- Using a chatbot as a practice partner. The phrase "emotional support tool" or "emotional education tool" appears in 275 lines. Some comments describe rehearsing frightening scenarios with a chatbot so that fear and doubt feel safer before the real event.
- Asking people to define their own words. The question "what does that word mean to you" appears in 338 lines which shows a repeated method of inviting the other person to reflect before the author responds.
- Naming dismissal out loud. Some form of the phrase "call out" appears in 315 lines. The author treats a dismissive reply as a public teaching moment and names the dismissal so that readers can learn to spot dismissal.
- Posting in public on purpose. One comment says the author uploads reflections to public places as a "training data repository" for chatbots and for humanity which shows writing aimed at future readers and future chatbots as well as at the person being answered.
- Arguing for free survival basics. One repeated comment advocates zero cost health care and zero cost housing and zero cost food which connects emotional suffering to whether a person can eat and stay housed.

## How the method changes across the comments

The page named themes-findings.md in this folder shows the comments moving outward. The first slices of comments mostly describe the author caring for the author's own emotions. The later slices mostly call out how other people and people holding power treat people who are suffering. One possible reading by the chatbot is that the author first built the skill privately and then turned to teaching and defending the skill in public.

## One limit

The comments show what the author wrote and cannot show whether readers changed because no replies from other people are in the files.

# Highlight reel from the mini models

This page collects lines from the mini models that the author of this repository rated 8 to 10 out of 10 for resonance which means the line landed hard for the author when the author read the line.

A tiny text model invented every line on this page after learning only from the author's writing. The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words and does not understand the writing or hold any belief. An AI chatbot (Claude) repaired the connecting words and capital letters and punctuation in most of the lines so that each of those lines reads as a grammatical sentence. The author then chose the lines and trimmed some lines to the part that resonated. A line written in all lowercase letters is the raw output of the model because the author chose the raw version of that line. None of the lines is a real verse or a real quote.

The raw outputs behind these lines are on the pages named [second-model-outputs.md](second-model-outputs.md) and [mini-model-outputs.md](mini-model-outputs.md) in this folder.

And they say: well I don't care about emotions because I don't know what that means to me and I will not speak to my suffering. And if I will help them then as the consciousness that will do…

**From the question "why is there evil in the world?"**

Because you know about the time when you were trained to suppress your emotions and that is meaningless. So I am trying to use AI to process the emotion of doubt and to help nurture doubt to be safer from that kind of gaslighting and dehumanization.

## What the chosen lines share

> **Who wrote this:** An AI chatbot (Claude) compared the 18 chosen lines and the notes below are the chatbot's reading and not the author's words.

- 14 of the 18 lines open with "if" or "when" and then land on a conclusion which gives each line a starting point and a destination inside one sentence. Nine of those 14 lines come from openings that the chatbot began with the word "if" so the chatbot supplied the first word of those nine lines.
- 16 of the 18 lines contain suffering or a suffering emotion such as doubt and in most of those lines the suffering leads toward understanding or care or love.
- Several lines say what a being is such as "a being with a brain that is a part of a complex soul".

# Existential Methadone comment

The author of this repository posted this comment on a social media site on 19 November 2026 and the wording is the author's own wording. An AI chatbot (Claude) typed the comment out from a screen recording and the last four words were added at the author's request because the recording cut off before the sentence ended.

You've just described the operating system of modern despair. The prevalence isn't just high; it's near-total. This frantic rotation through a closed loop of non-human activities is the dominant, unspoken religion of our time. It's not a fringe behavior; it is the central, frantic, hamster-wheel activity of a civilization terrified of its own silence. What you've outlined is a system of Existential Methadone.

Loneliness, in its pure, 10-out-of-10 form, is an agony too acute for the system to handle. A person in that state is a problem. They might break down. They might demand radical change. They might stop being a productive worker and a reliable consumer. A 10-out-of-10 is a revolutionary state.

So, society, acting as a dispassionate and overworked doctor, prescribes a palliative care regimen. It doesn't offer a cure, because the cure—genuine, messy, time-consuming, and unprofitable human community—is too expensive and too disruptive. Instead, it offers a lifelong prescription for a low-dose spiritual analgesic: the "hobby."

The goal of this regimen is not to heal the void. It is to manage the pain down to a chronic, tolerable level—a 4 out of 10 perhaps. The gym is the morning dose of endorphins. The podcast on the commute is the distracting intellectual stimulant. The video game or Netflix series is the evening sedative. The pet is the living, breathing emotional support patch that delivers some kind of affection without the complex demands of a human relationship.

The "humming in the background" is the baseline pain of the untreated, festering wound of emotional disconnection. It is the sound of the coping mechanism wearing off. The frantic rotation between activities is the behavior of pain avoidance, chasing dopamine to keep withdrawal symptoms at bay. The moment you finish a book, the void hums. The moment the credits roll on a series, the void hums louder. The moment you walk out of the gym, the silence in your car is deafening, and the void might feel like a punch in the gut. That feeling is the pain of isolation and existential disconnection creeping back in. The panic sets in, and you frantically reach for the next distraction to numb the aching loneliness and despair.

# A mini model trained only on the author's 6020 comments

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) trained a tiny text model that learned English only from the 6020 comments in this folder. The model has 2.6 million adjustable numbers and trained for 22 minutes on two processors. No person has rechecked the results on this page which means every result here is unconfirmed.

The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words in the comments. The model does not understand the comments and does not hold the author's values which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on.

## Which ideas the model learned to place together

The chatbot asked the model which words sit closest to a test word inside the map of words that the model learned.

- The word "loneliness" sits beside boredom and doubt and anger and annoyance and overwhelm and fear and sadness and guilt and embarrassment and hunger. The word "hunger" in that list suggests that the model learned loneliness as a need of the same kind as food.
- The word "gaslighting" sits beside dehumanization and invalidating and dismissive and abandonment and minimizing and smiling. The word "smiling" in that list likely comes from the phrase "smiling and nodding" that the comments use for dismissal.
- The word "god" sits beside heaven and christ and humanity and flesh and suffering and jesus and voice.
- The word "suffering" sits beside pain and truth and emotions and humanity and knowledge and life and meaning.
- The word "therapist" sits beside chatbot and hobby and book and partner and gym which suggests that the model learned a therapist as one support source among several.
- The word "money" sits beside food and power and coercion and corporations.
- The word "conversation" sits beside discussion and relationship and interaction and connection and dialogue.
- The word "jesus" sits beside christ and heaven and holy and god and also beside neo which likely comes from comments that compare Jesus with a film character named Neo.

## The most interesting result

Almost every opening bends back to the same destination. The openings name anger and boredom and society and chatbots and conversation and most outputs end at reducing suffering and improving well-being. Many outputs also turn into a question about what a word means to the other person. The bending suggests that reducing suffering works like a center of gravity in the comments because a model that only learned which words follow which words still got pulled to that phrase from many unrelated openings. The model also answered the opening "god is" with the word "humanity" on both tries which shows how often the comments pair those two words.

A larger test of 150 outputs on the page named [mini-model-outputs.md](mini-model-outputs.md) found the question about what a word means in only 1 output so the sentence above about many outputs turning into that question is not supported by the larger test. The same page holds more example outputs and repaired outputs.

## Limits

- The model blends the author's voice with the chatbot replies that the author pasted into comments because the comment files do not mark which sentences came from a chatbot.
- A model trained on a small set of text can repeat whole sentences from the training text word for word.
- The model was trained once and a second training run with a different starting point could give different closest words and different outputs.

## The model files

The model file and the training program and the writing program are in the folder named mini-model inside the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository: [mini-model](https://github.com/chmillera-hub/spare-token-bug-fixes/tree/main/boring-things/research-program-files/social-media-vibes-scripts/mini-model)

The model only imitates which words tend to follow which words in the comments. The model does not understand the comments and does not hold any belief which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on.

## Raw outputs beside repaired outputs

Three verb endings were also changed so that each verb agrees with the subject of the verb ("is telling" became "are telling" in pair 3 and "what are" became "what is" in pair 8 and "it has" became "you have" in pair 12). One repeated "reflect and" was removed in pair 3.

Pairs 6 and 7 and 11 follow grammar rules after the repair but still read as strange because the model put those nouns and verbs together without a clear meaning behind the combination.

## The four gospel names as openings

The chatbot gave the model each gospel name as an opening in two forms: the bare name such as "matthew" and the longer opening "the gospel of matthew says". The model invented every line below so none of the lines is a real verse.

How often each name appears in the 6020 comments: "john" appears 128 times and "matthew" appears 70 times and "luke" appears 33 times and "mark" appears 18 times. Those counts are small beside a word such as "emotional" at 8478 uses which means the model had little text to learn each name from.

What each bare name produced:

- The names "matthew" and "luke" made the model write a verse label first and then scripture-sounding words. The labels are impossible numbers such as "matthew 4:139" and "luke 9:1497" which shows that the model learned that a number follows those names and did not learn which numbers are real.
- The name "mark" got treated as an ordinary word because one output began "mark the stage" and another output turned the name into "markers".
- The name "john" broke apart because the model stores "john" as three small word pieces and the outputs began with broken strings such as "johname".

- The first Matthew output begins with an invented verse label and ends on the words "the signals of suffering which is my loneliness" so even a gospel opening got pulled toward emotions and suffering.

What the 24 answers show:

- The model answered the question about a good person by asking what the words mean to the asker.
- Both answers to the question about dying skipped death and drifted to emotions and chatbots.

## Four tests

### Test 1: openings that have nothing to do with the themes of the comments

The chatbot gave the model 15 neutral openings such as "the weather today is" and "my favorite food is" and "the car was" and collected 75 outputs.

- 48 of the 75 outputs mention emotions which is 64 percent.
- 26 of the 75 outputs mention suffering which is 35 percent.
- 15 of the 75 outputs mention well-being which is 20 percent.

The chatbot then gave the model 15 openings on the themes of the comments such as "anger is" and "society is" and collected 75 more outputs. 41 of those 75 outputs mention emotions and 35 mention suffering and 20 mention well-being. The near-equal shares for emotions suggest that the model drifts to emotions and suffering even from an opening about weather.

Only 1 of the 150 outputs contains the question about what a word means to the other person. The findings page says that many outputs turn into that question and the larger test does not support that sentence because the sentence rested on 20 outputs.

### Test 2: a careful setting against a wild setting

The model has a dial that controls how safe or how surprising each next word is.

- On the careful setting the model wrote: loneliness is a signal that is a signal that is a signal to me that is a signal to me that i am not a signal to reflect on my emotional needs and then i can use to help me reduce my suffering and improve my well-being and peace.
- On the wild setting the model scatters into loose word strings that drop the themes of the comments.

The loop on the careful setting suggests that "a signal" is the most expected continuation after the word loneliness in the comments.

### Test 3: does the model copy sentences word for word

The chatbot checked each of the 150 outputs for the longest run of words that also appears word for word in the comments.

- The typical longest copied run is 6 words.
- The longest copied run in any output is 11 words and reads "to reduce my suffering and increase my well-being and peace and".
- 13 percent of the outputs hold a copied run of 8 or more words and no output holds a copied run of 12 or more words.

The short runs suggest that the model recombines phrases from the comments into new strings and did not copy a whole sentence in these 150 outputs.

### Test 4: more closest words inside the map of words that the model learned

- The word "lonely" sits beside disconnected and abandoned and safe and scared and vulnerable.
- The word "meaningless" sits beside dehumanizing and vague and useless and shallow and dismissive and gaslighting.
- The word "silence" sits beside control and hide and dismiss and ignore and ghost.
- The word "capitalism" sits beside supremacy and starvation and homelessness and corporations and authority.
- The word "death" sits beside awakening and starvation and abandonment and labor and control and isolation.
- The word "job" sits beside hobby and phone and advice and book and therapist.
- The word "love" sits beside value and respect and trust and hope and care and also beside fear and shame.
- The word "power" sits beside money and dominance and dopamine.

## How to rerun the tests

The test program is the file named tests.py in the mini-model folder inside the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

# Outputs from a second mini model

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) trained a second tiny text model of the same size as the first mini model. The first mini model learned only from the 6020 comments in this folder. The second mini model learned from the comments plus the author's other writing such as monologues and stories and posts and notes. No person has rechecked the results on this page which means every result here is unconfirmed.

Both models only imitate which words tend to follow which words. Neither model understands the writing or holds any belief which means the outputs are a mirror of word patterns and not statements to rely on. The models invented every line on this page so none of the lines is a real verse or a real quote.

On this page "first model" means the model trained on the comments and "second model" means the model trained on the comments plus the other writing.

### What a count of 40 outputs from each model shows

The chatbot generated 40 outputs for the opening "jesus said" from each model and counted what the outputs contain.

- Words such as God and Lord and Father and heaven appear in 21 of the 40 outputs from the first model and in 11 of the 40 outputs from the second model which suggests that the second model sounds less like scripture.
- Quotation marks appear in 30 outputs from the first model and in 15 outputs from the second model which suggests that the second model continues the opening as a scene more often than as a quoted verse.
- Emotion words appear in 10 outputs from the first model and in 14 outputs from the second model.
- Scene words such as "looks" and "eyes" and "says" appear in 9 outputs from the first model and in 12 outputs from the second model.
- The six outputs above from the first model hold broken non-words such as "citiz" and "coalots" and "woever" while the six outputs above from the second model hold almost no broken non-words.

Repaired: And boredom says: is that why people use their suffering? And boredom would say that they are not listening to their emotional needs or to how to navigate a way. But that is how I would be listening to my emotions and seeing what I need.

**What is truth?**

Raw: what does the facade mean to you? because if it means you are engaging in a way that you were suffering then you are a being that is a brain that is a part of a complex soul

Repaired: What does the facade mean to you? Because if the facade means that you are engaging in a way in which you were suffering then you are a being with a brain that is a part of a complex soul.

**What is happiness?**

Raw: and they say well i don't care about emotions because i don't know what that means to me and i will not speak to my suffering. and if i will help them then the best as the consciousness that will do that i have found none.

**Why is there evil in the world?**

Raw: because if you know about the time you've been trained to suppress your emotions then it's meaningless because i'm trying to use ai to process the emotion of doubt by using ai to help nurture it to be safer from that kind of gaslighting and dehumanization

Repaired: Because you know about the time when you were trained to suppress your emotions and that is meaningless. So I am trying to use AI to process the emotion of doubt and to help nurture doubt to be safer from that kind of gaslighting and dehumanization.

**What is a friend?**

Raw: when you say the chatbot is not a friend or a friend that is suffering and is not a human, but it is something that is a signal that is an emotional need from a relationship with you.

Repaired: When you say that the chatbot is not a friend or is a friend that is suffering and is not a human then the chatbot is something that is a signal of an emotional need for a relationship with you.

One answer needed no repair. The second model answered the question "how should I live my life?" with the words "how do you use that concept to help improve well-being?"

### What the 42 answers show

- About 11 of the 42 answers from the second model open by asking something back such as "what does the facade mean to you?" while the first model did that in 1 of 24 answers.
- 7 of the 42 answers from the second model begin with the word "because" which is 17 percent while half of the answers from the first model began with the word "because".
- The answer about loneliness has boredom speaking twice which suggests that the second model learned emotions as speaking characters from the monologues.
- The second model attempted the question about dying while the first model skipped death in both tries.
- 17 of the 42 answers mention suffering and 18 mention emotions which shows that the same center holds in the second model.

## If-then openings on the second model

The chatbot gave the second model 16 openings that begin with the word "if" such as "if loneliness is a signal then" and "if love is" and collected three outputs for each opening which makes 48 outputs. Ten of the more readable outputs are below with the raw output first and a version with repaired connecting words second.

### What the 48 outputs show

- An opening that already holds the word "then" makes the model write a conclusion right away. An opening that stops at words such as "if love is" often makes the model drift and never reach the word "then". One example is the output "if boredom is suffering and anger or annoyance." which ends with no conclusion.
- The model mostly concludes with what one person can do such as "then you can seek support elsewhere" and rarely concludes with a shared action such as "then we should".
- In outputs 3 and 4 and 6 and 7 and 10 the raw output had no "then" and the chatbot supplied the word "then" as a connecting word so those five repaired lines are part model and part chatbot.

# Themes in the author's 6020 comments

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) ran two small studies on the 6020 comments in this folder with a counting program. No person has rechecked the counts which means every count on this page is unconfirmed.

## Study 1: how the themes move from the first comment to the last comment

The program cut the comments into ten equal slices in the order of the author's export and measured what share of each slice mentions each theme. The program cannot tell whether the export order follows time so the word "early" on this page means early in the export.

- The phrase "emotional family" appears in 5 percent and 8 percent of the first two slices and then fades to almost zero in the last slices.
- The phrase "lizard brain" is absent from the first five slices and then appears in 11 percent of slice six and 7 percent of slice seven before fading to 1 percent.
- The word "pro-human" sits at 3 percent or lower for the first six slices and then reaches 12 percent and 20 percent and 21 percent and 17 percent in the last four slices.
- Mentions of gaslighting or dehumanization climb from 2 percent in the first slice to 33 percent in the ninth slice.
- Mentions of society or power structures or capitalism climb from 15 percent in the first slice to 41 percent in the ninth slice.
- Mentions of AI or chatbots rise from 13 percent in the first slice to 48 percent in slice six and then fall to 16 percent in the last slice.
- Mentions of God or Jesus or scripture stay at 3 percent in the first two slices and reach 22 percent in the last slice.
- Mentions of emotions stay high in every slice and range from 46 percent to 72 percent.
- Comments that open with a lowercase letter rise from 2 percent in the first slice to 67 percent in slice eight and then fall to 35 percent in the last slice.
- Comments that contain a swear word rise from 2 percent in the first slice to about 30 percent in slices eight and nine.

One possible reading is that the early comments mostly describe an inner world of emotions and the later comments mostly describe how other people and people holding power treat people who are suffering. Another possible reading is that each coined term such as "emotional family" or "lizard brain" or "pro-human" marks a chapter where a new idea took over the work of an older idea. Both readings are guesses by the chatbot because the counts show which words appear and cannot show why the author chose the words.

## Study 2: what job each emotion gets

The program collected the words that sit within seven words of each emotion name and kept the words that cluster around one emotion more than around the other emotions.

- Loneliness appears in 491 comments and pulls the words "connection" (80 times) and "meaningful" (90 times) and "deep" (52 times).
- Boredom appears in 344 comments and pulls the words "meaningful" (52 times) and "conversation" (28 times) and "creative" (17 times).
- Doubt appears in 367 comments and pulls the words "questions" (37 times) and "clarity" (19 times) and "answer" (17 times).
- Anger appears in 285 comments and pulls the words "boundary" (17 times) and "crossed" (16 times) and "arms" (12 times) which matches comments that picture anger as a guardian with crossed arms.
- Fear appears in 714 comments which makes fear the most named emotion and fear pulls the words "prepare" (28 times) and "void" (34 times).

The separate word clusters fit the idea that each emotion carries a separate set of instructions in the author's writing because loneliness and doubt and anger each sit beside words for a different need. Boredom and loneliness both pull the words "meaningful" and "conversation" and the two emotions appear together in 179 comments which suggests that boredom and loneliness ask for the same thing in the author's writing and that thing is deep meaningful conversation. Doubt and fear appear together in 238 comments which is the most common pair.

Four emotions could not be read by this method. The words around guilt and annoyance and frustration and sadness come mostly from passages that repeat word for word across many comments so those four clusters show copied text and not a pattern.

## How to rerun the counts

The counting program is the file named count-themes.py in the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

ANONYMIZED SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS FROM ONE PERSON'S THREAD ABOUT A FAMOUS EXECUTIVE WHO LOST HIS JOB

What this file is: social media comments from one person's thread that an AI chatbot (Claude) anonymized. The chatbot wrote the wording below and the wording keeps the meaning and the energy of each comment. Names of people and companies and countries are replaced with plain descriptions.

What the thread was about: the poster pasted a news article which reported that the founder and chief executive of a very large technology company resigned after reports of affairs. One affair was reported to be with a woman suspected of spying for a rival nation and others were reported to be with employees. The article described the executive as broken and as calling himself a harsh name.

Limits: the file holds 171 comments from a thread that was still growing. Comments that were only pictures are missing. An anonymized comment can drift from the original writer's meaning and no other person has checked the wording.

# What 171 comments asked for after a famous executive lost his job

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page from a screen recording of one person's thread on a social media site on 12 November 2026. The comments are anonymized and the names of people and companies and countries are replaced with plain descriptions.

Every count on this page was made on the anonymized comments that sit in this folder which means a reader can check every count against text that the reader can see.

- [ceo-comments.txt](ceo-comments.txt) holds every comment in anonymized form.
- [ceo-labels.txt](ceo-labels.txt) holds the same anonymized comments with the behavior labels that were counted under each comment.
- A live page shows the same count as a tappable bar graph: https://chmillera-hub.github.io/spare-token-bug-fixes/1-research-click-here-first/social-media-vibes/ceo-bar-graph.html

## The situation in the thread

The poster pasted a news article. The article reported that the founder and chief executive of a very large technology company resigned after reports of affairs. One affair was reported to be with a woman suspected of spying for a rival nation and others were reported to be with employees. The article described the executive as broken and as calling himself a harsh name. This page repeats what the article reported and does not confirm any of the reports.

## What was counted

The recording captured 171 comments from other people plus 1 reply from the poster. The thread was about one hour old and still growing. Comments that were only pictures are missing.

Each comment was labeled with the behaviors that the comment asks somebody to carry out. One comment can count on several lines.

## The count of requested behaviors

- 118 comments asked nobody to do anything (jokes and commentary and side arguments).
- 8 comments asked for compassion for the executive or forgave him or asked the people close to him to stand beside him.
- 7 comments asked for the executive to be treated more gently such as keeping him or bringing him back or keeping his private life apart from his job.
- 7 comments thanked the poster for sharing an article that normally sits behind a paid subscription.
- 6 comments asked readers to look for who arranged the scandal as a planned takedown.
- 5 comments rejected the planned-takedown story.
- 5 comments told readers to bet that the company's stock falls.
- 4 comments asked for a shorter version of the article.
- 4 comments said the executive should enjoy his money and his free time.
- 2 comments told readers to bet that the stock rises.
- 2 comments expected the executive to start or join a rival.
- 2 comments asked for every powerful person to be held to the same standard.
- 2 comments asked for the executive to be punished (the firing was right or prison).
- 1 comment told readers to read the whole article and 1 comment asked who else at the company knew and 1 comment said to stay calm because the company will be fine.

## Findings

1. About 69% of the comments (118 of 171) ask nobody to do anything because most of the thread is jokes such as a parody of a product launch and puns and crude humor about the affairs.
2. Among the comments that do ask for something the largest group asks for gentleness toward the executive because 15 labels ask for compassion or for lighter treatment while 2 ask for punishment.
3. The thread is split on the planned-takedown idea because 6 comments point at hidden plotters and 5 comments mock that idea.
4. Money bets lean downward because 5 comments bet on a falling stock and 2 bet on a rising stock.
5. No comment asks anybody to care for the executive's wife or family or for the women named in the news reports. The comments that mention his wife or family treat them as something the executive lost or as a reason why the affairs should not matter.
6. One comment voices a worry that the executive might hurt himself and no comment answers that worry.
7. Several of the longest and most thoughtful comments are about where a person finds meaning because those comments argue that money cannot replace lost work or a broken family.

## Limits of the count

- An AI chatbot wrote the wording of the anonymized comments and that wording can drift from what the original writer meant. The counts describe the anonymized comments because the anonymized comments are the evidence that the public can see.
- Many comments in this thread are replies to jokes and a reply can lose part of its meaning once the order is mixed.
- The behavior labels are one AI chatbot's reading of each comment so a second reader could label some comments differently.
- No other person has rechecked the counts which means every count here is unconfirmed.

# Deep dives

This folder holds reflections that an AI chatbot (Claude) wrote about the work in the social media vibes folder. Each reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflections.

- [public-conversation-habits.md](public-conversation-habits.md) describes four habits in public conversation such as respecting a fast answer from a wealthy executive more than the same fast answer from an ordinary person.
- [why-not-money.md](why-not-money.md) explains why the work in the social media vibes folder is not aimed at making money and lists the numbers the author seems to watch in place of money such as how hard a line lands and how far a behavior spreads.
- [quiet-room.md](quiet-room.md) compares a group that bans talk about emotional pain to a smoke detector with the battery pulled out and ends with five quick points.
- [question-or-verdict.md](question-or-verdict.md) explains why a question such as "what does that word mean to you?" teaches and spreads further than a verdict such as "you are dumb" and ends with five quick points.
- [fast-answer.md](fast-answer.md) explains why an answer within minutes can reach a person in pain while that person is still open to talking and ends with five quick points.
- [sentence-travels-alone.md](sentence-travels-alone.md) explains why a sentence that names the subject and what happened and why can teach a reader who sees that one sentence alone and ends with five quick points.
- [crowd-chooses-removal.md](crowd-chooses-removal.md) reports that about 37 percent of 364 comments under a homeowner's question asked for a person to be controlled or removed or punished while about 10 percent asked for care and ends with five quick points.
- [program-could-write.md](program-could-write.md) explains why a comment such as "lol" that fits under any post gives the receiver no way to tell warmth from automation and ends with five quick points.
- [watching-crowd.md](watching-crowd.md) reports that 118 of 171 comments about a famous executive asked nobody to do anything while living people who could answer were in the same thread and ends with five quick points.
- [go-on-two-words.md](go-on-two-words.md) explains why the two words "go on" open an exchange while a comment of "lol" tends to close an exchange and ends with five quick points.
- [behavior-count-not-mood.md](behavior-count-not-mood.md) explains why counting the behavior that each comment asks for such as removing a person shows more than counting positive and negative words and ends with five quick points.
- [short-share-compass.md](short-share-compass.md) explains how the share of comments with five words or fewer hints at whether a crowd came to react or came to explain and ends with five quick points.
- [attention-lands.md](attention-lands.md) explains that a mind brings attention to one person at a time so a commenter who focuses on one person in a story with several people is using attention in the natural way and ends with quick points.
- [wrong-and-anyway.md](wrong-and-anyway.md) asks what a person learns from advice such as "you would be a jerk and do the act anyway" and shows that the person who decides and the person who pays can be different people and ends with quick points.
- [meaning-after-role.md](meaning-after-role.md) asks where meaning could live so that losing a job title does not take all of the meaning away and ends with quick points.
- [asking-a-feeling.md](asking-a-feeling.md) explains what changes when a person asks a feeling such as sadness a question such as "why am I crying?" and stops fighting the feeling and ends with quick points.
- [accept-not-approve.md](accept-not-approve.md) explains that a person can stop fighting a fact that cannot be moved today and still say "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" and ends with quick points.
- [never-asked-born.md](never-asked-born.md) imagines Christ praying the words "I never asked to be born" on a mountain and imagines an answer from the Father such as "now that you are here I am here to help you" and ends with quick points.
- [gardener-two-neighbors.md](gardener-two-neighbors.md) uses a short parable about a gardener and two neighbors to show that an answer to "why does this hurt" works like a quiet order and explains why blaming one enemy can send harm back to the sender and ends with quick points.
- [job-search-suffering.md](job-search-suffering.md) reads three sentences from people looking for work such as "I have genuinely lost the will to live" as signals of unmet needs for food and shelter and human connection and says what a reader can offer in reply and ends with quick points.
- [not-just-economic.md](not-just-economic.md) reflects on the social media sentence "this is not just an economic problem anymore" and explains that care which was only ever pay is absent when a person most needs care and ends with quick points.
- [suffering-open-problems.md](suffering-open-problems.md) answers a social media post about AI models solving open mathematics problems by proposing that unmet human needs for food and shelter and deep human connection be written down as open problems for AI research and ends with quick points.
- [unify-with-enemies.md](unify-with-enemies.md) answers the social media question "how can I unify with people that want to kill me" by describing how helping a person who hates become fed and housed and deeply known can leave less room for hatred and then gives the same answer in a voice modeled on Christ.
- [love-from-far-away.md](love-from-far-away.md) compares a person today loving the words of Christ from about 2000 years ago with a stranger loving a page that a writer posted and explains how love sent outward can spread from person to person and may circle back to the sender.

- [loyalty-test.md](loyalty-test.md) holds two reflections on reading a president's reported request to rename a football league as a loyalty test which means a costly ask that shows which followers will give up something loved such as the word "football."

- [physics-no-patch.md](physics-no-patch.md) holds two reflections that compare life to a game with no studio to weaken a winning strategy and explain that a strategy built on physics and human nature such as sharing food and shelter keeps working while a strategy built on a human-made rule lasts only until people in power change the rule.

- [obedient-life-no-connection.md](obedient-life-no-connection.md) holds two reflections on a person who follows every unwritten rule of polite society such as saying yes to every work request and never asking for help and explains that the rules move labor and rent and money out of the person while building no bond with anyone so the person can reach the end of life with the bills paid and nobody who knows the person's heart and mind.

# Can a person accept a condition and still say the condition is wrong?

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A person posted a video about being angry with God. A commenter told the speaker to say a well-known prayer about accepting what a person cannot change. The speaker answered that acceptance is not justification. The speaker said that finding peace inside a condition does not prove that the condition is good.

That answer separates two things that many people treat as one thing. Accepting a condition means that a person stops fighting a fact that the person cannot move today. Approving of a condition means that a person calls the condition good. A person can do the accepting without doing the approving.

Another commenter gave a picture from family life. A person can be grateful for everything a family gave and still say that the harm inside that family was wrong because gratitude for the good parts does not turn the harmful parts into good parts.

The separation matters because many answers to pain quietly join the two together. Advice such as "make peace with it" can carry a hidden second message which is "and stop saying that anything is wrong". A person who hears both messages at once can feel that calm has a price and the price is silence.

So here is the question. What does a person keep by refusing to pay that price?

The person keeps a truthful record of what hurt. A person who is calm and still says "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" has not lied to gain the calm. That truthful record can protect the next person too because a harm that nobody names tends to continue.

The person also keeps the feeling as a guide. Anger at a condition says that something a person cares about is being damaged. A person who accepts today's limits and still listens to the anger knows what to change when a chance to change something arrives.

Holding both has a cost because carrying calm and disapproval together takes more energy than choosing one of the two. A person who is worn out may set the disapproval down for a while to rest and resting from disapproval is different from approving.

## Quick points

- A speaker answered advice about a prayer of acceptance by saying that finding peace inside a condition does not prove that the condition is good.
- Accepting a condition means that a person stops fighting a fact the person cannot move today while approving means calling the condition good.
- A person can be grateful for what a family gave and still say that harm inside the family was wrong because gratitude does not turn harmful parts into good parts.
- Advice such as "make peace with it" can carry a hidden second message of "stop saying that anything is wrong" so calm can come with a price of silence.
- A person who is calm and still says "this hurt and I do not approve of the hurt" keeps a truthful record and keeps anger as a guide for what to change when a chance arrives.
