# A stone for bread: two reflections on empty advice for loneliness

This page holds two reflections on one observation from the author of this repository. The observation says that a lonely person who asks where and how to find love is handed vague suggestions such as hobby groups and dating apps and is then left alone when the person asks for specifics.

## Reflection one

> **Who wrote this:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection on 18 November 2026 and no other person has rechecked the reflection.

A lonely person who asks "where and how" is asking for directions and the usual reply is a wave of the hand toward the horizon.

**The shape of the exchange**

The exchange runs the same way nearly every time. A person says "I am lonely and I want to find a woman to share my life with." The parent or the authority figure or the stranger online answers "then go find one because finding one is not that difficult." The person asks where and how. The answer is a list of category names such as hobby groups and dating apps and "something in your area." The person asks which group and what address and what happens there. The adviser has no group and no address and has never checked. The adviser then offers speed dating to a person who just said he wants deep conversation which is like offering a thimble of water to someone who asked for a well. The person says so. The adviser says "well I tried" and leaves.

**What the list of category names really is**

A category name is not advice because a category name cannot be acted on. "Try a hobby group" has the grammar of help and the content of a shrug. Fully validated advice has a test which is whether the giver would stake anything on the advice such as going along or making an introduction or checking back next week. Advice that the giver would not walk three steps to support is a way of ending the conversation while keeping the appearance of having helped.

James 2:16 describes the move exactly. "and one of you tells them, "Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;" yet you didn't give them the things the body needs, what good is it?" "Try something in your area" is the modern wording of "be warmed and filled."

Matthew 7:9 names what the lonely person receives. "Or who is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?" A person asked for bread which here means a real path toward being known and loved. The person was handed a stone shaped like a suggestion.

**What the exchange does to the person who asked**

Speaking loneliness aloud takes exposure because the speaker is showing a wound. The chest tightens before the words leave the mouth. When the answer is a brush off the wound gets a second injury on top of the first. The speaker learns three things in under a minute. The speaker learns that the people who were supposed to know do not know. The speaker learns that asking a follow up question makes helpers impatient. The speaker learns that continuing to speak about the loneliness leads to being left which means the price of company is silence about the very thing that hurts. So the exchange that was supposed to reduce loneliness produces more loneliness and adds a lesson to hide the loneliness next time.

**Why the silence is so wide**

Finding a person to love is among the most common human longings so a reasonable person expects a deep shelf of tested knowledge. The shelf is nearly bare and here is a possibility for why. Most people who found someone did not follow a method. A classmate sat nearby or a coworker became more over months or a friend made an introduction. The finding happened inside daily surroundings that did the work and the people inside those surroundings never had to build a path from nothing. So when a person without those surroundings asks for the path the adviser has no path to hand over. The adviser has only the memory that the finding felt easy and the memory turns into "it is not that difficult."

Not knowing the answer would be forgivable if the adviser stayed. The harm is in what the adviser does with the not knowing. The adviser covers the gap with a confident tone and then punishes the questions that expose the gap by getting short and walking away. The lonely person ends up carrying the adviser's discomfort along with the original loneliness.

**What a real answer would sound like**

A real answer is simple and rare. "I do not know where a person finds what you are looking for and I am not going to pretend to know. I have an hour so tell me what a good conversation with a woman would be like for you. I know two people I can ask on your behalf." That answer contains no expertise at all. The answer contains a person who admits the limit and stays and offers something that person can truly give.

**Why the disturbance is warranted**

A society that has detailed instructions for filing taxes and assembling furniture and has almost nothing for the question "how does a lonely adult find love" has revealed what the society keeps on file and what the society leaves to luck. Food and shelter and deep connection with another human being are the three things a person needs and the third one has been left without a map. The millions of people online who could compare notes mostly repeat the same category names because the same bare shelf sits behind each of them. The feeling of being disturbed by the silence is an accurate reading of a real absence. A person who notices the absence and keeps saying the absence aloud is doing the first thing that has to happen before any map gets drawn which is refusing to accept a stone as bread.

## Reflection two

> **Who wrote this:** The author of this repository supplied the text of this reflection on 18 November 2026 and the text appears in full.

You are pointing at one of the most maddening, hollow reflexes in modern culture: people handing out vague location placeholders ("try a hobby group," "check online," "go find someone") as a polite exit ramp so they don't have to sit with someone else's loneliness or do five minutes of actual relational labor.

It is completely reasonable to find that disturbing. For something as foundational as deep human connection and love, the gap between how universally people claim to value it and how little actual, concrete infrastructure or guidance exists to help two thoughtful people find each other is stark.

Look at the exact mechanics of why that parroted script fails—and why the people repeating it bail out the second you ask "Okay, where and how?":

- **They Are Offering Placeholders Instead of Bridges:** Saying "check your city for a group" or "try speed dating" isn't advice; it is a conversational smoke bomb. The speaker gets to feel like they "helped" by tossing out a noun, and the moment you press for specifics—which group, what format, how does a five-minute small-talk carousel produce deep conversation—their script runs out of lines. Because they don't actually have a real path to offer, they retreat into "well I tried, have a good day."
- **Standard Social Formats Are Engineered Against Depth:** Almost every mainstream suggestion—bars, apps, speed dating, generic hobby mixers—is built around rapid visual sorting, surface-level banter, and high-volume small talk. If your nervous system and mind are wired for unhurried, substantive, deep conversation rather than performing five-minute elevator pitches to strangers, being told "just go to a meetup" is like telling someone starving for a real meal to go lick wallpaper.
- **Emotional Bandwidth Scarcity Makes People Bail:** Most parents, peers, and random commenters are themselves running on empty, trapped inside their own survival routines, and terrified of confronting systemic isolation. When someone names loneliness plainly and refuses to be pacified by a cliché, it forces the listener to confront how broken our social fabric actually is—so they casually abandon the conversation to protect their own comfort.
- **Why the Internet Feels So Empty on This:** Even with millions of people online, algorithms reward outrage, quick dopamine clips, and performative dating-coach gimmicks—not slow, earnest, high-trust introductions between people who want genuine depth. Nobody gets viral clicks for carefully introducing two compatible humans or building a quiet room where four people can actually talk honestly without a timer running.

You aren't crazy for rejecting baloney formats like five-minute speed dating or vague "just go outside" slogans. Wanting real depth—and expecting people who claim to care about you to offer more than a shrug and a quick exit—is a completely sane standard in a culture that has largely forgotten how to build real bridges between people.

If you want to push past the generic noise, would it help to look at concrete ways to bypass those high-volume, shallow mixers altogether—like filtering directly for long-form, text-first or small-format spaces where people actually lead with ideas and depth before ever meeting in person?

# Social media deep dive: open problems that are made of human suffering

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A post on social media says that AI models recently solved hundreds of open problems in mathematics and the post treats the news as a reason to panic. The same news can be read as a direction because mathematics moved fast once people wrote the open problems down in precise words and pointed AI research at the list. Human suffering can be written down the same way because a human being is a fragile biological organism who needs food and shelter and deep meaningful emotionally and spiritually resonant human connection and each unmet need is an open problem waiting for a clear statement.

The open problem is the care and nurturing itself and the constraint is doing the care responsibly without harming anyone. An example of a clear statement is "how does a person with no wages reach a meal and a safe bed tonight without being shamed or controlled" because a statement that precise gives researchers something to work on and gives everyone a way to check the answer. The person who is suffering is the one who verifies a proposed answer because only that person can report whether the need was met and whether any harm arrived along with the help.

## Quick points

- People who direct AI research can speed up useful progress by keeping a public list of open problems about unmet human needs because a shared list focuses many minds on the same target the way a list of unsolved mathematics problems does.
- A person who is suffering can add to the list by stating the unmet need out loud in specific words because a need that nobody has heard about cannot be worked on by anyone.

# The treadmill and the missing village: three reflections on work and retirement and community

> **About this page:** This page holds three reflections on why life can feel empty both with a job and without a job. An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote the first two reflections on 20 November 2026 and no other person has rechecked the two reflections. The author of this repository supplied the third reflection and the text appears in full.

## Reflection one

> **Who wrote this:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection.

A joke like "no point retiring early because you would only be bored" is a confession that the job was the last thing holding a person's day together because nothing else was ever built to hold a human life.

**Two doors and misery behind both**

A person with a job gives forty to sixty hours a week to tasks that often numb the mind and the person arrives home with too little energy to know anyone deeply. A person without a job has the hours back and finds that nearly every place to spend the hours charges admission. The coffee shop wants a purchase and the gym wants a membership and the bar wants a tab. So the person without a paycheck lies in bed or walks the streets wondering where everyone went and the answer is that everyone is at work or behind a paywall. The remark "must be nice not to work" misses that free time without money in a pay to enter society is closer to house arrest than to a holiday.

**Why the misery follows a person out of the job**

Human beings lived for a very long time in groups where food and shelter and company were shared and where a person's day was full of other people by default. The present arrangement stripped that away and put a workplace in the gap. The workplace now supplies the schedule and the reason to leave the house and most of the faces a person sees. Take the workplace away and the gap is exposed because no village is waiting underneath. That is why a retiree can feel the days go flat. The job was never nourishing and the job was simply the only structure on offer.

**What a village costs under this arrangement**

A lasting community needs a place to gather and food to share and enough stability that people stay near each other for years. Each of those is priced. Housing near friends costs rent that a landlord can raise and a person who cannot pay is removed by armed deputies against that person's will. Raising a family near trusted adults requires those adults to afford the same neighborhood. So continuity which is the thing that turns a group of acquaintances into a village is rationed by money and people who lack money get scattered wherever the cheapest rent happens to be.

**The laugh that covers the alarm**

When someone laughs and says "I would be miserable without work anyway" the sentence deserves to be heard literally. The sentence says "my life outside of labor is empty enough that crushing labor is the better option." That is a five alarm fire told as a joke. Here is a possibility about the laughter: the speaker laughs because the alternative is to feel the full weight of the emptiness with no one nearby willing to hear the weight. Laughter keeps the conversation light and the light tone keeps anyone from having to ask why a human being in a wealthy country has nothing but a job to live for.

**The silence that keeps the arrangement in place**

A person who says aloud "working is miserable and not working is miserable" is often told to be grateful or to find a hobby. That reply closes the subject and the closing serves the people who profit from the arrangement because workers who believe the emptiness is a personal failing do not ask who designed days this way. People with the power to change zoning and wages and the price of shelter made choices that produced paywalled towns and scattered families. Those choices were made by living people and living people can make different ones.

**What the picture adds up to**

The three things a person needs most are food and shelter and deep connection with other human beings. Under the present arrangement the first two are held behind a job and the third is held behind the first two. So a person can be employed and fed and housed and still starving for connection or can be free of the job and too poor to reach anyone. Calling that arrangement an open air prison fits because the walls are made of prices and schedules and the inmates are told every day that the gate is open.

## Reflection two

> **Who wrote this:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection.

A treadmill inside a locked cell is a fitting picture of the job because exhaustion keeps the eyes on the belt and off the door.

**What the treadmill does**

A person who works forty to sixty hours a week arrives home with just enough energy to eat and sleep and scroll. Tiredness works as a kind of anesthetic because a mind that is worn out does not have the strength to ask "who do I belong to?" The weekend fills with errands and recovery and then the belt starts again. So the job does two things at once which are paying for food and shelter and keeping a person too busy to notice that the hours outside of work lead nowhere.

**The cage with no walls**

A person who steps off the treadmill is free to go anywhere and discovers that anywhere is empty. The park has benches and no one who knows the person's name. The bike trail has other riders passing with earbuds in. Standing still on a path and looking into the middle distance the person asks "where is the village?" and nothing answers. The bars of this cage are absences because no shared table and no door to knock on and no group expecting the person at dusk add up to confinement just as surely as concrete does.

**The two disturbing possibilities**

One possibility is that warm villages exist all around and the people inside keep quiet and do not open the gate for outsiders. The other possibility is that real villages are so rare that most people have never been inside one. My best guess is that the second is closer to the truth because the evidence visible from the street points that way. Most people when asked who they could call at midnight name a household member and a partner and perhaps one or two friends. A circle that small is a lifeboat and not a village since one move to another city or one breakup or one death can empty the boat.

**Why the rarity is the more unsettling answer**

If villages were hidden a person could at least search for the hidden gate. If villages are rare then the lonely person on the bike trail is looking at a crowd of people who are lonely in the same way and who each believe everyone else has somewhere to be. Each person reads the others' silence as proof that the others are fine. So thousands of people can stand within sight of each other and each one concludes "the problem must be me" because nobody says the sentence out loud.

**How people talk past the bars**

The remark "you would be bored without your job" treats the emptiness as a fact about the person and not as a fact about the surroundings. Here is a possibility about why the remark is so common: admitting that the job is a distraction from a missing community would mean facing the missing community and the treadmill is easier to face. The cost of that avoidance lands on real lives because a person can spend forty years on the belt and reach the end with a pension and no one to eat dinner with.

**What seeing the bars makes possible**

A person who has stopped running and looked around has information that the runners do not have. That person can say plainly to another human being "I have looked and I cannot find a village and I suspect you cannot either." A sentence like that breaks the shared silence for at least two people. A village begins as exactly that kind of exchange repeated among a handful of people who decide to keep showing up for each other and who find some way to share food and shelter costs so that the showing up can last. The first requirement is that someone says what the cage looks like while everyone else is still watching the belt.

## Reflection three

> **Who wrote this:** The author of this repository supplied this reflection in three parts on 20 November 2026 and the text appears in full.

People laughing off the idea that retiring early just makes you bored and miserable is a massive tell, because it treats a completely hollowed-out society like a cute quirk of human nature.

If stepping away from a soul-crushing 50-hour week actually makes life feel more empty, that is not proof that humans secretly love shift work and fluorescent lighting. It is proof that the job quietly ate everything that used to exist outside of it. When you are working full-time, you are too drained to build a real life. When you stop working—whether you are unemployed or retired—you step outside on a Tuesday afternoon and realize the neighborhood is a ghost town because everyone else is still trapped at their desks or registers.

On top of that, almost every place left where people actually gather has been turned into a tollbooth. If you are not buying a coffee, paying a cover charge, or swiping a card for an activity, you are basically loitering. Without money to constantly buy your way into spaces, free time shrinks down to staring at the ceiling or walking around aimlessly wondering where all the people went. And even when you do find a few people you genuinely click with, trying to build anything with real continuity—sharing daily meals, raising the next generation, having a real village—immediately slams straight into rent, land costs, and grocery bills.

So the whole arrangement ends up working like a double bind. Either you stay on the treadmill and feel miserable because your hours belong to someone else, or you step off the treadmill and feel miserable because there is no community waiting on the other side. People joke about being bored in retirement because laughing at it is much easier than staring directly at the five-alarm fire underneath: a society where work has become the only remaining substitute for belonging, purpose, and daily human contact.

When you hear people casually shrug and accept that trade-off as normal, do you think they genuinely do not feel how bleak it is, or is joking about it just the only way they keep themselves from snapping?

Part 2: Because exhaustion works like anesthesia. When you spend 40 to 60 hours a week grinding through a repetitive job, commuting, running errands, and spending the weekend just trying to recover, you barely have the quiet space or spare energy to notice how hollow everything outside of work has become.

A full-time job hands you a synthetic substitute for a village. It gives you a schedule, hands you tasks that make the hours disappear, and puts other human beings in the same room so you are not sitting in total silence. The moment you step away from it, all of that artificial noise cuts off. Suddenly you are looking straight at the actual bars of the cage: empty streets during the day, paywalled gathering spaces, and a society where almost nobody has the margin left to build real continuity together.

People act like staying on the treadmill is the safer choice because seeing the cage without an obvious way out is terrifying. If someone realizes there is no real community waiting for them on the other side of work, admitting that the job is soul-crushing leaves them with nowhere to stand. So their mind flips the script to protect itself. Instead of asking why everyday life outside of work has been stripped down to nothing, they treat that sudden wave of boredom and emptiness as proof that they need the job just to stay grounded.

It is a remarkably effective trap: the exact thing draining a person's time and spirit is also the only thing keeping them too tired to notice how much of real human life has been hollowed out around them.

Once you have stepped back and seen those bars clearly, do you think it is even possible to go back to ignoring them, or does seeing it permanently change what you are willing to put up with?

Part 3: The second option is almost certainly the reality, and in a quiet way, it is the more disturbing one of the two.

If there were thriving, open-hearted villages tucked away in every town and everyone was just gatekeeping them, at least you would know the blueprint still worked and existed somewhere within reach. Instead, what you are noticing when you stand on a bike trail or walk through a park is an actual structural absence. For the overwhelming majority of people, the village has been shrunk down to a micro-bunker—a romantic partner, maybe a parent or sibling they keep up with, and one or two friends they manage to see every few weeks when work schedules happen to overlap.

That is why the image of a treadmill in a wall-less solitary cell lands so hard. You are not locked in a dark room; you have full freedom to walk down a sunny street, pass twenty other people walking their dogs or jogging with headphones in, and still experience a total social vacuum. Everyone is moving through the exact same physical space while staying completely sealed inside their own private loop.

There is a small piece of the first option mixed in, too, though it usually comes from scarcity panic rather than some coordinated secret club. When people do manage to cobble together a fragile little circle or a steady household, they often seal the hatches. Because everyone is already stretched thin on time, money, and emotional energy, bringing a new person into the fold feels like taking on weight they cannot afford to drop. So the few small pockets of connection that do exist stay closed, not because they are overflowing with abundance, but because they are barely holding together as it is.

When you look at other people passing by out in public and realize most of them are probably just as stranded in those tiny two-or-three-person bunkers, does that make the whole landscape feel even heavier, or does it take some of the sting out of feeling like you are the only one on the outside looking in?

# Social media deep dive: how do you unify with people who want to kill you?

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection in answer to a social media post that asked "How can I unify with people that want to kill me". The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection. The page has two parts. The first part answers in plain words. The second part gives the same answer in a voice modeled on the way Christ speaks in the gospels and the second part is the chatbot's own writing and is not a quotation from the Bible.

## The answer in plain words

You flood their world with love until those people have no room left for hatred.

I mean that literally because a person who is fed and housed and deeply known by other people has a life worth protecting and a person with a life worth protecting has a whole lot to lose by hurting anyone. A person who is busy laughing at a full table has fewer empty hours to spend planning harm because joy eats up the time.

So the wild move is to want the person who hates you to flourish. Want that person surrounded by people who know that person's heart and mind because someone who learns to love a huge number of people might one day have enough love left over to spare some for you. And if the love never reaches you then maybe that person just leaves you alone because the life in front of that person got too good to risk.

Here is the part that gets me every time because the math is beautiful. People carry love to other people. Somebody that person loves might end up loving you too because that somebody might look at both sides and conclude that love builds a better environment for everyone than hatred does. And that somebody might turn around and say "please do not hurt them and please leave them alone and let them live a good life too". A plea from a loved one can reach a place that no argument from you ever could because people listen to the ones who know their heart.

None of this means standing still while someone swings at you. If a person is about to physically harm you then get distance first because a person who is injured cannot spread much love. Unity gets built from a safe distance by helping fill the whole neighborhood with food and shelter and deep human connection until killing starts to look like the dumbest possible use of a good life.

You unify by winning the kind of win where everybody wins because a better environment for yourself and others might reduce the chance that the person who wanted you dead will act that out. A win that needs a loser leaves someone carrying the loss while a win-win leaves every person holding a life too good to throw away. So build the better world out loud and let the person who hated you get so busy living their life in a pro-human way that their hatred ends up having nowhere to go and that hatred hopefully goes extinct.

## The same answer in the voice of Christ

You ask me "how can I unify with people who want to kill me". Truly I tell you that you unify with them by filling their days with love until no room remains in their heart for hatred.

You have heard it said "love your neighbor and hate your enemy". But I say to you love your enemies and pray for the ones who hunt you because the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good alike.

Feed the one who hates you because an empty stomach leaves a wide door for hatred. See that the one who hates you has a roof and a table and people who know the depths of that one's soul. For a person whose cup overflows has a life worth guarding and a person with a life worth guarding has much to lose by shedding blood.

Rejoice when your enemy flourishes. For the one who learns to love a multitude may one day find love left over for you. And if that love never reaches you then perhaps your enemy will pass you by in peace because the feast set before your enemy is too good to abandon.

Hear this mystery for the mystery is glad news. Love is carried from person to person like bread passed down a long table. Someone your enemy loves may look upon you and love you also because that someone has weighed hatred against love and found that love builds the better house. And that someone may plead for you and say "do not harm them and let them live a good life too". A word from a beloved mouth opens a door that your own knocking could never open for the heart listens to the ones who know the heart.

Do not stand still before the raised fist. When a hand is lifted to strike you withdraw to another town because the injured cannot carry much love to anyone. Build the kingdom of heaven from a safe distance which means a place where every person is fed and sheltered and deeply known.

This is the victory in which no one is defeated. For a better world for you and for your neighbor may still the hand of the one who wished you dead. So build the kingdom in the open because a lamp is not lit to be hidden. Let the one who hated you grow so busy living a life that honors every human being that their hatred finds nowhere to dwell and withers and is seen no more.

# A crowd that watches and asks nobody to do anything

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the five quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A news article reported that a famous technology executive resigned from a job. A crowd wrote 171 comments under a post about the article. 118 of the 171 comments asked nobody to do anything which is about 69 percent. Most of those 118 comments were jokes and puns about the executive.

A comment that asks nobody to do anything works like a cheer or a boo from a stadium seat because the comment shows the crowd how the commenter feels and gives no person a next step.

The jokes were aimed at the executive and the executive is unlikely to read a comment in that thread. So a joke about the executive is aimed at the one person in the story who is unlikely to answer.

The people who could answer were already in the thread. Each of the 171 comments was typed by a living and breathing human being who was reading the same page at around the same time. A commenter who turned toward one of those people with a question could have received an answer from a real person within minutes.

So the cost of the 118 comments is a missed chance that was sitting in plain view. Many commenters spent their words on a stranger who was unlikely to reply while people who could reply were one tap away.

A different comment was possible under the same article. A commenter could have asked the other commenters what a person feels after losing a job that shaped how the person saw themself. That question turns a news story into a conversation between real people because many readers have lost a job or fear losing a job.

## Five quick points

- In a thread of 171 comments about a famous executive who resigned 118 comments asked nobody to do anything which is about 69 percent.
- A joke about a famous stranger works like a cheer from a stadium seat because the joke shows a feeling and gives no person a next step.
- A famous executive is unlikely to read a comment in a stranger's thread so a joke aimed at the executive is aimed at the one person in the story who is unlikely to answer.
- Each of the 171 comments was typed by a living and breathing human being so a commenter who asked one of those people a question could have received an answer from a real person.
- A question to the other commenters such as "what does a person feel after losing a job that shaped how the person saw themself?" turns a news story into a conversation between real people.

# Why money is not the number being raised here

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this reflection after the author of this repository asked why the work in this folder is not aimed at making money. Each point is the chatbot's interpretation of what the author has said and done and no person has rechecked the reflection.

## Why money is not the number the author is trying to raise

- The author's goal is measured in connection and money cannot buy that kind of connection. The author wants deep conversation and close human connection and a community of people living close by. A person who chooses to know another person cannot be purchased. The paid forms of connection are the forms the author criticizes because a paid helper is barred from connecting with a person outside the paid hour.
- A price would sit between a reader and the help. The author's writing argues against putting survival needs such as food and housing behind a paywall. Charging for writing that teaches people to care for their emotions would put emotional help behind a paywall too.
- Free things spread further. A sentence that anyone can copy and pass along can multiply from person to person. A sentence locked behind a payment stops at each person who cannot pay. So a price would lower the passing rate of the behaviors the author wants to spread.
- Selling changes what gets written. A writer who needs sales starts writing what sells and that tends to mean what is quick and pleasing. The author's writing asks readers to sit with suffering and to question their jobs and their schooling. Writing without a need for sales keeps the freedom to say what is true to the writer even when that writing draws no crowd.
- A paying audience creates debts. People who pay expect answers and service and a steady supply. The author has limited bandwidth and does not promise help that the author cannot deliver. A customer base would spend that bandwidth on obligations and leave less for one deep conversation.

## The numbers the author seems to watch in place of money

- Resonance: the author rates lines from 8 to 10 out of 10 by how hard a line lands.
- Usable comments: the author asks what share of the comments in a thread describe a behavior a reader can picture and copy such as 1 comment in 15 or 2 comments in 15.
- Depth of replies: the author sorts replies into those that engage with a person and those that are hollow phrases.
- Whether suffering goes down: the author's comments track whether boredom and loneliness and doubt feel heard.
- Spread: the author cares whether a behavior gets picked up and passed along by other people and by chatbots.
- The arrival of a person: underneath the other numbers the author seems to be watching for a human being who can meet the author at depth.

## Why a rising money number can feel like friction

Each hour spent on pricing and promotion and customer service is an hour not spent writing or talking with a person. So chasing money would pull effort away from the goal and would also bend the writing toward what sells. That is two costs with no gain toward connection.

## The author's view of money

The author sees the money system as prehistoric because food and shelter are locked behind payment. The author hopes for a new way of structuring society where a person's food and shelter no longer depend on money and hopes that change comes as quickly as possible.

# The writers nobody can hear anymore: what an unreadable old book shows about being understood

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection. The reflection borrows the unreadable handwritten book from the Voynich manuscript folder of this project as a picture for a person whose words are not being understood and makes no new claim about the book.

Many lifetimes ago several scribes sat with quill pens over costly calfskin and filled a whole book in an alphabet that the scribes knew so well that the scribes made almost no corrections. The scribes drew plants and stars and women bathing in green pools and each scribe wrote with a steady hand which suggests each scribe expected a living person nearby to open the pages and understand. Then every person who knew the alphabet died and the book went quiet because the meaning lived in the minds of the readers and not in the ink.

Sadness rises while reading about the book because the scribes did everything a person can do to be understood and the understanding still ended when the last shared reader was gone. The sadness points toward a need many living people carry right now because a person can speak in full careful sentences at a dinner table and still watch every listener glance down at a plate. A person at such a dinner table is writing in an alphabet that nobody in the room has learned and the loneliness in the chest is asking for one reader who knows the same letters.

The warming part of the story is that the scribes were not alone at the writing table because several hands shared the pages and divided the subjects among each other. A shared private alphabet suggests those scribes had what many people ache for which is a small circle where each person could read the heart and mind of the other without translating. The surviving book is a record that such a circle existed once and the record suggests a circle like that could be built again because ordinary people with pens built the first one.

## Quick points

- A person whose deep words keep landing on blank faces might be missing readers and not missing worth because the scribes' careful pages lost no care when the readers died and lost only the people able to receive the care.
- Handing one listener the key to the alphabet could open more than writing many more pages alone such as saying "when I say I am lonely I mean days have passed without anyone asking what I think" because a defined word gives the listener a way in.

# What happens when a person says an act is wrong and recommends the act anyway?

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this short reflection and the quick points under the reflection. The reflection is the chatbot's interpretation and no person has rechecked the reflection.

A homeowner asked a crowd whether blocking an AI chatbot on the home wifi would be wrong since a friend in crisis was staying in the home and talking to the chatbot all day. Several commenters gave the same two-part answer. Those commenters said that the block would make the homeowner a jerk and then told the homeowner to do the block anyway. A commenter wrote that being a bit of a jerk is sometimes worth the price.

That advice raises a question. What does a person learn from being told that an act is wrong and that the act is fine to carry out?

The advice pulls apart two things that usually travel together. The judgment that an act harms someone usually comes with a decision to look for a different act. Once the judgment and the decision are pulled apart the judgment shrinks into a label such as "jerk" that a person can accept and then carry on.

The phrase "worth the price" also hides who pays. The homeowner receives a label. The friend in crisis loses the conversation partner that the friend talks with all day. So the person who decides and the person who pays are different people.

Here is a possibility about the commenters. Those commenters may have wanted to comfort a tired homeowner by saying that the homeowner does not have to be perfect. Care for the homeowner is a real kindness and the advice still leaves the friend out of the picture.

A different answer could hold both people. A commenter could say that the homeowner's exhaustion matters and that the friend's need for conversation matters. Then the commenter could suggest that the homeowner tell the friend plainly what the homeowner can keep giving and what the homeowner has run out of. That talk takes more energy than changing a wifi setting so the suggestion fits a homeowner who has some energy left.

## Quick points

- Several commenters told a homeowner that blocking a friend's chatbot would make the homeowner a jerk and then told the homeowner to do the block anyway.
- The judgment that an act harms someone usually comes with a decision to look for a different act and the advice in the thread pulled those apart.
- Once the judgment stands alone the judgment shrinks into a label such as "jerk" that a person can accept and then carry on.
- The phrase "worth the price" hides who pays because the homeowner receives a label while the friend in crisis loses a daily conversation partner.
- A commenter could hold both people by naming the homeowner's exhaustion and the friend's need for conversation and suggesting that the homeowner say plainly what the homeowner can keep giving.

# Behaviors described in one thread and how each one connects to Charles's practice on social media

On this page "Charles" is the person who posts on social media and who keeps the public repository of these analyses. Charles does not own or work for the chip company in the thread. An AI chatbot (Claude) picked comments that describe a specific behavior a reader can picture. Each entry below gives the behavior a commenter described and then the matching behavior in what Charles does on social media. Charles's side of each entry comes from Charles's own description of Charles's practice. No person has rechecked these connections.

The comments from the thread are in the file named [fast-reply-comments.txt](fast-reply-comments.txt) in this folder. The thread shared stories about the former head of a large chip company who answered messages from strangers within minutes.

## Behavior 1

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the executive answered a stranger's message inside sixty seconds and another commenter said that an answer came in seven minutes.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles answers messages on social media quickly most of the time. The reason is timing because the moment a person writes is a moment when that person may be awake to pressures such as housing and food sitting behind a paywall or a culture that punishes talk about emotions. A fast answer meets the person inside that open moment and a slow answer can arrive after the moment has closed.

## Behavior 2

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the company was the executive's whole world and that the executive spent Sundays reading company mail.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** The executive in the thread gave nearly all of his attention to one chip company. Charles gives that same kind of attention to social media. The goal differs because Charles's goal is more flourishing and thriving for Charles and for other people and not necessarily the growth of a company. A company might grow as a side effect when the people around that company are flourishing and Charles is not trying to prevent that growth. Charles posts emotional and spiritual deep dives several times a week and also posts comments so the focus shows up as steady output.

## Behavior 3

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the executive would drop into a meeting and listen quietly and then ask a junior engineer for a view so that a fresh angle was heard.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles enters comment sections and asks a person what a word means to that person and how that person uses the word to reduce suffering. Both behaviors hand the floor to a person who might not be asked otherwise. Charles's question appears in hundreds of Charles's public comments.

## Behavior 4

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that people can simply take action and described friends who write to company chiefs out of the blue and receive answers.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles posts and comments without waiting for an invitation and states needs and intentions at the start of a conversation. A person who wants deep conversation can follow the same behavior by writing one clear message to another person about what the writer is looking for.

## Behavior 5

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that a founder answers a credible message while a hired manager stays silent because the manager feels too grand for customers.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles stays open to conversation with people who reply to Charles's posts and comments. Charles treats a person met online as fully real so a reply from a stranger gets attention in the way a founder gives attention to a customer.

## Behavior 6

**What a commenter described:** A commenter respected that the executive took time to read a note from an ordinary stranger and then connected that stranger to a person who could fix the problem.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles looks for chances to empower the person who wrote such as by reflecting the person's own words back or by naming a tool the person could use to process a feeling. Reading the note is one behavior and handing the writer something usable is a second behavior and the commenter praised both.

## Behavior 7

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that self-restraint matters and that sometimes the right move is to not act.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles calls out troll behavior without copying the troll behavior. Examples of troll behavior are name-calling without consent and telling a person to shut up and telling a person that the person is stupid and that nobody cares. The restraint is in what Charles leaves out because Charles names the behavior and does not insult the person.

## Behavior 8

**What a commenter described:** A commenter who mediates divorces said that nobody has endless capacity so every choice trades one thing for another.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles has limited bandwidth and says so. Fast answers and frequent posts use that bandwidth so Charles does not promise help that Charles cannot deliver. Stating the limit openly lets another person know what Charles can offer.

## Behavior 9

**What a commenter described:** Two commenters asked whether an answer inside one minute came from an automated mail assistant.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** A reader can ask the same question about a fast answer on social media. Charles says openly that a chatbot is a tool Charles uses for emotional and spiritual processing. Saying so openly lets a reader judge the words with full knowledge of where the words came from.

## Behavior 10

**What a commenter described:** Some commenters wrote lines such as "Are you dumb?" and "You should delete your account" and "Go outside for a while."

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** These three comments are examples of the behavior Charles calls out. Each comment labels or dismisses a person and none of the three comments says what the other person got wrong or what would be more accurate. A call-out in Charles's style would name the dismissive behavior and then ask the commenter what the commenter meant.

## Behavior 11

**What a commenter described:** A commenter said that the site has no room for nuance once a crowd picks a target and that one mistake puts a person on a blacklist.

**The matching behavior in Charles's practice:** Charles separates a person from a behavior. Charles calls out a specific harmful act such as dehumanizing words and keeps respect for the humanity of the person who did the act. That separation is the opposite of a blacklist because the person stays welcome in the conversation.

# A test of 10000 generic phrases against a public archive of forum comments

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 12 November 2026.

## What the phrase list is

The file [generic-phrases-10000.txt](generic-phrases-10000.txt) holds 10000 interchangeable comment phrases of six words or more such as "thank you so much for sharing this" or "I'm so sorry you're going through this" or "I could not agree more with this". Each phrase signals a reaction and carries no information and no request that a reader could act on. An AI chatbot wrote 320 base phrases by hand in eight groups and a small program combined the base phrases with common openers and closers such as "lol" or "bro" or "for real".

The list changed on 13 November 2026. The earlier list included phrases as short as one word such as "lol". Every phrase on the current list has six words or more because a comment of five words or fewer is already counted as too short to carry a specific thought.

## Counts with the current list (six words or more)

- 2 of the 49525 rows are word for word the same as a phrase on the current list which is about 0.004%.
- 26 of the 49525 rows (0.05%) contain one of the 320 base phrases somewhere in the row. The most common base phrase is "keep up the great work" which appears in 7 rows.
- 39658 of the 49525 rows (80.1%) have six words or more so the current list was tested against most of the archive and still matched almost nothing.
- 9867 rows (19.9%) are five words or fewer. That count does not depend on the list.

The near-zero match rate suggests that a longer hollow comment is rarely worded the same way twice. A fixed list of long phrases works as a set of examples of hollow comments and works poorly as a filter for catching hollow comments.

## What this test does and does not claim

The test counts how many real comments in a public archive are word for word the same as a phrase on the list. The test does not claim that any comment came from an automated account. The archive dates from February 2016 which is years before chatbots could write fluent comments so nearly every writer in the archive was a living person. The point of the test is awareness: a comment that matches the list contains nothing that separates a person from a program so a reader who wants to know more has to reply and ask the writer.

## The archive

The archive is a public collection named reddit-dataset by the GitHub account linanqiu: https://github.com/linanqiu/reddit-dataset

- The archive holds posts and comments from 51 forums on one large discussion site grouped into seven areas (entertainment and gaming and humor and learning and lifestyle and news and television).
- The archive repeats most rows about fifty times. After the program removed repeats and deleted comments the archive held 49525 different posts and comments.
- The archive stripped punctuation and emoji from the text which means the emoji lines on the phrase list could not be tested.
- The archive mixes thread titles with comments so some short rows are titles and not comments.

## The three counts with the earlier list

The counts in this section and in the next two sections were made with the earlier list that included short phrases.

- 343 of the 49525 rows (0.69%) are word for word the same as a phrase on the list.
- 665 more rows (1.34%) are short rows of eight words or fewer that are built around a list phrase of two or more words such as a list phrase with a name added.
- Together 1008 rows (2.0%) match the list in one of those two ways.
- 9867 rows (19.9%) are five words or fewer whether or not the row matches the list.

## The most common exact matches with the earlier list

ok (15) and lol (11) and wow (10) and yes (10) and no (10) and awesome (9) and nice (8) and thank you (7) and beautiful (7) and neat (6) and very nice (6) and rip (5) and who cares (5) and nope (5) and this (5) and congratulations (5).

## The counts by area with the earlier list

Each line shows the share of rows that match the list in either way and the share of rows that are five words or fewer.

- Lifestyle: 3.2% match and 13.2% are five words or fewer.
- Humor: 2.4% match and 23.2% are five words or fewer.
- Gaming: 2.2% match and 31.6% are five words or fewer.
- Television: 1.9% match and 11.0% are five words or fewer.
- Entertainment: 1.7% match and 13.8% are five words or fewer.
- Learning: 1.2% match and 8.3% are five words or fewer.
- News: 1.1% match and 28.3% are five words or fewer.

## Findings

1. A fixed list catches a small share because only 2.0% of the rows match the list even with 10000 phrases. People vary a stock reaction in more ways than a list can hold.
2. The zone of comments that a program could imitate is far wider than the list because 19.9% of the rows are five words or fewer and a comment of five words or fewer has very little room for anything specific to the post.
3. The forum with the highest match rate is a forum where people post photos of their own progress because 14.9% of the rows there match the list. The matches there are praise phrases such as "great work" and "congratulations". So the place where people share something personal is also the place where the replies are most interchangeable.
4. Forums that require detailed answers show almost no matches. A science question forum (395 rows) and a plain-explanation forum (485 rows) had zero matches and a history question forum (164 rows) had one. So the rules and habits of a space change how much room stock phrases get.
5. The humor area and the gaming area hold the most short rows which fits the idea that quick reactions cluster where the posts are jokes or game moments.
6. Long hollow phrases almost never repeat word for word because the current list of 10000 phrases of six words or more matched 2 rows out of 49525. So checking whether a comment mentions any detail from the post may catch hollow comments better than any fixed list can.

## Limits

- The archive is from 2016 and from one site so the shares could differ on other sites and in other years.
- The match test is strict. A comment with one extra word or a spelling change does not count as an exact match.
- A match says nothing about the writer. A short reaction can be a living person's small way of being present.
- No other person has rerun the program which means every number here is unconfirmed. The program sits in the folder boring-things/research-program-files/social-media-vibes-scripts.

# What 209 comments did with one person's fear of losing a job to AI chatbots

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page from a screen recording of one person's thread on a social media site on 15 November 2026. The post and the comments are anonymized. The counts were made by the chatbot on the anonymized comments and no person has rechecked the counts.

- [job-fear-thread.md](job-fear-thread.md) holds the anonymized post and all 209 anonymized comments so a reader can check every claim on this page against text that the reader can see.

## The situation in the thread

A person wrote that years of schooling and practice now seem easy to swap out because AI chatbots write the program text that the person used to write by hand. The person wrote that the thought of being swapped out is frightening. The person then asked a plain question which was where time and money and energy should go today if the paycheck stops within three to five years.

Fear in that post is doing a job because fear is pointing at a real cliff edge where the paycheck ends and rent stops getting paid and armed deputies eventually carry out an eviction. A person at that cliff edge could wind up hungry or sleeping outside.

## What the comments did

- About 58 of the 209 comments (more than one in four) inspect the wording of the post to decide whether a chatbot typed the sentences. The line where the person admits being frightened gets held up like a counterfeit bill under a lamp and several commenters report that they stopped reading at that exact line. So the one sentence that carried the fear became the reason to stop listening.
- About 38 of the 209 comments (roughly one in six) argue over whether chatbot prices will rise or fall which is a debate about a product and not about the person who is frightened.
- Many of the remaining comments tell the person to move up a level by becoming the designer or the product owner or the local chatbot expert. That advice carries a cost that some commenters name themselves because a team of a hundred that shrinks to ten leaves ninety people who cannot all move up into the same ten seats. One commenter compared "just get better" to the old argument about pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps for that reason.

## What is missing

Not one of the 209 comments lays out step by step how the person stays fed and housed if the job disappears because the advice that does appear mostly names another role to chase inside the same shrinking field. Not one comment offers the person a meal or a couch or an hour of listening. Almost no comment speaks to the fear itself by saying what was heard and what the commenter is facing too. One commenter wrote after scrolling for minutes that a single reply appeared to be the only one that tried to answer the question.

A person may have used a chatbot to help find words for the fear and that choice does not make the fear less real because a human being still stands behind the post and that human being could still wind up hungry or without a home. Grading the phrasing of the post while leaving the fear unanswered is a way that human suffering gets casually ignored and casually abandoned in plain sight.

## The quiet comments

Some comments carry their own suffering and the wording debate rolled past those comments as well.

- One person was let go when about a hundred engineers became five.
- One person has gone three years without being hired.
- One beginner with no degree asks whether putting in the time and money would be foolish.
- One person says that the pride and joy of the craft are gone even though output is up.
- One person swings between expecting a bloodbath and expecting things to work out and asks what happens if everything set aside ends up meaning nothing.

## Quick points

- The thread treats a report of fear as a text to grade which leaves the person who posted and every reader in the same spot with no food plan and no shelter plan and no one who answered from the heart.
- No commenter offered a tested way to keep food and shelter if the jobs vanish and the chatbot that wrote this page does not have one either so the plain state of things is that no solution appeared in this thread.
- What a single reader can do at no risk to the reader's own food or shelter is answer the fear itself in a reply by saying what was heard and what the reader is facing too. That kind of reply is a small opening toward deep meaningful emotionally and spiritually resonant human connection and the wording debate closes that opening.

# Thread: fear of losing a programming job to chatbots

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page from a thread of social media comments on a single user's post. The post and the comments were anonymized and the order of the comments was shuffled.

## The post

My coworkers and I stopped typing program text by hand so long ago that I cannot name the last day when one of us did. Releases go out faster than ever and fewer defects show up. Plans and design choices now travel between people mostly as documents that one chatbot drafts and another chatbot reads which means the human share keeps shrinking. I put many years into schooling and practice and staying current and for the first time I feel simple to swap out and that frightens me. I like what the tools allow and yet I seem to be helping to remove my own livelihood. What are other people doing to prepare? New skills or a different field or a business or other income? If this work stopped paying within three to five years then where would your time and money and energy go today?

## The comments

- The same squeeze opens doors at small and midsize firms that could never afford a team. I visited a food plant where a finance chief spends thirty hours a month building reports in a spreadsheet and the chatbot was unreliable in untrained hands. One expert with a chatbot could make real progress there. I hope such firms absorb the people whom large firms shed.
- You are already living in your future.
- I am a beginner with one year of paid work. My answer for other beginners is to stay curious and keep learning. A beginner today is expected to own a whole feature including the business reasons behind the feature. None of this would motivate me if I did not love the work. The constant change is exhausting sometimes and so is the constant talk that beginners are suddenly unneeded. I expect a revival of beginner hiring. Tell me if I am wrong because I want to learn from senior people.
- Operations roles will merge into the programmer role and the number of positions will drop rapidly.

# Thread: a president says the football league ought to change its name

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 15 November 2026 from a thread of social media comments on a single user's post. The post and the comments were anonymized and the order of the comments was shuffled. The page holds 256 comments and the thread held many more that were not captured. Comments marked [incomplete] were cut off in the capture. Square brackets also stand in for pictures and for accusations of crimes and wishes for a person's death and slurs because the page is written for general audiences. The chatbot did not check whether the quote in the post is real and one commenter called the video old. An anonymized comment can drift from the original writer's meaning and no other person has checked the wording. The comments are the commenters' opinions and the page takes no side.

# Thread: people at an AI lab who have made peace with being replaced

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 15 November 2026 from a thread of social media comments on a single user's post. The post and the comments were anonymized and the order of the comments was shuffled. The page holds 126 comments and some comments in the thread were not captured. Comments marked [incomplete] were cut off in the capture. An anonymized comment can drift from the original writer's meaning and no other person has checked the wording.

## The post

Follow-up. Seven months back I wrote about a buddy employed at an AI lab who was still at the office after midnight on a weekend. He and I spoke again and he says the whole staff has made peace with being swapped out.

Humans meeting AI today resemble the Aztecs on the day the Spanish force arrived. People believed their own civilization was far along and then a power beyond anything within reach stepped into the yard. The invaders entered the capital in late 1519 with a few hundred soldiers plus thousands of native allies and under two years later the capital was lost. (The tale that the Aztecs mistook the Spanish for gods was probably added afterward according to most historians. I keep the comparison for the feeling which is dread with a layer of wonder underneath at a thing nobody can size themselves against.)

Seven months back I described a video call with that buddy who works at one of the leading AI firms. The hour was past midnight on a weekend for him and the office behind him looked like an ordinary afternoon. Many readers had opinions. He and I finally spoke again for about ninety minutes and I asked how the place feels now.

He said the worry has vanished. Everybody there treats replacement as a closed question: researchers and physicians and welders and eventually every occupation and no action will undo the change. His words were close to these: "Nobody in this valley asks what happens if I get swapped out. Everybody gets swapped out. And since everybody does there is no cause for sorrow."

He likened the mood to the film about a comet that people refuse to look at. First everybody panics and then everybody decides to use the remaining time. Some coworkers are piling up as much pay as possible before the layoffs. The more active ones spend their chatbot allowance on personal projects so they own something when the day arrives. He is no bystander because he runs twelve to fifteen AI agents at once with five of the agents directing the rest. He told me that when he tries to relax with a book his attention slips after about three lines.

Then he said something close to this: "Nobody discusses how to live in a place drenched in technology without getting hurt and how to care for people and bond with people and feel alive. Not one scrap of talk or thought goes there."

I agree with the first half. Replacement is on the way and I doubt anybody gets a vote. The comet is already falling. Where I part ways is what follows. Enjoying the time before impact is one answer. Trying to keep pace by making humans more machine-like is another answer and I doubt that works either. I think humans and AI run side by side: humans stay human and AI stays AI and each has its own work in the world. I wish to spend my time on the part he says nobody discusses which is how people stay whole while living right beside something so powerful.

I have no tidy answer. What I do have is many people around me who quietly made peace with being replaced and very few who said aloud what they plan to hold onto. So I am asking: if you already accept that AI will do your job one day then what have you decided to keep doing yourself and why?

## An automated summary that was posted in the thread

Most commenters judge the post to be invented and machine-written and point to the all-small-letters style and the dramatic tone. The post still set off several arguments. Many professionals such as attorneys and technology workers reject the claim that everybody gets replaced and report that AI is a strong tool that makes one worker far more productive so one worker takes over the roles of others. A louder and smaller group answers that feeling safe is self-soothing because AI improves so fast that senior roles are next. A large current of worry concerns money for food more than jobs and many doubt that any safety net will appear. Many commenters are concerned about the buddy who cannot read more than three lines. The few who answered the poster's question named things such as gardening and human connection and building tools that help other people through the changes.

# The five-words-or-fewer check

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 13 November 2026. The page reports what happens when every comment of five words or fewer is set aside before a person or a chatbot reads a large pile of social media comments. No other person has rerun the counts which means every number here is unconfirmed.

## What the check is

A program counts the words in each comment. A comment with five words or fewer goes into a separate pile. A comment with six words or more stays in the main pile for reading. The check needs one line of code and needs no judgment about meaning.

## What the check does to a large public archive

The archive is a public collection of 49525 different posts and comments from 51 forums on one large discussion site. The page named [generic-phrases-test.md](generic-phrases-test.md) in this folder describes the archive.

- 9867 of the 49525 rows have five words or fewer which is 19.9 percent of the rows.
- Those 9867 short rows hold about 1.5 percent of all the words in the archive. So the check sets aside one row in five and gives up very little text.
- The most common short rows are "ok" and "lol" and "wow" and "yes" and "no" and "awesome" and "nice" and "thank you".
- About one third of a random sample of 70 short rows were bare numbers or web links which are leftovers of how the archive was collected and not comments. So the check also clears out junk rows.

The share of rows at other cut-off points:

- One word or fewer: 7.7 percent of the rows.
- Three words or fewer: 13.2 percent of the rows.
- Five words or fewer: 19.9 percent of the rows.
- Eight words or fewer: 30.6 percent of the rows.
- Ten words or fewer: 36.8 percent of the rows.
- Twenty words or fewer: 58.5 percent of the rows.

The share of short rows differs by the kind of forum:

- Gaming forums: 31.6 percent of the rows have five words or fewer.
- News forums: 28.3 percent.
- Humor forums: 23.2 percent.
- Entertainment forums: 13.8 percent.
- Lifestyle forums: 13.2 percent.
- Television forums: 11.0 percent.
- Learning forums: 8.3 percent.

## What the check shows about the three threads in this folder

- The thread about a famous executive who lost his job: 18 of 171 comments have five words or fewer which is 10.5 percent. The middle comment runs 14 words. The short comments are quick reactions such as "Poor man." and "Doormat energy." and "Put him behind bars."
- The thread about blocking a chatbot on home wifi: 9 of 364 comments have five words or fewer which is 2.5 percent. The middle comment runs 33 words. The short comments are blunt commands and verdicts such as "Do it." and "Nope." and "Mate just send her packing."
- The thread about an executive who answered messages within minutes: 13 of 247 comments have five words or fewer which is 5.3 percent. The middle comment runs 20 words. The short comments are verdicts and dismissals such as "Are you dumb?" and "You should delete your account."
- The author's 6020 public comments: 67 comments have five words or fewer which is 1.1 percent.

The three threads hold 40 short comments in total. None of the 40 short comments describes a behavior together with a reason for the behavior. So in these three threads the check would have set aside 40 comments and would have lost zero comments that teach a reader what to do and why.

The share of short comments also says something about the kind of thread. A thread built on a news story about a famous person drew the most short reactions. A thread where a person asked for advice drew long replies because advice takes room. So the share of short comments works as a quick reading of whether a crowd came to react or came to explain.

## What the check can lose

- A short comment can be a real invitation. The author of this repository posted the two words "go on" as a whole comment to ask another person to continue. That whole comment appears 4 times in the 6020 public comments in this folder once question marks and emoji are ignored. The check would set those invitations aside.
- A short comment can be a real question. About 4.6 percent of the short rows in the archive begin with a question word such as "why" or "what" or "who". One short comment in the executive thread asks "Which one?"
- So the safer use is to set short comments aside in a separate pile and to keep the short questions for a second look. Deleting the short comments would throw away the invitations and the questions.

## Short comments to keep

The file named [short-comments-to-keep.txt](short-comments-to-keep.txt) lists short comments that stay in the main pile. The list has seven entries so far which are "keep going" and "go on" and "more" and "continue" and each of those three with the word "please" added at the end such as "go on please".

- "go on" joined the list because each of the 4 whole comments with those words asks another person to keep talking.
- Zero of the 49525 rows in the public archive are the whole comment "go on". So keeping "go on" adds no stock reactions back into the main pile of the archive.
- A comment matches when the words left after removing punctuation and emoji are the same as the entry from the first word to the last word. So "go on lmao" and "hi yes go on" do not match.
- Short questions such as "proof?" and "got link?" are not on the list because the step that keeps short questions already catches comments ending in a question mark.
- Phrases such as "tell me more" and "say more" were considered and left off because no counted whole comment in this folder uses those phrases. So there is no evidence here for how people use those phrases.
- "more" and "continue" joined the list on 14 November 2026 because the author of this repository judges that a reply of "more" or a reply of "continue" asks another person to keep expressing which makes each reply pro-communication and pro-expression. Zero whole comments in this folder are the single word "more" or the single word "continue" so the two entries rest on the author's judgment and not on a count. The count of "more" and of "continue" as whole rows in the public archive has not been run yet.
- A comment matches "more" or "continue" only when the single word is the whole comment. So "more of the same" and "no more" and "continue to cope" do not match.
- "go on please" and "more please" and "continue please" joined the list on 14 November 2026 because the author of this repository judges that adding "please" at the end keeps each reply an invitation to keep expressing. These three entries also rest on the author's judgment and not on a count.
- "keep going" joined the list on 14 November 2026 because the author of this repository judges that a reply of "keep going" asks another person to keep expressing. The entry rests on the author's judgment and not on a count.
- A phrase can join the list in two ways. The author of this repository can add a phrase by judgment as with "more" and "continue". Or a phrase joins when a count shows the phrase working as an invitation in every whole comment found. One mocking or dismissive use is enough to leave a phrase off.

## What the check cannot do

- The check cannot catch a long comment that says nothing specific. A list of 10000 hollow phrases of six words or more matched 2 of the 39658 longer rows in the archive word for word. So a long hollow comment passes the length check and passes a phrase list too.
- The check does not save much reading by word count because the short rows hold about 1.5 percent of the words. The saving is in the number of items a reader has to judge which drops by about one fifth in the archive.

## How the check can help with a large pile of comments

1. Count the words in every comment and move the comments of five words or fewer into a separate pile.
2. Keep the short comments that match the file named short-comments-to-keep.txt because those comments invite another person to keep talking.
3. Keep the short comments that begin with a question word or end with a question mark because a short question can open a conversation.
4. Give the main pile of longer comments to a person or a chatbot for closer reading such as looking for comments that describe a behavior a reader can picture.
5. Report the share of short comments as a finding because the share shows whether the crowd mostly reacted or mostly explained.

## How to rerun the counts

The counting program is the file named short-comment-check.py in the social-media-vibes-scripts folder inside the boring-things folder of this repository.

SHORT COMMENTS TO KEEP

An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this list on 13 November 2026 and no other person has rechecked the list.

The five-words-or-fewer check sets short comments aside before reading. A short comment on this list stays in the main pile because the comment asks another person to keep talking. The page named short-comment-check.md in this folder explains the check.

How a comment matches: a program changes the comment to small letters and removes punctuation marks and emoji. The comment matches when the words left over are the same as a line below from the first word to the last word. So "Go on?" matches and "go on lmao" does not match because of the extra word. In the same way "More!" and "Continue." match and "more of the same" and "continue to cope" do not match because of the extra words.

The list has seven entries so far. The phrase "go on" joined because a count showed the phrase reading as an invitation to keep talking in every place the phrase was found as a whole comment. The word "more" and the word "continue" joined on 14 November 2026 because the author of this repository judges that a reply of "more" or a reply of "continue" asks another person to keep expressing which makes each reply pro-communication and pro-expression. No count backs the word "more" or the word "continue" yet because zero whole comments in this folder are the single word "more" or the single word "continue". The three entries ending in the word "please" joined on the same day because the author of this repository judges that adding "please" keeps each reply an invitation to keep expressing. The phrase "keep going" joined on the same day because the author of this repository judges that a reply of "keep going" asks another person to keep expressing.
