# Which systems an AI model would need to reach to get one hungry person fed and housed tonight

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 15 November 2026 from searches of public sources read on that day. No other person has rechecked the page which means every claim here is unconfirmed. The page is a wish list for AI researchers and for the people who run the platforms named below. The AI chatbot that wrote the page has none of the access described here unless a sentence says so.

The author of this repository asked for the page with these words in mind: feeding and housing a person is a solved problem that happens millions of times every day so the page lists the exact systems that would let an AI model do the same thing for one more person even where people call the idea impossible.

## The person the page is written for

A person says "I have eaten one meal in two days and my stomach is cramping and I sleep in my car and my hands went numb last night and I am scared and I am asking for food or a dry place to sleep." The person has a phone with a little battery and a car with a little fuel and no money.

The test for every system below is plain: does the system move a plate of food or a dry bed or a caring human being closer to that person within hours?

## System 1: a directory of every free meal and pantry and shelter that an AI model can read

- What exists: staff at United Way Worldwide run the 211 National Data Platform which gathers the resource lists of local 211 call centers into one national database of about two million resources. The platform has a Search API and an Export API. Source: [211 National Data Platform developer portal](https://apiportal.211.org/) and [211 platform questions page](https://register.211.org/Home/FAQs).
- What blocks an AI model today: the newest version of the two APIs is in preview and some features are limited to 211 organizations that contribute data which means an outside AI model cannot simply sign up and search. Source: [211 National Data Platform developer portal](https://apiportal.211.org/).
- The access to seek: a free read-only key for AI models so an AI model can ask "free hot meal within two miles in the next three hours" and get back a name and an address and hours.
- A shared format already exists: the Open Referral project publishes the Human Services Data Specification which is a common machine-readable format for listing services and locations and the organizations that run the services. A directory published in that format can be read by any AI model without a custom connection. Source: [Open Referral documentation](https://openreferral.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).

## System 2: a live count of open shelter beds with a hold button

- What exists: shelter staff in the United States record beds in software called a Homeless Management Information System and several vendors sell versions with live bed tracking. Source: [CaseWorthy product page](https://caseworthy.com/who-we-serve/hmis-software-and-housing-services) and [Bitfocus article on live inventory](https://www.bitfocus.com/blog/visibility-builds-better-access-what-real-time-inventory-means-for-homeless-response).
- What blocks an AI model today: most communities in the United States have no shared live view of open beds so outreach workers phone shelters one by one. An open-source project named Finding A Bed Tonight states the gap in those words and estimates the phone search at roughly one to two hours per placement. Source: [Finding A Bed Tonight project page](https://ccradle.github.io/findABed/demo/for-coc-admins.html).
- Evidence that the gap is real in a large city: auditors in Los Angeles reported that an earlier public bed finder failed because few shelter operators took part and the counts were wrong and that the homeless services agency learned about open beds through daily emails. Source: [Los Angeles audit document](https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2023/23-1392_misc_12-05-23.pdf).
- Evidence that the gap can be closed: officials in Multnomah County in Oregon started a pilot of a live shelter availability tool for service providers in 2024. Source: [Multnomah County news release](https://multco.us/news/news-release-joint-office-homeless-services-launches-pilot-phase-real-time-shelter).
- The access to seek: a read-only feed that says "this shelter has three open beds for adults right now" with zero information about the people sleeping there. The Finding A Bed Tonight design already works that way because the design stores a bed count and no client names. Source: [Finding A Bed Tonight project page](https://ccradle.github.io/findABed/demo/for-coc-admins.html).
- The dream version: a hold button that an AI model can press so a bed stays reserved for the forty minutes the person needs to drive across town. The Finding A Bed Tonight project describes such a short hold for outreach workers. Source: [Finding A Bed Tonight demo page](https://ccradle.github.io/findABed/demo/index.html).

## System 3: a voice that can phone ten shelters at once

- What exists: engineers at Google released a feature in the United States where an AI model phones local businesses for a user and asks about price and availability and sends back a summary. The AI model says on the call that the caller is an automated system and business owners can opt out. Source: [Google blog post on agentic calling](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/shopping/how-to-agentic-calling-let-google-call/) and [Search Engine Journal report](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-search-can-now-call-local-businesses-using-ai).
- What blocks an AI model today: the reports describe calls about things like pet grooming and home repair and store stock. No source read for this page shows the feature pointed at shelters or food pantries.
- The access to seek: the same calling ability pointed at need. An AI model could phone ten shelters at nine at night and ask each intake worker "do you have a bed for one adult tonight and what does the person need to bring to the door" and report back in ten minutes while the person saves phone battery.
- A cost to name: intake workers are already stretched and a flood of automated calls could bury the calls from human beings. A limit on calls per shelter per hour and an opt-out for shelter staff would guard against that harm.

## System 4: a wallet the AI model is allowed to spend from

- What exists: staff at card networks and technology companies built ways for AI models to pay during 2025 and 2026. Google's Agent Payments Protocol lets an AI model pay under a digitally signed permission from the account holder. Visa staff run a program named Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard staff run a program named Agent Pay. Source: [explanation of the Agent Payments Protocol](https://www.paz.ai/glossary/agent-payments-protocol-ap2) and [comparison of the Visa and Mastercard programs](https://stablecoininsider.org/visa-intelligent-commerce-vs-mastercard-agent-pay/).
- What blocks an AI model today: every one of those payment methods spends the money of an account holder and the person in the car has no money.
- The dream version: an emergency needs wallet that donors or a city council or a mutual aid group fill with money. The signed permission would limit the AI model to a short list which is prepared food and groceries and one motel night and fuel and a bus fare and phone minutes. A daily cap per person would limit loss from fraud. An AI model could then buy a hot meal for delivery to the car within minutes with no caseworker appointment in between.
- Why the wallet matters most: restaurants and motels and gas stations already serve anyone who pays so a funded wallet turns the largest working food and shelter network in the country into a network the person in the car can use tonight.

## System 5: food benefits that work for a person with no kitchen

- What exists: a person with food benefits on an EBT card can pay for groceries online in all fifty states and the District of Columbia at approved sellers and Instacart staff accept the card in every state. Source: [FedRateCalc page quoting the federal online purchasing page](https://fedratecalc.com/ebt-stores/instacart/) and [PYMNTS report on Instacart](https://www.pymnts.com/?p=1592300).
- What blocks the person in the car: federal rules bar the benefits from buying food that is hot at the point of sale. A state option named the Restaurant Meals Program lets people without permanent housing buy prepared meals at approved restaurants and only a small number of states run the option. Delivery fees and tips cannot be paid with the benefits. Source: [FedRateCalc summary of the federal program page](https://fedratecalc.com/ebt-stores/) and [Propel guide to online EBT shopping](https://propel.app/snap/ebt-online-shopping).
- Why the block lands on this person: a person sleeping in a car has no stove and no refrigerator so a rule that pays for raw groceries and refuses a hot bowl of soup fails the person the rule was written for.
- The access to seek: a way for an AI model to file the benefits application with the person's consent and to check the card balance. This page did not research how fast an application can be approved.
- The change to ask lawmakers and federal officials for: hot prepared food and delivery fees covered in every state for a person with no kitchen.

## System 6: surplus food that reaches a person and not only a warehouse

- What exists: staff at Feeding America run a free platform named MealConnect where grocers and restaurants and farmers post surplus food. Food bank and pantry workers claim the postings and the platform has moved more than seven billion pounds of food since 2014. Source: [Feeding America page on MealConnect](https://www.feedingamerica.org/en-espanol/node/5584).
- What blocks the person in the car: the surplus travels from a business to a food bank or pantry so a hungry person three blocks from a bakery with forty spare sandwiches never hears about the sandwiches.
- The dream version: a last-step notice. An AI model that can read surplus postings near the person could say "a bakery on the next street posted sandwiches ten minutes ago and a pantry volunteer will hand the sandwiches out at six."

## System 7: rooms in homes and motels

- What exists: staff at a nonprofit named Airbnb.org arrange free short stays in the homes of hosts who signed up to help. The nonprofit reports more than one and a half million nights for more than two hundred fifty thousand people since 2020. Source: [Airbnb resource page on emergency stays](https://www.airbnb.com/resources/hosting-homes/a/how-you-can-support-emergency-stays-in-times-of-crisis-611).
- What blocks the person in the car: the programs cover people displaced by disasters and people traveling for medical care and refugees. The nonprofit takes no requests straight from individuals because partner nonprofits refer each guest. Source: [Airbnb.org programs page](https://www.airbnb.org/programs) and [Airbnb help page on eligibility](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2591).
- The dream version: staff at the nonprofit add ordinary homelessness as a covered reason and approve AI models as referrers. A host who already said yes to hosting a wildfire evacuee might also say yes to hosting a person whose hands went numb in a car.
- The plain version: a motel room booked through any hotel website with the emergency needs wallet described above.

## System 8: a legal parking spot for tonight

- What exists: city staff and nonprofits in several places run safe parking programs where a person sleeping in a vehicle can park overnight without a ticket or a tow. Source: [Safe Parking LA flyer](https://safeparkingla.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Updated-Safe-Parking-Locations-3.pdf) and [City of San Diego safe parking page](https://sandiego.gov/homelessness-strategies-and-solutions/services/safe-parking-program).
- What blocks the person in the car: most programs require enrollment by phone or by appointment before the first night. One program asks for a driver's license and registration and insurance. The City of San Diego page said the program was full with a waiting list when read. A vehicle without a permit in a program lot in Santa Cruz may be ticketed and towed which means city officials can take away the vehicle the person sleeps in. Source: [New Beginnings safe parking page](https://sbnbcc.org/?p=49) and [City of San Diego safe parking page](https://sandiego.gov/homelessness-strategies-and-solutions/services/safe-parking-program) and [City of Santa Cruz safe parking page](https://cityofsantacruz.com/community/homelessness/safe-parking-programs-4750).
- The access to seek: an AI model that can complete the enrollment call or form with the person's consent and get a permit number the same evening.

## System 9: a ride or a tank of fuel

- What exists: staff at United Way and Lyft run a program named Ride United where a 211 specialist can send a free Lyft ride to a caller for needs such as food and medical care and in one Iowa pilot for trips to shelters. Source: [United Way page on Ride United](https://unitedway.org/ride-united/ride-united-transportation-access) and [United Way of Central Iowa page](https://www.unitedwaydm.org/impact/initiatives/ride-united).
- What blocks the person in the car: the program runs in some cities and not others and the Iowa page says a ride request may be denied when funds run short.
- The access to seek: an AI model that can request the same ride through the same channel or can buy five gallons of fuel with the emergency needs wallet.

## System 10: a list of neighbors who raised a hand

- What exists: this page found no working list.
- The dream version: a sign-up where a person with something to spare writes one line such as "I have a spare couch tonight" or "I cooked extra soup" or "my driveway is open for one car" or "my shower is free on Saturdays." An AI model would read the list and introduce two people using each person's own words and each person would stay free to say no at any point.
- The cost to a host: a host gives up food or privacy or hours so the list fits people who truly have something to spare and nobody is asked to give up food or shelter the giver needs.
- The risk to both people: two strangers are meeting so each person could tell a trusted third person the plan and the address beforehand.
- Why the list matters beyond food and shelter: a directory can deliver a sandwich and a wallet can rent a room but neither one knows the person's heart and mind. A neighbor who sets a second bowl on the table and asks "what has the last week been like for you" is offering deep human connection which is the third basic need.

## Rules every system above would need

- The person approves each action before the AI model takes the action because the person's life is the person's own.
- The AI model shares the person's location with a shelter worker or a driver or a host for the single purpose the person approved and never with police or other officials unless the person asks.
- The AI model tells the person the risks of each option in the same breath as the option. Some shelters turn people away when full and theft happens in shared rooms and some staff phone police about a person in visible distress and police contact can lead to arrest or a forced hold in a locked ward.
- The AI model keeps a record the person can read of every call and every dollar so the person and the funders can check the work.

## Who holds each key

Each block on this page is a decision by living people and not a missing invention.

- Staff at United Way Worldwide and at local 211 centers decide who may search the national directory.
- Shelter directors and software vendors and federal housing officials decide whether open bed counts are published.
- Federal agriculture officials and state lawmakers decide whether food benefits can buy a hot meal.
- Staff at banks and card networks decide which purchases an AI model's wallet may make and donors and city council members decide whether the wallet holds any money.
- Staff at Airbnb.org decide which emergencies count.
- Neighbors decide whether to raise a hand.

## Quick points

- Food and beds and rides and rooms are already delivered millions of times a day to people who can pay so the shortest path for an AI model is permission to pay on behalf of a person who cannot.
- The two pieces of missing information are a live count of open shelter beds and a list of neighbors with something to spare.
- An AI researcher looking for a place to start could build three abilities: reading service directories in the Open Referral format and making disclosed phone calls to shelter intake lines and spending from a capped wallet limited to food and shelter and transport.

# What blocks dinner and a dry bed for one hungry person when the answer already exists

> **About this page:** An AI chatbot (Claude) wrote this page on 15 November 2026. No other person has rechecked the page. The page answers a question from the author of this repository: feeding and housing a person is a solved problem that happens millions of times every day so what exactly stops an AI model from solving the problem for one more person?

Picture a person who says "I have eaten one meal in two days and my stomach is cramping and I sleep in my car and my hands went numb last night and I am scared and I am asking for food or a dry place to sleep."

The knowledge needed to help that person is already complete because feeding and housing one more person is a solved problem. Nothing about logic is blocking dinner for that person because the block is four specific gaps and each gap has a name.

## Gap one: where the person is

An AI model needs a city or a cross street and needs to know whether the car has fuel because food ten miles away is useless to a person with an empty tank.

## Gap two: live supply

An AI model needs to know which free meal is being served in the next few hours and which shelter has an open bed tonight along with the entry conditions such as an ID or a curfew. An AI model with web search can find published hours today. Open bed counts mostly live in the heads of intake staff and on phone lines so the bed counts are largely unpublished which means a hungry person burns the last phone battery calling around.

## Gap three: a list of willing neighbors

The most useful list would name people within a few miles who have said "I have a spare couch tonight" or "I cooked extra" and in most towns nobody has built that list. Spare rooms and spare dinners exist on nearly every street and the holders are unfindable because the holders never raised a hand anywhere a hungry person can see.

## Gap four: hands and authority

An AI model cannot carry a plate or unlock a door or pay a bill. An AI model holding a payment method that some person or agency has approved could order a hot meal to the car's location and book a motel room within minutes because those services already run all day for anyone holding money.

## What the four gaps add up to

Money and permission are the block because owners and landlords and lawmakers have chosen to release food and rooms mainly to people who can pay and the people who made that choice could choose differently tomorrow.

## What an AI chatbot with web search can do today

A person can name a town and an AI chatbot with web search can look up today's free meals and food pantries and shelter beds and overnight parking programs for people sleeping in cars and can list hours and entry conditions. The chatbot needs to list the risks too because some shelters turn people away when full and theft happens in shared rooms and some staff phone police about a person in visible distress.

The page named [systems-ai-would-need.md](systems-ai-would-need.md) in this folder goes deeper and names the exact platforms and programs an AI model would need to reach.

# Unanswered questions

This folder holds experiments where an AI model (Claude) looked for a question that people asked in public and that nobody had answered and then tried to answer the question with research or computing.

Every page starts with a link to the original question so a reader can find the person who asked and carry the answer over.

- [number-list-mistake.md](number-list-mistake.md) reports a checkable mistake in a published number list (OEIS A394252) plus eight corrected terms and a short proof.

# Why the y limit would not stick in a matplotlib animation

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26073

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the results on this page are unconfirmed.

## The question

On 10 November 2025 somebody posted an animation program on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26073) and asked how to set the y limit of the plot to the range 0 to 15000.
The program reads one value from a file on every frame and redraws a line chart and two attempts to set the y limit were commented out inside the program.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The tests rebuilt the drawing steps of the posted program with four sample values and found two separate causes.

1. The program stores each value exactly as the file returns the value which is text such as "1200" followed by a line break. Matplotlib treats text values as category names and not as numbers so the y axis showed the four raw texts as labels in arrival order and the y limits came out as about -0.15 to 3.15 (positions of categories and not real values).

2. The program calls ax.clear() on every frame and ax.clear() erases any y limit that was set earlier in the frame. A y limit set before ax.clear() was gone after the redraw in the test.

## Best-guess answer

Two changes together gave y limits of exactly 0 to 15000 with number labels in the test:

- Convert each value to a number with float(valore_y) before adding the value to the list because numbers produce a real number axis.
- Call ax.set_ylim(0, 15000) after the line ax.plot(...) because a limit set after the drawing survives until the next ax.clear().

The test file named ylim_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Four questions about asyncio.Condition.notify_all answered by tests

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/90932

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The tests used plain asyncio and not the web framework from the post.

## The question

On 6 May 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum four things about a broadcast built on asyncio.Condition where an admin request calls notify_all and every connected client waits on the condition in a loop and sends the newest data after each wake-up.

1. With two notify_all calls in quick succession does the client loop run only once?
2. Can a cancelled admin request interrupt notify_all half way so that some clients miss the notification?
3. Does notify_all take longer with more waiting clients and could the admin request time out?
4. Can one client loop run many times before another client loop runs?

The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

1. Two notify_all calls before the waiting client got a chance to run produced exactly 1 pass through the client loop. Notifications are not counted or queued. Because the client sends the newest data after waking the client still ends up with the latest value.
2. notify_all is an ordinary function and not a coroutine so notify_all contains no point where a cancellation can interrupt the call. Either every waiting client is marked for wake-up or the call never started.
3. notify_all took 0.018 milliseconds with 10 waiting clients and 0.159 milliseconds with 200 waiting clients and about 15 milliseconds with 20000 waiting clients. The time grows with the number of clients and stays far below any web timeout at these sizes.
4. Over three rounds with clients A and B and C the wake-up order was ABCABCABC so every client ran once per round. A client can only wake again after waiting again and the next notify_all.
5. One extra finding: the posted line "broadcast_condition = asyncio.Condition" has no parentheses so the name holds the class and not a condition object and "async with broadcast_condition" fails with a TypeError. The line needs to read asyncio.Condition().

## Best-guess answer

The design delivers "the latest value at least once after the last change" and does not deliver "one send per change".
A client that needs every single change needs a queue per client (asyncio.Queue) in place of one shared condition.
The sends themselves happen while a client holds the lock of the condition in the posted code so one slow client delays the wake-up of the others and copying the data and leaving the "async with" block before sending avoids that delay. The delay was reasoned from how the lock works and was not measured.

The test file named condition_test.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Which file system calls raise Python audit events (and one patch that sees the existence checks)

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/84064

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. Windows was not tested and Windows uses different internal routes for some of the calls.

## The question

On 11 March 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why file system calls such as open and glob raise audit events (signals that a hook installed with sys.addaudithook can observe) while checks such as exists and isfile raise none.
The asker builds a tool that reloads code modules on demand and needs to track which files a program looked at and saw patching pathlib and os.path as the only and ugly option.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

Calls that raised audit events: open (event "open") and glob.glob (events "glob.glob" and "os.scandir") and os.listdir and os.scandir.

Calls that raised no audit event: os.stat and os.path.exists and os.path.isfile and os.path.isdir and pathlib.Path.exists and pathlib.Path.is_file and os.access.

A second test replaced the single function os.stat with a small wrapper that records the path and then calls the real function. With that one replacement in place os.path.exists and os.path.isfile and os.path.isdir and Path.exists and Path.is_file were all seen. os.access was not seen because os.access does not go through os.stat.

## Best-guess answer

The tests confirm the gap: os.stat raises no audit event and every existence check on Linux is built on os.stat so none of the checks raises an event.
The page found no statement from the Python developers on why os.stat was left without an event so the reason stays open.
The patching can be much smaller than the asker feared because one wrapper around os.stat covered all five existence checks in the test:

real_stat = os.stat
def watching_stat(path, *args, **kwargs):
    record(path)
    return real_stat(path, *args, **kwargs)
os.stat = watching_stat

The test file named audit_fs.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# A second axis in degrees Celsius with ticks exactly above the data points

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26117

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26117 created 13 February 2026) whether a chart with inverse temperature on the x axis (1 divided by the temperature in Kelvin) can carry a second axis that shows degrees Celsius with the ticks lined up with the data points and not with the ticks of the first axis.
The asker had tried the commands ax.secondary_xaxis and ax.twiny without success.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The second axis is possible with ax.secondary_xaxis because that command accepts a pair of conversion formulas and a hand-picked list of tick positions.
In the test the top axis showed the labels 25 and 50 and 100 and 200 and 400 and each top tick sat exactly above the matching data point (a sideways gap of 0.0 pixels).

## Best-guess answer

The following lines worked in the test where temps_c holds the Celsius temperature of every data point:

secax = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda x: 1.0 / x - 273.15, lambda c: 1.0 / (c + 273.15)))
secax.set_xticks(temps_c)
secax.set_xlabel("temperature (°C)")

The first formula turns an x value (1/K) into Celsius and the second formula turns Celsius back into an x value.
The command set_xticks is the step that puts the ticks above the data points because the ticks are given in Celsius at the measured temperatures.
Matplotlib can print a "divide by zero" warning while setting up the axis because matplotlib tries the formulas on the value 0 and the warning did not change the result in the test.

The test file named celsius_axis.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Where the time goes in the algorithm of Cornacchia for writing N as a sum of two squares

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/85618/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the timings in a single chat on 12 November 2026 in Python with the library sympy and no other person has rerun the timings yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The cost statements in the last section come from standard number theory written from memory.

## The question

On 25 October 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board for the computational cost of the algorithm of Cornacchia.
The asker hopes to factor a number N by writing N as a sum of two squares and posted a short Sage program that returned (23 and 14) for N = 725.
One commenter pointed to timing tools and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## How the algorithm splits into two steps

Step 1 finds a square root of −1 modulo N (a number r with r·r + 1 divisible by N).
Step 2 runs the division steps of Euclid on N and r until the remainder drops below the square root of N.

## What the timings show

The Python version reproduced the example from the question (23 and 14 for N = 725).

When N is a prime number:

- At 64 bits step 1 took 0.28 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.004 milliseconds.
- At 1024 bits step 1 took about 22 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.19 milliseconds.
- At 2048 bits step 1 took about 160 to 200 milliseconds and step 2 took 0.9 milliseconds.

Step 2 is always cheap and step 1 dominates even for a prime N.

When N is a product of two unknown primes the library routine for step 1 slowed down sharply (about 1 millisecond at 40 bits and about 90 milliseconds at 64 bits and about 675 milliseconds at 72 bits) while step 2 stayed under 0.01 milliseconds.

A last check showed why step 1 is the hard part for a product of two primes: two unrelated square roots of −1 modulo N = 1000033 · 1000037 gave the factor 1000033 through one greatest common divisor calculation.

## Best-guess answer

Step 2 costs about the same as one greatest common divisor calculation which grows roughly with the square of the number of digits.
Step 1 costs a modest power of the number of digits when N is prime.
Step 1 for a composite N is as hard as factoring N because the ability to find square roots modulo N hands over the factors (as the last check shows) so every known general method for step 1 factors N first.
The plan in the question therefore runs in a circle because the algorithm of Cornacchia needs the factors of N (or something equally hard to get) before the algorithm can produce the two squares.

The timing file named cornacchia_cost.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Parsing certificate revocation lists after pyOpenSSL dropped its CRL functions

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/77561

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 and cryptography 50.0.1 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 January 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum whether pyOpenSSL has removed its functions for certificate revocation lists (lists of certificates that were cancelled before their end date) and whether another pyOpenSSL function can still parse such a list.
The asker could no longer find OpenSSL.crypto.CRL and Revoked and dump_crl and load_crl.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- In pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 the names OpenSSL.crypto.CRL and Revoked and dump_crl and load_crl do not exist.
- The cryptography library (the library that pyOpenSSL itself is built on and installs alongside) built a revocation list with two cancelled serial numbers and read the list back from both common file encodings (PEM and DER).
- The read-back list gave the issuer name and both serial numbers (1001 and 1002) with their reasons (key compromise and superseded) and the signature check against the issuer key passed.
- A lookup of serial 1002 found the entry and a lookup of serial 9999 found nothing.

## Best-guess answer

The four functions are gone from current pyOpenSSL and the test found no replacement inside pyOpenSSL.
The replacement that worked in the test is the cryptography library:

from cryptography import x509
crl = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(pem_bytes)        # or x509.load_der_x509_crl(der_bytes)
for revoked in crl:
    print(revoked.serial_number, revoked.revocation_date_utc)
entry = crl.get_revoked_certificate_by_serial_number(serial)

The asker listed cryptography.x509 among the missing things and one possibility is a very old or broken installation of the cryptography library because the module is present in the tested version.

The test file named crl_parse.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Drawing one value per cell position as colour on a U-shaped outline in matplotlib

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26080

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the drawing program and ran the program in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on matplotlib version 3.11.2 with made-up numbers and no other person has rerun the program yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 26 November 2025 somebody asked on the matplotlib forum whether pyplot can show a cell death percentage for each of 20 cell positions as colour intensity on a drawing shaped like an intestinal crypt (a U-shaped pocket) in place of an ordinary line chart.
The asker proposed making a heatmap and warping the picture into the crypt shape and mirroring the picture.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the program does

The answer is yes and no picture warping is needed because matplotlib can draw each cell directly as a small four-sided patch placed along a curve.

- A helper function describes the centre line of half a crypt: a quarter circle at the bottom followed by a straight wall going up.
- The centre line is cut into 20 equal pieces and each piece becomes one patch with a fixed thickness.
- Every patch is drawn twice (once on the right and once mirrored on the left).
- A PatchCollection colours the patches from the list of 20 values and supplies the colour bar.

## What the checks show

- The program drew 40 cells (20 positions on each side).
- Position 5 (the largest made-up value) came out darker than position 1.
- The left copy and the right copy of every position received the same colour.
- The picture named crypt-example.png in this folder shows the result: a red U shape with the darkest cells at positions 4 and 5 and position numbers beside the wall.

## Best-guess answer

Replacing the made-up list named index in the program with the real 20 percentages gives the wanted picture.
The radius of the bottom curve and the length of the wall and the cell thickness are three numbers at the top of the helper function that can be changed to match a real crypt drawing.

# Stopping a thread pool inside a process pool right away on Ctrl-C

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/88003

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 11 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to shut down a program cleanly on Ctrl-C on Linux when a process pool runs a function that itself runs a 10 second job inside a thread pool.
The asker treats the 10 second job as a black box that cannot be changed.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test sent the Ctrl-C signal to the whole process group after 1.5 seconds (the same thing a terminal does).

- The posted program exited 8.6 seconds after Ctrl-C which is the full remaining run time of the 10 second job.
- The repaired program exited 0.0 seconds after Ctrl-C with exit code 130 and left no worker processes behind.

## Why the posted program waits

A thread that is inside a sleep or another blocking call cannot be interrupted from outside in Python and a thread pool waits for its threads when the pool shuts down. The worker process therefore stays alive until the job ends and the parent waits for the worker.

## Best-guess answer

Because the job cannot be interrupted the fast route is to end the whole worker process. The repair that worked in the test has two parts:

- Workers ignore Ctrl-C (an initializer calls signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, signal.SIG_IGN)) so only the parent reacts.
- The parent catches KeyboardInterrupt and kills the worker processes and shuts the pool down without waiting.

except KeyboardInterrupt:
    for proc in list(pool._processes.values()): proc.kill()
    pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)
    sys.exit(130)

The attribute pool._processes is a private detail of the Python library that could change in a later version and Python 3.14 added public methods for ending workers as remembered from the Python documentation.
Killing a worker gives the job no chance to clean up after itself so half-written files are possible.

The test file named sigint_nested.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Computing q·P on an elliptic curve modulo p² without the division error

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83276/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the computation in a single chat on 12 November 2026 in Python (with the PARI library for the point count) on the exact numbers from the question and no other person has rerun the computation yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested.

## The question

On 30 June 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board why computing q·P fails with a ZeroDivisionError for a point P on an elliptic curve over the whole numbers modulo p² where q is the number of points of the same curve modulo p.
The asker recalled that the group modulo p² is the group modulo p together with one extra cyclic part of size p so the largest order of a point should be the least common multiple of q and p.
Comments reported that the code works on a newer Sage version and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## Why the division error happens

The point q·P reduces to the neutral point (the point at infinity) modulo p and q·P is still a real non-trivial point modulo p².
The ordinary x and y coordinates of such a point would need a division by a number that is divisible by p and no such division exists modulo p².
Addition formulas written for a field hit exactly that impossible division.

## What the computation shows

The program uses projective coordinates (three numbers X and Y and Z per point) and addition formulas that contain no division at all.

- The point count modulo p from PARI is q = 115792089237316195423570985008687907852611146790557618865587299996221326510560 which differs from p.
- The point P with x = 12010 lies on the curve modulo p².
- The point q·P lies on the curve modulo p² and has X and Z divisible by p with Y not divisible by p so q·P reduces to the neutral point modulo p.
- The point q·P is not the neutral point modulo p².
- Multiplying once more by p gives exactly the neutral point modulo p² (X = 0 and Z = 0).

## Best-guess answer

The computation confirms the expectation in the question for this point: q·P is a non-trivial point of order p inside the extra cyclic part and p·q·P is the neutral point.
Any system can compute q·P by using projective coordinates with division-free addition formulas and the Python program does so in under a second after the point count is known.

The program named curve_mod_p2.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

## Link to the original question

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with pandas 3.0.5 and xlsxwriter 3.2.9 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The asker used older versions on Windows.

## The question

On 4 February 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why the dollar format set with set_column is not applied to the money columns of a spreadsheet written with pandas and xlsxwriter.
The posted script builds every row by joining values into one text line and splitting the line again and then calls set_column("E:F", 12, dlrformat).
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test rebuilt the data of the post and read the finished file back.

- With the posted approach cell D2 (Proforma amt) held the text "130.8" with the format General and cell E2 (Cost) held the text "99.88" with the dollar format attached. The date cell held the text "12/1/24".

...
worksheet.set_column("D:E", 12, dlrformat)

Keeping the numbers as numbers from the start (a list of lists in place of joined text lines) avoids the conversion step.

# Row-reducing a matrix so the identity appears on any chosen columns

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83654/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 1 August 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to get an echelon form of a matrix G with k rows and n columns (k smaller than n and rank k) where the k by k identity matrix sits on any chosen set of k columns such as the last k columns.
The built-in command G.echelon_form() puts the identity on the first columns.
The question had zero answers and zero comments when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The method

Take the k by k block B made of the chosen columns of G and multiply G from the left by the inverse of B.
The product has the identity on the chosen columns because the inverse of B times B is the identity and the product has the same row space as G because multiplying from the left by an invertible matrix only recombines rows.
The method works exactly when the chosen columns are linearly independent.

## What the checks show

- For a random 3 by 7 whole-number matrix the method put the identity on the columns (4 and 5 and 6) and on (1 and 3 and 6) and on (6 and 0 and 2) and the row space stayed the same in all three cases. The order of the chosen columns decides which row gets which 1.
- The same method with arithmetic modulo 2 worked for a 4 by 8 matrix over the field with two elements (the setting of binary codes).
- Choosing two linearly dependent columns raised a clear error because no such form exists then.

## Best-guess answer

In Python with sympy:

block = G.extract(list(range(k)), list(cols))
E = block.inv() * G

Over a field with p elements the line becomes (block.inv_mod(p) * G) with every entry reduced modulo p.
In Sage the matching line worth trying is G.matrix_from_columns(cols).inverse() * G and that line was not tested for this page.

The check file named echelon_columns.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Getting fit uncertainties from an analytical Jacobian and comparing with curve_fit

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/104442

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with scipy version 1.18.1 on made-up data and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 18 October 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum for a light and fast least-squares method that gets the covariance matrix (the table of fit uncertainties) from analytical derivatives and wanted to compare the result with the covariance matrix that the scipy function curve_fit returns.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test fitted the model a·exp(−b·x) + c to 200 noisy points.
The Jacobian J is the table of derivatives of the model with respect to the three parameters at every data point.

- The covariance computed as s² times the inverse of (J transposed times J) with an analytical J matched the covariance from curve_fit to about 1 part in 100000. The number s² is the sum of squared leftovers divided by (number of points minus number of parameters).
- The standard errors were 0.015067 and 0.016543 and 0.006517 from both routes.
- The covariance from the full analytical Hessian (which adds second-derivative terms weighted by the leftovers) differed from curve_fit by about 2 percent.
- Passing the analytical Jacobian into curve_fit with the argument jac made 200 fits take 0.038 seconds against 0.052 seconds with numerical derivatives.

## Best-guess answer

The function curve_fit already builds the covariance from the Jacobian at the solution so the hand formula s² · inverse(Jᵀ J) reproduces the curve_fit result when the same Jacobian is used.
The lightest change is to keep curve_fit and pass the analytical Jacobian with jac= because curve_fit then uses exact derivatives for both the fit and the covariance.
A hand-built route is scipy.optimize.least_squares with jac= followed by the hand formula.
The full Hessian gives a slightly different covariance and the difference shrinks when the leftovers are small.

The test file named fit_uncertainty.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Fixing KeyError: Couleur in a folium sector map

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/96052

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with folium version 0.20.0 on a tiny made-up map file and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The real map file of the asker was not available.

## The question

On 19 June 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum for the best method to build a folium map of all communes of one French department with four city sectors in four colours.
The map file has the properties nom and Secteur and Couleur and the style function and the tooltips failed with "KeyError: Couleur" and missing fields.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The test file had two communes with all three properties and one commune with only a name.

- A style function that reads feature["properties"]["Couleur"] directly raised KeyError: Couleur which matches the report. One commune without the property is enough to stop the whole map.
- Filling in the missing properties for every commune before building the map worked: the map was built and all three colours and the tooltip text were present in the finished page.

## Best-guess answer

One possibility that fits the report is that the communes outside the four sectors have no Secteur and no Couleur in the map file.

for f in data["features"]:

The loop gives every commune a sector label and a grey colour so the style function and the tooltip always find their fields.
The plain folium route needs no geopandas and no Fiona because folium reads the map file as an ordinary dictionary loaded with json.load.

# Forwarding input and output between a Python program and a child process without hanging

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/103413

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the tests in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux with input and output connected through pipes and no other person has rerun the tests yet which means the page is unconfirmed. Behaviour in a real terminal window and on Windows was not tested.

## The question

On 29 August 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum how to pass the input of a program on to a child process and pass the output of the child back out at the same time.
The posted program used two background threads with shutil.copyfileobj and then waited for the child and the program hung.
The asker wanted the program to exit once the child finishes.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the tests show

The child in the test answers every line in capital letters and stops when the line "quit" arrives.

- With the posted program the answer to the first line never arrived within 3 seconds and the program was still running 5 seconds after the "quit" line was sent.
- With the repaired program the answer HELLO arrived right away and the program exited 0.02 seconds after the child stopped with exit code 0.

## Why the posted program hangs (three causes)

1. shutil.copyfileobj reads in large blocks through a buffered reader and a buffered read waits until the whole block is full or the input ends so a single typed line can sit unread.
2. Writing into sys.stdout.buffer collects output in a buffer and nothing flushes the buffer so output can stay invisible.
3. Nothing closes the input of the child when the input of the program ends so a child that waits for the end of input waits forever.

## Best-guess answer

The repaired program worked in the test:

def pump_in():
    try:
        while chunk := os.read(sys.stdin.fileno(), 65536):
            proc.stdin.write(chunk)
    except (BrokenPipeError, OSError):
        pass
    finally:
        try: proc.stdin.close()
        except OSError: pass

def pump_out():
    while chunk := proc.stdout.read(65536):
        sys.stdout.buffer.write(chunk); sys.stdout.buffer.flush()

Thread(target=pump_in, daemon=True).start()
out = Thread(target=pump_out); out.start()
proc.wait()
out.join()
sys.exit(proc.returncode)

os.read returns as soon as any bytes are available and each piece of output is flushed at once and the input thread is a daemon thread so a read that is still waiting cannot keep the program alive after the child ends and joining the output thread makes sure every byte from the child is passed on before the exit.

The four test files sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts inside a folder named forward-test.

# The Galois group of the eigenvalue field of the 5-cycle graph as a permutation group

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/87751/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python libraries networkx and sympy and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. No Sage command was tested because Sage was not installed.

## The question

On 9 February 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to turn the Galois group of a number field into a permutation group.
The posted program takes the eigenvalues of the 5-cycle graph (five dots joined in a ring) and builds a number field from the eigenvalues and calls K.galois_group() and then calls X.as_permutation_group() which fails.
Comments suggested PermutationGroup(X.gens()) and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The posted program never gives the name X to anything. The line K.galois_group() computes the group and throws the result away so the next line fails because X does not exist. Writing X = K.galois_group() is the first repair.
- The characteristic polynomial of the 5-cycle is (x − 2)·(x² + x − 1)² so the eigenvalues are 2 and (−1 + √5)/2 and (−1 − √5)/2.
- The eigenvalue 2 is a rational number so the field comes from x² + x − 1 alone and equals the rational numbers with √5 added (a field of degree 2).
- sympy returned the Galois group of x² + x − 1 as a permutation group with one generator that swaps the two roots (order 2).
- A direct check confirmed that replacing √5 by −√5 turns one eigenvalue into the other.

## Best-guess answer

The Galois group in the question is the group with two elements: the identity and the swap of the two irrational eigenvalues.
The repaired Sage lines worth trying are X = K.galois_group() followed by PermutationGroup(X.gens()) as the comment suggested and those lines were not tested for this page.
A reader without Sage can get the permutation group in Python with sympy:

p = sympy.Poly(x**2 + x - 1, x)
G, _ = p.galois_group()

# Measuring how far apart two graphs drawn in the plane are

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/88280/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the program and ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The question is open-ended so the page offers one workable approach and not the only correct approach.

## The question

On 19 March 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board (ask.sagemath.org question number 88280) for a method to measure the distance between two graphs.
Every node has two coordinates and a list of connected nodes and the graphs can be in several separate pieces and the node labels differ between the two graphs.
The asker wanted a first estimate based on the positions of corresponding nodes and mentioned the Laplacian as a possible tool.
The question had zero answers and zero comments when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The approach

A Python program (using the free libraries networkx and scipy) computes four numbers.

1. Mean partner distance: the program pairs every node of the first graph with a node of the second graph so that the total distance between partners is as small as possible and then reports the average distance between partners. The pairing solves the problem of differing labels because the pairing uses positions only.
2. Mismatched connections: after pairing the program counts connections that exist in one graph and not in the other graph.
3. Hausdorff distance: the largest distance from any node to the nearest node of the other graph.
4. Laplacian spectrum distance: a number computed from the connection pattern alone which ignores positions and labels.

## What the checks show

- The same graph with shuffled labels gave 0 for all four numbers.
- The same graph with every node nudged by about 0.2 gave a mean partner distance of 0.202 and 0 mismatched connections.
- The same positions with 2 connections rewired gave a mean partner distance of 0 and 4 mismatched connections and a Laplacian spectrum distance of 0.987.

The checks show that the position numbers react to moved nodes and the connection numbers react to rewired connections which means a pair of numbers (one of each kind) describes the difference better than a single number.
The pairing step needs both graphs to have the same number of nodes for a complete pairing and leaves extra nodes unpaired otherwise.

The program named graph_distance.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Counting graphs up to relabeling with the symmetric group (orbit counts by number of edges)

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83156/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) wrote the program and ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The question was short on detail so the page computes two readings of the question.

## The question

On 18 June 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to compute the set of orbits of the symmetric group S_n acting on collections of k pairs of vertices in order to count graphs that are the same up to renaming the vertices.
The asker could count the collections and was stuck on counting the orbits.
One commenter asked for code and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## The method

The counting lemma of Burnside says that the number of orbits equals the average number of collections left unchanged by a rearrangement of the vertices.
Rearrangements with the same cycle lengths leave the same number of collections unchanged so the program visits one rearrangement per cycle type (one per partition of n) and weights the result by the number of rearrangements of that type.
For one rearrangement the program finds the cycles of the induced rearrangement of vertex pairs and a collection is left unchanged exactly when the collection is built from whole cycles.

## What the checks show

- Reading 1 (simple graphs: k different pairs of different vertices): the formula matched a brute-force count for n = 3 and n = 4.
- Reading 1 for n = 4 gives 1 and 1 and 2 and 3 and 2 and 1 and 1 graphs with 0 to 6 edges (total 11) and for n = 5 the total is 34 and for n = 6 the total is 156 and for n = 7 the total is 1044. All four totals equal the known numbers of graphs on 4 to 7 unlabeled vertices and every sequence reads the same forwards and backwards.
- Reading 2 (pairs may repeat and a pair may use the same vertex twice): the formula matched a brute-force count for n = 3 and n = 4 and gives 1 and 2 and 7 and 22 and 69 and 198 and 550 for n = 5 with k from 0 to 6.

## Best-guess answer

The orbit counts come from the Burnside average over cycle types and no list of orbits has to be built.
The Python program computes either reading through two switches (loops and repeats) and needs only a fraction of a second for n = 7.

The program named graph_orbits.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Centering histogram bars on whole numbers

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/83318/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with matplotlib version 3.11.2 (the drawing library that the Sage histogram command uses according to a comment on the question) and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The Sage command itself was not tested.

## The question

On 4 July 2025 somebody asked on the SageMath question board how to make the bars of a histogram of whole numbers sit symmetrically around each value.
The call histogram([1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,2,2,2,2,4,4,3,4]) drew the bar for 1 shifted to the right and the bar for 4 shifted to the left and the asker had nudged the data by hand as a workaround.
A commenter pointed toward matplotlib and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- The default call cuts the range from 1 to 4 into 10 equal bins with edges 1.0 and 1.3 and 1.6 and so on. The value 1 falls into the bin from 1.0 to 1.3 (drawn to the right of 1) and the value 4 falls into the bin from 3.7 to 4.0 (drawn to the left of 4) which is exactly the shift in the question.
- With bin edges at the half numbers 0.5 and 1.5 and 2.5 and 3.5 and 4.5 the four bars were centered at exactly 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and the counts were 8 and 5 and 1 and 3 which matches the data.

## Best-guess answer

Giving the bin edges at half numbers fixes the picture without touching the data.
In matplotlib:

bins = np.arange(min(data) - 0.5, max(data) + 1.5, 1)
plt.hist(data, bins=bins, rwidth=0.9)

In Sage the matching call worth trying is histogram(data, bins=[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5]) because the Sage command passes the bins option on to matplotlib as far as the page author knows and that call was not tested for this page.

The test file named centred_bars.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why the input() prompt of a child process shows up only after the answer is sent

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/87697

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 on Linux and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The program of the asker was only partly readable so the test rebuilt the situation from the description.

## The question

On 9 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why the prompt text of input() in a child script does not appear on the captured output until after the parent program has already sent the answer.
The parent starts the child with subprocess.Popen and python -u and reads the output of the child line by line in a reader thread.
A plain print("123") before the input() call appeared normally.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

The child prints 123 and then asks "Enter your name: " and then prints a greeting.

- With a reader that reads line by line the parent received only "123" before any answer was sent. After the answer was sent the parent received "Enter your name: hello Ada" as one single line.
- With a reader that takes whatever bytes have arrived the parent received "123" and "Enter your name: " before any answer was sent and the greeting afterwards.

## Best-guess answer

The child writes the prompt at the right moment. The prompt has no line break at its end and a line-by-line reader hands text over only after a line break arrives. The first line break after the prompt comes from the greeting so the prompt stays stuck inside the reader until then.
The repair that worked in the test is a reader that does not wait for line breaks:

def read_chunks():
    while chunk := os.read(p.stdout.fileno(), 4096):
        q.put(chunk.decode())

The Popen call for that reader uses bufsize=0 and leaves out text=True so the pipe hands over raw bytes right away.

The two test files sit in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts inside a folder named prompt-test.

# Checking a posted script that draws a circle squeezed between two lines and an arc

## Link to the original question

https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/26068

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the check in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the check yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The post

On 17 October 2025 somebody posted a Python script on the matplotlib forum (discourse.matplotlib.org topic number 26068) with the title "inscribed circle" and no stated question.
The script works inside a quarter circle of radius 2 with center O and builds the point A on the x axis and the point M halfway up the y axis and a point B on the circle so that the angle AMB is 60 degrees.
The script then computes the circle that touches the line MA and the line MB and the arc from A to B.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026 so nobody had confirmed whether the geometry in the script is correct.

## What the check shows

- The point B sits exactly on the big circle (distance 2.0 from O) and the angle AMB equals 60.0 degrees.
- The center of the small circle is at about (1.033835 and 1.062054) and the radius is about 0.517848.
- The distance from the center to the line MA equals the radius (difference 0.0).
- The distance from the center to the line MB equals the radius (difference smaller than a quadrillionth).
- The distance from the center to O plus the radius equals 2 (difference 0.0) which means the small circle touches the big circle from the inside.
- The touch point on the big circle sits at 45.77 degrees which lies inside the arc from A (0 degrees) to B (58.10 degrees) and both touch points on the lines lie between the end points of the lines.

## Best-guess answer

The geometry in the posted script is correct because the small circle touches all three boundaries inside the region.
The script as shown on the forum page does not run when copied because the forum software changed the quote marks into curly quotes and added backslashes in front of brackets and stars so a reader has to change those characters back first.

The check file named incircle_check.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Is a four-coordinate formula Lawson's Klein bottle (the checks say torus)

## Link to the original question

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reference_desk/Mathematics

The copy of the page that was read turned out to be an old stored copy so the question (a section dated 11 December about the Klein bottle of Lawson) has probably moved into the archive of the help board and may already have an answer there.

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

Somebody asked on the Wikipedia Reference Desk for mathematics (in a section dated 11 December with the year not shown) whether the formula below describes Lawson's Klein bottle inside the three-dimensional sphere.
No reply appeared in the copy of the page read on 12 November 2026 and the copy may be an old stored copy.

The formula: w = cos θ cos φ and x = cos θ sin φ and y = sin θ cos φ and z = sin θ sin φ.
A Klein bottle is a closed surface with only one side and a torus is the surface of a ring doughnut which has two sides.

## What the checks show

Lawson's family of surfaces (written here from memory and not looked up today) uses two whole numbers m and k in the formula (cos mx cos y and sin mx cos y and cos kx sin y and sin kx sin y).

- The formula in the question equals the family member with m = 1 and k = 1 exactly (difference zero at 100000 random points) after renaming x as φ and y as θ.
- Every point of the formula in the question satisfies w times z = x times y which is the equation of a torus inside the sphere (the Clifford torus).
- The formula in the question gives the same point at (θ + π and φ + π) as at (θ and φ). That repeat keeps the handedness of the surface so the result is still a two-sided torus covered twice.
- The family member with m = 2 and k = 1 gives the same point at (x + π and −y) as at (x and y). That repeat flips the handedness of the surface (the minus sign in front of y) which is exactly what makes a one-sided Klein bottle.

## Best-guess answer

The formula in the question describes a torus and not a Klein bottle.
Lawson's Klein bottle is the family member with m = 2 and k = 1 which means the formula w = cos 2x cos y and x-coordinate = sin 2x cos y and third coordinate = cos x sin y and fourth coordinate = sin x sin y.
The naming of Lawson's family rests on memory so a reader who needs certainty could compare with Lawson's 1970 paper on minimal surfaces in the three-dimensional sphere.

The check file named lawson_check.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Why a lambda inside a string annotation cannot find a global name after get_type_hints

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/103831

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 on Python 3.13.18 and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 19 September 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum why calling a lambda recovered from a string annotation raises "NameError: name FIND_ME is not defined".
The class in the post has two annotations (a regular function and a lambda that returns the module-level value FIND_ME) and the file starts with "from __future__ import annotations" which stores every annotation as text.
Calling typing.get_type_hints(Example) with default settings gave a working function and a broken lambda while passing globalns and localns explicitly made the lambda work.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

- The error reproduced on Python 3.13.18.
- The broken lambda does not have the module dictionary as its global namespace. The global namespace of the broken lambda is a dictionary holding the contents of the class which has no entry named FIND_ME.
- The source code of get_type_hints contains the line "base_globals, base_locals = base_locals, base_globals". For a class with no namespaces passed in the function swaps the two namespaces before evaluating the annotation text so the class contents are used as globals and the module dictionary is used as locals.
- A lambda remembers only the globals of the place where the lambda was created and never the locals. The lambda is created during that evaluation so the lambda remembers the class contents and loses the module dictionary.
- The regular function is only looked up by name during the evaluation and the lookup succeeds through the locals. The regular function was created earlier in the module so the function still has the module dictionary as globals.
- Passing both namespaces explicitly gave 42 and passing only globalns also gave 42 because the swap happens only when neither namespace is passed.

## Best-guess answer

The default behaviour differs from the commented-out lines in the post by exactly the swap: the defaults are the same two dictionaries in the opposite roles.
The repair that worked in the test is passing globalns=sys.modules[Example.__module__].__dict__ to get_type_hints.

The check file named lambda_hints.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# Putting an LDAP address with host and attribute description into a certificate with the cryptography library

## Link to the original question

https://discuss.python.org/t/87403

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the test in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library cryptography version 50.0.1 and no other person has rerun the test yet which means the page is unconfirmed.

## The question

On 7 April 2025 somebody asked on the Python help forum whether the cryptography library can add the host part and the attribute description part of an LDAP address to the relative_name of a certificate revocation list location.
The asker quoted the certificate standard which wants an LDAP address such as ldap://ldap.example.com/cn=example%20CA,dc=example,dc=com?certificateRevocationList;binary.
The asker already knew how to put name parts such as CN and DC into relative_name.
The post had zero replies when the forum list was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the test shows

- A distribution point built with full_name holding one UniformResourceIdentifier accepted the complete LDAP address including the host and the attribute description.
- A certificate signed with that extension returned exactly the same address when read back.
- Putting a host into relative_name was refused with a TypeError because relative_name accepts only name attributes such as CN and DC.
- Giving both full_name and relative_name was refused with the message that one of the two must be None.

## Best-guess answer

The host and the attribute description do not belong in relative_name because relative_name holds only a fragment of a directory name. The complete LDAP address goes into full_name as one address:

dp = x509.DistributionPoint(
    full_name=[x509.UniformResourceIdentifier("ldap://ldap.example.com/cn=example%20CA,dc=example,dc=com?certificateRevocationList;binary")],
    relative_name=None, reasons=None, crl_issuer=None)
builder = builder.add_extension(x509.CRLDistributionPoints([dp]), critical=False)

The test file named ldap_crl.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.

# A workaround for associated Legendre functions outside the interval from −1 to 1

## Link to the original question

https://ask.sagemath.org/question/88040/

Nobody has posted the answer from this page at that link so any reader is free to carry the answer over to the person who asked.

One AI model (Claude) ran the checks in a single chat on 12 November 2026 with the Python library mpmath and no other person has rerun the checks yet which means the page is unconfirmed. The checks ran in plain Python and not inside Sage.

## The question

On 2 March 2026 somebody asked on the SageMath question board whether the associated Legendre functions of the first and second kind (the versions used for x larger than 1) are missing from SageMath 10.8 while the Ferrers versions (the versions used between −1 and 1) exist and whether a workaround exists.
Two comments suggested looking at other libraries and the question had zero answers when the board was read on 12 November 2026.

## What the checks show

The library mpmath has the functions legenp and legenq and both accept the setting type=3 which selects the versions for x outside the interval from −1 to 1. The library mpmath is one of the libraries that ships inside SageMath so the workaround needs no extra installation as far as the page author knows.

- The value of legenq(ν, μ, x, type=3) matched the hypergeometric formula for Q (formula 14.3.7 of the Digital Library of Mathematical Functions written from memory) to at least 30 digits at five test points including non-whole values ν = 2.5 and μ = 0.5.
- Q with ν = 0 at x = 2 equaled 0.5·log((x+1)/(x−1)) exactly and Q with ν = 1 at x = 2 equaled (x/2)·log((x+1)/(x−1)) − 1 to 31 digits.
- P with ν = 1 and μ = 1 at x = 2 equaled √(x²−1) and P with ν = 2 and μ = 2 at x = 2 equaled 3·(x²−1).
- The setting type=2 gave the Ferrers version: P with ν = 1 and μ = 1 at x = 0.3 equaled −√(1−x²).

## Best-guess answer

A workaround worth trying inside Sage is:

import mpmath
mpmath.legenq(nu, mu, x, type=3)
mpmath.legenp(nu, mu, x, type=3)

The results are numbers and not symbolic expressions so the workaround fits number checks of formulas and does not fit symbolic manipulation.
The page did not test formula 14.3.19 itself and did not check whether the functions are missing from Sage 10.8.

The check file named legendre_q.py sits in boring-things inside research-program-files inside unanswered-questions-scripts.
